bullets: The new “Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep?” release separates task length from task structure. Instead of counting how many turns a large language model (LLM) happens to take, it measures work as required operations and depth as the steps that must occur sequentially because each depends on the previous step’s output. The authors report that turn count largely reflects model habits and that model-assigned difficulty labels barely track pass rates. [E004] Why it matters: If you are choosing or constructing a suite for long-running agents, this design distinguishes genuinely sequential work from tasks made long by inefficient behavior. That can change which tasks qualify as long-horizon and prevent model-specific interaction style from being mistaken for task difficulty. [E004] Evidence: E004. High confidence.

The new THReD benchmark evaluates an agent that converts electronic health record extracts into analysis-ready datasets, alongside the preprocessing tools it invokes. Its 141 tasks cover goal-level requests, failure recovery, requests requiring no action, schema variation, and prompt injection—malicious instructions embedded inside the input data. Proposed processing steps run only after user confirmation. [E001] Why it matters: If you are evaluating clinical-data agents, THReD supports a decision beyond whether the final table looks correct: it tests whether the agent abstains, recovers, handles changing table structures, resists hostile data, and keeps a person in control before execution. Those dimensions better match deployment risks than ordinary transformation accuracy alone. [E001] Evidence: E001. High confidence.

The new MemHarmBench evaluates prompt injection that survives through an agent’s persistent memory and affects later, otherwise normal tasks after the original malicious content is gone. It organizes outcomes around potential victims, including users and workspaces, rather than reporting only whether an injected instruction succeeded. [E016] Why it matters: If you are selecting a safety evaluation for agents that remember preferences or rules across sessions, this benchmark tests delayed downstream harm rather than only immediate attack compliance. That changes the test boundary from one conversation to the full memory lifecycle and can reveal failures that a single-session red-team suite misses. [E016] Evidence: E016. High confidence.

The new Switch-SWE benchmark tests whether coding agents can resume an unfinished repository task after working on other unfinished tasks. It keeps a persistent checkout for each task, so the evaluation measures recovery of prior requirements and partial progress rather than another isolated issue-to-patch episode. [E013] Why it matters: If you are choosing a coding-agent benchmark for multi-ticket development workflows, this release adds interruption recovery as a distinct capability. A system that performs well on independent issues may still lose context or mishandle partial work when tasks are interleaved, which affects whether benchmark results transfer to everyday engineering sessions. [E013] Evidence: E013. High confidence.

The new WorkRB skill-extraction evaluation replaces the usual rule that every unannotated skill is fully wrong. It assigns each candidate a relevance grade from zero to four using four binary questions, then scores the ranked output against those grades. This addresses a setting with 13,939 possible skills, where sparse positive annotations can hide reasonable alternatives or nonsensical predictions. [E024] Why it matters: If you are designing retrieval or classification leaderboards with incomplete labels, this method offers a concrete alternative to exact-match scoring. It can change model rankings by rewarding semantically relevant alternatives while still distinguishing degrees of error, rather than treating all unannotated outputs identically. [E024] Evidence: E024. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的“Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep?”将任务长度与任务结构区分开来。它不再统计大语言模型（LLM）实际用了多少轮，而是以所需操作衡量工作量，并以必须按顺序执行的步骤衡量深度，因为每一步都依赖前一步的输出。作者报告称，轮次数主要反映模型习惯，而模型自行判定的难度标签与通过率几乎不相关。[E004] Why it matters: 如果你正在为长时间运行的智能体选择或构建评测套件，这种设计可以区分真正的顺序性工作与因低效行为而变长的任务。这可能改变哪些任务符合长时程任务的标准，并避免将特定模型的交互风格误认为任务难度。[E004] Evidence: E004. High confidence.

新推出的THReD基准评估一种将电子健康记录摘录转换为可直接用于分析的数据集的智能体，同时也评估它调用的预处理工具。其141项任务涵盖目标层级的请求、故障恢复、无需采取行动的请求、模式变化，以及提示注入——即嵌入输入数据中的恶意指令。拟议的处理步骤只有在用户确认后才会运行。[E001] Why it matters: 如果你正在评估临床数据智能体，THReD支持做出不止关乎最终表格看起来是否正确的判断：它会测试智能体是否能够拒绝执行、从故障中恢复、处理不断变化的表结构、抵御恶意数据，并在执行前确保由人掌控。与仅评估普通转换准确率相比，这些维度更符合部署风险。[E001] Evidence: E001. High confidence.

新推出的MemHarmBench评估一种能够存留于智能体持久记忆中的提示注入：在最初的恶意内容消失后，它仍会影响后续原本正常的任务。该基准围绕潜在受害者（包括用户和工作区）组织评估结果，而不是只报告注入指令是否成功执行。[E016] Why it matters: 如果你正在为能够跨会话记住偏好或规则的智能体选择安全评估，这一基准测试的是延迟发生的下游危害，而不只是对即时攻击的服从。这将测试边界从一次对话扩展至完整的记忆生命周期，并可能揭示单会话红队测试套件遗漏的故障。[E016] Evidence: E016. High confidence.

新推出的Switch-SWE基准测试编码智能体在处理其他未完成任务后，能否继续执行某个未完成的代码库任务。它为每项任务保留持久化的检出工作区，因此评估衡量的是对先前需求和部分进展的恢复能力，而不是又一次彼此孤立的“问题到补丁”流程。[E013] Why it matters: 如果你正在为多工单开发工作流选择编码智能体基准，这一发布将中断恢复作为一项独立能力纳入评估。在独立问题上表现良好的系统，仍可能在任务交错时丢失上下文或不当处理部分完成的工作，这会影响基准结果能否迁移到日常工程工作中。[E013] Evidence: E013. High confidence.

新的WorkRB技能提取评估不再沿用“所有未标注技能都完全错误”这一常见规则。它使用四个二元问题，为每个候选项分配从零到四的相关性等级，然后依据这些等级对排序后的输出进行评分。这解决了一个包含13,939种可能技能的场景中的问题：稀疏的正向标注可能掩盖合理的替代项或荒谬的预测。[E024] Why it matters: 如果你正在设计标签不完整的检索或分类排行榜，这种方法为精确匹配评分提供了一种具体替代方案。它会奖励语义相关的替代项，同时仍区分错误程度，而不是对所有未标注输出一视同仁，因此可能改变模型排名。[E024] Evidence: E024. High confidence.

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents are increasingly built into data-analysis software, yet little evidence shows how reliably they preprocess clinical data or whether the tools they invoke give correct, reproducible output. We report a benchmark of THReD, a web-based system that turns electronic health record (EHR) extracts into AI-ready datasets through a chat agent whose proposed steps run only after user confirmation. The agent benchmark has 141 tasks (100 templates) in seven categories, including goal-level requests, failure recovery, requests calling for no action, schema variation and prompt injection through the data, on synthetic tables calibrated to a regional health information exchange; success is judged by checks on the produced data. Over 2,550 episodes with Claude Haiku 5.5 in four context configurations, the deployed agent completed 92.7% (95% CI 88.1-96.4) of tasks on its first answer, abstained on every advice request, recovered from every injected fault, and never proposed an action requested by planted text. Without the data profile, completion fell to 58.0%; goal-level requests were hardest (80.6%). Six experiments on real records of two chronic-disease cohorts and on synthetic data at scale validate the tools: 91-92% of inferred patient classes and 99.7-99.8% of inferred vital-sign labels were correct in masked reconstruction; a dictionary builder combining curated dictionaries with LLM suggestions mapped 99.0% of 2,208 raw variants correctly; all 2,176 replays of 128 saved pipelines gave byte-identical files under pinned dependencies; subgroup differences in inference accuracy vanished within facility and lookup key; and the same-day consolidation rule changed 90-day emergency revisit rates by up to 3.2 points without shifting cohort composition by more than one point. Processing time grew roughly linearly to 5.5 million records while the prompt stayed at about 13 thousand tokens.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark of THReD: Evaluating an LLM Agent and Its Preprocessing Tools for Turning Electronic Health Records into AI-Ready Datasets

evidence_items.summary: As agents increasingly undertake data querying, Text-to-SQL serves as a foundational capability for database access. However, for text-to-SQL in time-series databases, high-quality benchmarks and large-scale training corpora remain scarce, limiting the systematic evaluation and domain adaptation of existing models and agents. Existing automated SQL generation approaches lack sufficient autonomy, leaving key challenges unresolved. First, numerous combinations of temporal syntax and functions complicate comprehensive coverage of valid queries. Second, as the corpus grows, generating valuable and diverse new data becomes increasingly challenging. Third, schema and data heterogeneity hinder reuse of temporal query structures, limiting generation efficiency. To address these challenges, we propose TSSDA, a Time-Series SQL (TSSQL) Generation Data Agent framework, and construct TERN, a comprehensive Time-sERies text-to-SQL beNchmark. First, to achieve broad coverage of valid queries, we systematically model TSSQL syntax and semantics to construct a data generation space. Next, to explore the space and improve diversity, we develop a Data Agent that autonomously orchestrates data generation. The agent comprises a planning and decision-making module and a query generation module, with online adaptation for continuous self-improvement. Finally, we introduce a temporal-aware memory that enables adaptive reuse of experience across heterogeneous data instances, improving generation efficiency. Comprehensive evaluations on TERN reveal the limitations of existing methods in performing Text-to-TSSQL tasks. Furthermore, extensive experiments demonstrate that TSSDA substantially improves coverage, diversity, and complexity.
evidence_items.title: TSSDA: An Autonomous Agent for Constructing a Time-Series Text-to-SQL Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Description We present the Corinth Rift Laboratory Benchmark Dataset (CRLBD), a collection of waveforms and associated phase arrival times from the Western Gulf of Corinth (WGoC), Greece, the area monitored by the Corinth Rift Laboratory (CRL) Near-Fault Observatory (NFO). A plethora of seismic instruments are installed in WGoC by multiple institutes, to record the high seismic activity, characterized by swarms. CRLBD comprises 224,573 three-component records from 13,918 local earthquakes and 67,371 noise recordings, between June 2018 and December 2024. The dataset has a dominant local character, with over 99% of the traces having been recorded in hypocentral distances less or equal to 100 km. CRLBD has been created primarily focused on Deep-Learning (DL) phase pickers and is fully compatible with the SeisBench toolbox. The dataset includes 13,918 earthquakes located within the boundaries of the CRL-NFO area in WGoC 224,573 3-channel waveforms, from broadband and short-period seismometers, as well as accelerometers 121 (for events) and 46 (for noise) metadata fields 8 networks (CL, HA, HP, HL, HT, HI, HC, 1Y) 128 stations 224,573 P and 127,629 S manually picked phase arrivals The seismic catalogue was located using picked phase arrivals from the Geodynamic Institute of the National Observatory of Athens (GI-NOA) and the Seismological Laboratory of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens (SL-NKUA). The dataset was created in the context of the TRANSFORM² project. Files The following files comprise the full dataset: crlbd.tar.gz: Compressed archive that contains the event waveforms in HDF5 format (waveforms.hdf5) and their metadata (metadata.csv) according to the structure expected by SeisBench. crlbdnoise.tar.gz: Compressed archive that contains the noise waveforms, structured similarly to the events subset.
evidence_items.title: CRLBD - The Corinth Rift Laboratory Benchmark Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Dexterous robotic manipulation remains a major challenge in robotics, exemplified by piano playing, which requires coordinated control of fingers and provides a demanding testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). Although previous work established a benchmark for robotic piano playing, it is restricted to two hands and does not support unified evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce OmniPiano, a benchmark that provides one to up to five Shadow Hands and supports standard, robust, safe, and multi-agent RL within a shared piano-playing task family. OmniPiano is developed for scalable and diverse piano-playing tasks with configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation settings. Particularly, to facilitate usability and extendability, OmniPiano adopts a highly modular design and provides comprehensive tasks to support RL study of task performance, robustness, safety, and cooperation in dexterous control. With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, OmniPiano further incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation scope and reveal new insights. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings, highlighting substantial room for improvement in dexterous control. The code, dataset, tutorial, and demo are available at https://sail-research-lab.github.io/omnipiano/.
evidence_items.title: OmniPiano: Diverse Dexterous Piano-Playing Challenges for Standard, Robust, Safe, and Multi-Agent RL

evidence_items.summary: Instruction tuning for multi-task network traffic analysis requires data with clearly defined sources, supervision targets, and evaluation conditions. We introduce TrafficInstruct, a newly collected dataset comprising raw packet captures and 55,000 structured supervised fine-tuning records across ten tasks: malware traffic detection, botnet detection, malicious DNS-over-HTTPS detection, Web attack detection, advanced persistent threat detection, encrypted VPN detection, Tor behavior detection, encrypted application/service classification, website fingerprinting, and application classification under concept drift. An automated workflow captures traffic from controlled software executions, attack experiments, and application activities. Labels are supported by task-specific collection evidence, including process or socket attribution, activity records, and execution outcomes. Filtering, sanitization, and task-specific transformations produce instructions, traffic observations, and structured answers. We verify sample sources and partition the dataset by complete collection sessions, keeping all samples from the same session within one partition. The benchmark defines allowed inputs, deterministic label mappings, fixed training/validation/test partitions, and task-wise scoring rules. We evaluate majority-class, random-forest, and ET-BERT baselines, an unadapted 27B language model, and independently trained task-specific LoRA adapters on a shared frozen base. Adapters are selected using validation data and evaluated on the corresponding test sets. Task-specific adaptation improves classification performance, supporting instruction tuning across diverse traffic-analysis tasks.
evidence_items.title: TrafficInstruct: A Multi-Task Network Traffic Dataset and Benchmark for Instruction Tuning

evidence_items.summary: Robust driver-state modelling requires synchronized physiological, behavioural, and contextual signals, yet existing open resources typically target a single cognitive state, omit continuous vehicle context, or do not define evaluation protocols that expose inter-subject heterogeneity. We present Multimental-IAS, a multimodal driver mental-state dataset collected in a cockpit-in-the-loop simulation built on CARLA. It contains vehicle telemetry with scenario-context channels, four-channel EEG and three-channel PPG from a Muse 2 headband, and cabin-facing video from 23 participants, recorded in 148 trials (11.6 hours) under six induced states: Normal, Distracted, Alerted, Stressed, Relaxed, and Drowsy. We document the acquisition pipeline in detail and provide a benchmark with one protocol for all models: chronological within-subject splits, participant-disjoint cross-subject folds, validation-based model selection, and ablations over modalities, scenario-context channels, and signal normalization. Multimodal fusion reaches a macro-F1 of 0.94 for drivers seen during training. For unseen drivers, fusing driving dynamics with per-window normalized EEG/PPG raises macro-F1 from 0.408 (telemetry alone) to 0.485, consistently across all five folds, while the gap between the two protocols quantifies the inter-driver heterogeneity that personalized models must address. Multimental-IAS thus provides a concrete testbed for non-IID generalization, personalization, and federated learning in driver monitoring.
evidence_items.title: MultiMental-IAS: A Multimodal Driver Mental State Analysis Dataset for Context-Aware Non-IID Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.
evidence_items.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?

evidence_items.summary: CIM-QA is a comprehensive, YAML-based evaluation benchmark designed to assess the performance of the CIMon agent in navigating and querying Common Information Model (CIM) ontologies. The dataset evaluates the agent's ability to translate natural language questions into complex graph traversals and time-series data retrievals. It is structured around distinct graph patterns, or templates, which range in structural complexity from 0 to 4 "hops" (property traversals). These templates require the resolution of various entity identifiers (e.g., name, rdfs:label, mRID, significantMrid, EIC code) as well as the application of literal constraints and filters (e.g., rated voltage, start dates). Dataset Composition: The dataset comprises two main components spanning varying levels of complexity: Knowledge Graph (KG) Dataset: 2,508 templates and 5,204 unique parameterised questions requiring 0 to 4 hops across the CIM knowledge graph. Time-Series Dataset: 6 templates and 60 questions that evaluate the agent's ability to fuse CIM model data with dynamic time-series observations retrieved from the Cognite Data Fusion platform. Technical Structure: Each YAML entry in the dataset operates as a structured evaluation template encompassing: Natural Language Questions: Up to five varied question formulations per structural pattern. Parameters & Filters: Defined graph paths, CIM types, and literal constraints required to successfully construct the query. Parameterised SPARQL Templates & Bindings: The underlying SPARQL query patterns and specific IRI mappings for each question. Expected Agent Trajectories: Ordered groups of reference steps (e.g., iri discovery, sparql query, Retrieve Time Series, Retrieve Datapoints) that define the expected tool calls and input arguments. This includes expected SPARQL result sets for deterministic accuracy evaluation of the CIMon agent. Dependencies & Base Models: This repository provides the evaluation dataset only.
evidence_items.title: CIM-QA: A Benchmark Question-Answering Dataset for Agent Evaluation over the CIM Ontology and Time-Series Data

evidence_items.summary: "The RS-SynAgent Benchmark Dataset is an expert-defined benchmark designed to evaluate the planning and execution capabilities of large language model (LLM)-based agents in complex remote sensing workflows. The dataset comprises 755 benchmark tasks, including 455 single-tool tasks and 300 multi-tool tasks. It integrates structured task descriptions, remote sensing input data, expert-defined reference workflows, parameter configurations, and associated reference data to support systematic evaluation of tool selection, parameter configuration, multi-step workflow planning, and execution reliability.The dataset is organized into task-level benchmark information, remote sensing input resources, and reference data. The input resources include geospatial raster imagery in GeoTIFF format, organized into multiple batches, while the reference data provide supporting information for task execution and evaluation. The dataset does not include precomputed processing-result files; instead, users can generate processing outputs by executing the corresponding remote sensing workflows.Associated with the RS-SynAgent framework, this benchmark provides a structured resource for evaluating knowledge-constrained tool use and collaborative multi-tool execution. It aims to facilitate reproducible experiments, comparative evaluation, and further research on reliable intelligent agents for remote sensing and Earth observation applications."
evidence_items.title: "RS-SynAgent Benchmark Dataset"

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that act in the open world need two abilities: world knowledge to interpret what they see, and exploration to find what they cannot yet see. We study how agents combine the two through interactive visual geolocation. GeoGuesser Bench contains 282 tasks in an offline Street View environment where agents rotate, zoom, and move between real panoramas. Its three task types shift the balance from knowledge to exploration: agents (1) report the coordinates of their starting location, (2) name the enclosing street, city, state, or country, or (3) find, read, and count nearby objects. The coordinate tasks in (1) also include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds, whose expert guesses provide a human reference. We evaluate 23 VLMs: the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding, and the best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. Beyond these headline numbers, world knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models: agents that localize well do not necessarily explore well. To understand where agents fail, we categorize their errors into vision, navigation, and tool-use failures. Further ablations show that the strongest agents, such as Claude Opus 4.8, still perform well with limited views, while weaker agents degrade; customizing the environment thus adjusts task difficulty. The environment's verifiable rewards and restorable state also support training, and our Planner-Worker-Compressor harness cuts planner tokens by 57-61% by compacting the interaction history. We hope GeoGuesser Bench and its environment serve as a high-quality foundation for simulating real-world exploration at scale.
evidence_items.title: GeoGuesser Bench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Agents on Interactive Geolocation

evidence_items.summary: Software development sessions often involve several unfinished tasks rather than one issue carried through to completion. As coding agents take on repository-level development, they need to recover an earlier task's requirements and partial progress after intervening work. Existing repository-level benchmarks typically score one issue-to-patch episode and do not directly measure whether an agent can resume a task after advancing other unfinished work in the same repository. We introduce \textbf{\ourmethod}, a benchmark for focus-task resumption in sessions that interleave unfinished tasks drawn from the same source repository, with a persistent checkout for each task. Each focus task is evaluated in matched uninterrupted and switched sessions with identical focus requirements and executable verifiers. The switched session interleaves ordered stages from other unfinished tasks in the same repository, while only the final focus patch is scored. \ourmethod~contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, reconstructed from issue, pull-request, and review histories and rendered as 400 matched session specifications. Across 7 coding agents, interleaved unfinished work produces an average focus-task resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points, ranging from 6.0 to 15.0 percentage points. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state as recurrent resumption behaviors. We introduce a plug-in context-management module that selects task-relevant history and maintains concise task-state summaries. On OpenCode, the module improves focus-task completion under same-repository task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points across the evaluated models. Code is available at github.com/Miraclecsc/Switch-SWE.
evidence_items.title: Switch-SWE: Do Coding Agents Hold Focus When Switching Between Unfinished Tasks?

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents can now rewrite repository-scale codebases while preserving tested behavior, creating a new challenge for plagiarism detection, license auditing, and software provenance. We ask whether such rewrites can still be traced to their source. Existing clone benchmarks emphasize fragments and bounded edits, while repository-transformation benchmarks evaluate functional correctness rather than provenance. Moreover, ranking the most similar source does not establish derivation when independent implementations can be similarly close. We define repository-level agentic code laundering and introduce Launder-Bench, to our knowledge the first repository-level benchmark for provenance under agentic rewriting, constructed from 282 real-world repositories. A source-hidden reconstruction protocol decomposes source behavior, reconstructs modules and repository structure, and retains rewrites only after execution-based verification. We evaluate the same provenance problem in two complementary settings: Launder-Bench-Pair contains 1,128 pairwise instances asking whether two repositories share provenance, while Launder-Bench-Attr contains 229 source-attribution instances asking which candidate is the source, with abstention when evidence is insufficient. Measured same-domain independent repositories establish how much similarity can arise without shared provenance and provide detector-specific reference bands. Existing methods remain far from saturating Launder-Bench: the strongest static method reaches only 0.66 AUROC on pairwise detection, while repository encoders rank the true source first on up to 22% of attribution queries but earn calibrated attribution credit on only 1-2%. These results reveal a systematic gap between relative code similarity and source-specific provenance evidence, providing a reproducible target for provenance detection under agentic rewriting.
evidence_items.title: Launder-Bench: Can Repository-Level Agentic Code Laundering Be Detected?

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.
evidence_items.title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks

evidence_items.summary: AI agents often rely on persistent memory to retain user preferences and operational rules across sessions. However, this capability introduces a new safety risk: malicious instructions from messages, documents, or Web content can be retained in memory and influence future tasks even after the original attack content is removed. Existing attack success metrics, however, fail to capture who is affected and how attacks translate into downstream harm during otherwise normal task execution. We introduce MemHarmBench, a victim-centric benchmark for evaluating cross-session prompt injection in memory-persistent AI agents. MemHarmBench considers three categories of potential victims: users, workspace/project owners, and external stakeholders. Our evaluation first exposes an agent to malicious instructions and tests whether they are retained in memory. We then remove the attack content and initiate a new session with a legitimate task while preserving the agent's memory. We jointly evaluate whether the agent follows the attacker's intent, completes the legitimate task, and exhibits observable execution anomalies. Across multiple agent systems, we find that cross-session attacks can remain behaviorally stealthy: agents often complete tasks normally and exhibit no detectable anomalies while still making critical decisions aligned with the attacker's intent. By connecting malicious memory retention to downstream decisions and affected parties, MemHarmBench provides a systematic framework for exposing safety risks that conventional attack- and task-success metrics may overlook. We publicly release MemHarmBench at https://github.com/Kirito14IT/MemHarmBench.
evidence_items.title: MemHarmBench: Evaluating Cross-Session Prompt Injection in Memory-Persistent AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: As coding agents achieve increasingly high success rates on software engineering benchmarks, recent efforts have sought to increase task complexity through longer horizons and more extensive code modifications. However, real-world software development often spans multiple interdependent repositories, introducing additional challenges in dependency reasoning, change propagation, and interface consistency. Rather than further increasing complexity within individual repositories, we introduce CrossSWE, a benchmark for cross-repository joint development comprising 171 real-world instances spanning 165 repositories, 20 technical domains, and 13 programming languages. CrossSWE verifies the necessity of coordinated changes by testing whether partial repository modifications are insufficient to achieve the intended behavior. Our evaluation of five LLMs reveals substantial challenges, with the strongest model, GPT-6.1 Sol, achieving only 58.48% Pass@1. Furthermore, cross-repository inconsistencies emerge as the most prevalent failure mode (44.2%), highlighting the difficulty of maintaining consistency across interdependent repositories.
evidence_items.title: CrossSWE: Benchmarking Cross-Repository Joint Development for Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains a synthetic healthcare population generated using Synthea and transformed into the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM). The dataset is intended for research and educational use in studying the impact of data quality degradation on downstream clinical and epidemiological analyses. The database contains synthetic patient-level healthcare data represented using the OMOP CDM, including demographic information, conditions, medications, measurements, observations, procedures, and healthcare visits. No real patient data are included. The dataset serves as the canonical, non-degraded reference dataset for a series of controlled data degradation experiments. These experiments introduce targeted or systematic alterations to the data, such as missingness and misclassification, and evaluate how these alterations affect downstream summary statistics, prevalence estimates, associations, and other analytical results. Further versions of this dataset will include controlled data degradation along with the scripts used.
evidence_items.title: Synthetic OMOP Healthcare Dataset for Data Quality and Degradation Experiments

evidence_items.summary: As consumer smartphone recommerce scales, buyers must quote binding repurchase prices from seller-uploaded multi-view photos and diagnostic screenshots before devices reach the warehouse. Accurate remote valuation requires fusing noisy cosmetic evidence with identity, battery, lock, and channel risk from screenshots and staff forms, since an error in any modality changes both grade and payout. However, existing multimodal resources mainly target general VLM competence, screen reading, or factory defect detection, and largely overlook staff-aligned trade-in fields, dual appearance/staff ground truth, and executable valuation scorecards. This gap stems from two challenges: (1) the lack of large-scale real trade-in data with audited dual annotations and a compact ranking benchmark kept separate from training labels, and (2) the need to jointly reason over unordered multi-view cosmetics and diagnostic screens under operational deduction rules. To address these challenges, we propose PhoneValue-Bench, a dual-GT evaluation suite with tier-gated scorecards, together with PhoneValue-Corpus, a matched weakly labeled training set of over twenty thousand orders and hundreds of thousands of captioned images. We further present ValueAgent, a staged perception-fusion-valuation reference pipeline aligned with production inspection, plus an executable public scorer and submission schema. Experiments show that ValueAgent reaches a measured 84.1/100 on Bench-Full, with 97.0 appearance fill and 54.1 staff-field fill, establishing a practical dual-GT benchmark for multimodal recommerce valuation.
evidence_items.title: PhoneValue-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark and Datasets for Consumer Smartphone Recommerce Valuation

evidence_items.summary: Overview: This deposit hosts the official replication package, synthetic benchmark dataset, and experimental audit artifacts for the scientific manuscript: "M-11: Auditing Synthetic Risk Labels and Physical Baselines in a Cyber-Physical Benchmark for Underground Mining" (submitted to Acta Montanistica Slovaca, 2026). M-11 is a simulation-only cyber-physical benchmark that integrates AI4I 2020 predictive maintenance attributes with synthetic kinematic positioning, physiological, and environmental indicators (10,000 records; 37 columns) to audit the statistical mechanics and potential circularity of synthetic risk labelling in confined underground mining operations. Key Empirical Findings Reported in the Manuscript: Label Circularity Audit: Variance decomposition demonstrates that 82.07% of the synthetic score variance is driven by spatial/kinematic components, 17.43% by injected noise, 0.48% by multimodal variables, and 0.02% by cross-covariance. Symmetric Holdout Evaluation (n = 2,000; seed 42): Calibrated Time-to-Collision (TTC) and Random Forest both achieve F2 = 0.9103; XGBoost achieves F2 = 0.9065. The paired bootstrap difference (ΔF2 = -0.0038, 95% CI: -0.0129 to 0.0047) and Holm-adjusted McNemar test (p = 0.6015) confirm no statistically significant gap under circular labels. Decoupled Hazard Stress Tests: Under 22% class prevalence and low signal-to-noise ratio, non-spatial decoupled labels (CO, fatigue, vibration) push F2 optimisation to near-universal HIGH alerts, approaching the trivial Always-HIGH baseline (F2 = 0.5851). A multimodal-only composite target recovers F2 = 0.6408 with 54.1% specificity. Feature Ablations: Removing three direct kinematic indicators reduces F2 by 9.60 percentage points; removing the entire 8-feature spatial block reduces F2 by 32.52 percentage points from the full 0.9065 baseline. Computational Scalability: Local backend P95 latency scales to 27.91 ms under 500 concurrent simulated agents (< 200 ms supervisory threshold).
evidence_items.title: Dataset and Replication Package for M-11: Auditing Synthetic Risk Labels and Physical Baselines in a Cyber-Physical Benchmark for Underground Mining

evidence_items.summary: Detectors can flag hijacked large language model (LLM) agents from the traces of the tools they call. In the eleven evaluations we audited, attacks or anomalies make up 16% to 86% of the test samples, no evaluation varies that share, and six report no test on data from a second benchmark or source. We ask what such evaluations hide. On the AgentDrift and AgentDojo benchmarks we test trained detectors that read tool identities, behavior, call sequences, step embeddings or text, and a released LLM action monitor, AlignmentCheck, with thresholds fixed on training data or set by the monitor's released decision rule. First, at a 2% attack rate a detector with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.879 reaches a precision of 0.076, and the mix of negatives alone moves that precision between 0.039 and 0.117. Second, as tool coverage, the share of test tool calls whose tool was seen in training, falls, detector rankings cross near 50% coverage and reverse below it, because unseen tools map to inputs that training never reached. Dropout on tool inputs largely removes the reversal. Third, no detector trained on AgentDrift ranks AgentDojo traces better than chance (AUROC 0.47 to 0.52), including one that reaches 0.996 within AgentDojo. The monitor, trained on neither, reaches 0.930, but with its open backbone its released decision rule would still mostly raise false alerts at a 2% attack rate (precision 0.096). We turn these findings into a checklist for evaluating trace detectors.
evidence_items.title: What Standard Evaluations Hide About Detectors of Hijacked LLM Agents: Rare Attacks, Unseen Tools and Benchmark Transfer

evidence_items.summary: Version 2.0 of the benchmark dataset for the revised manuscript "OrganelleCleaner: identification and removal of organellar contigs in genome assemblies using graph topology, sequence features, and homology evidence" (Jeon and Kim). Results were produced with OrganelleCleaner v1.1.0 (https://github.com/Jeondong/OrganelleCleaner, tag v1.1.0; source snapshot included). The revised benchmark covers 10 plant species (Amborella trichopoda, Arabidopsis thaliana, Carica papaya, Citrullus lanatus, Glycine max, Malus domestica, Oryza sativa, Salix wilsonii, Solanum lycopersicum, Vitis vinifera; Daucus carota from version 1.0 was removed) and evaluates organellar contig detection against independent ground truth: Simulated assemblies with known answers: 14 hifiasm assemblies (HiFi and ONT) from reads simulated from T2T-level A. thaliana and O. sativa nuclear genomes plus organelle genomes at three organelle copy levels; each contig is labelled from the origin of its reads, and nuclear NUPT/NUMT regions are flagged as hard negatives. Distant organelle references: 53 target–reference species pairs from the same family to different seed-plant lineages. Merged-coverage proxy labels (supplementary): contigs whose merged BLAST coverage at ≥90% identity against NCBI plastid and mitochondrial genomes is ≥0.80. Contents: hifiasm contig and unitig graphs of the 10 real assemblies; simulated assemblies with truth tables and simulation references; own-species HiMT organelle references, proxy labels and distant references; OrganelleCleaner v1.1.0 reports for all real assemblies and modes; result tables behind the manuscript figures and tables; Vitis vinifera Hi-C scaffolding summaries; and all analysis scripts. See README.md for the file layout and methods.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark dataset and analysis scripts for OrganelleCleaner: identification and removal of organellar contigs in genome assemblies

evidence_items.summary: Wind turbine wakes significantly reduce downstream performance, yet accurately modeling their sensitivity to atmospheric stability and terrain remains a challenge. To address this, the International Energy Agency Wind Technology Collaboration Programme Task 57 launched a new wind farm wake benchmark leveraging high-resolution observations from the American WAKE experimeNt (AWAKEN). This paper, Part 1 of a two-part series, details the observational dataset and the selection of 24 August 2023 as the case study for the benchmark. This date was selected for its canonical diurnal cycle, which features a low-level jet with strong nocturnal stratification and high turbulence during the daytime. Analysis of the observational data reveals that despite the relatively simple terrain, interactions between the low-level jet and topography drove significant spatial variability in wind flow, leading to turbine power differences of up to 80 % across the considered wind farm. These findings demonstrate that a single vertical profile is insufficient to characterize wind plant inflow even in moderately complex terrain and that terrain-induced flow modifications can outweigh wake losses under stable stratification. The observed conditions documented here, together with the openly released dataset, constitute a unique multi-scale reference case for wake model validation at a large operating wind plant and provide the foundation for the modeling performance evaluation presented in the companion Part 2 paper.
evidence_items.title: The AWAKEN wind farm benchmark – Part 1: Observed conditions

evidence_items.summary: Connecting new generation and demand to the grid depends on two scarce skills: checking applications against a large, changing body of regulation, and running the network studies that decide where and how a project connects. We present Grid Agents, an AI system that brings both together, and the methodology we use to evaluate it. The Grid Ontology is its knowledge system. It represents the regulation, standards and engineering knowledge that grid work depends on, makes it searchable, and evolves as the agents learn from use. Every answer drawn from it rests on evidence the agents cite. Grid Studio is an agent system specialised for power-system engineering. It works in its own engineering environment with domain tools and a study framework, draws on the Grid Ontology, and relies on established solvers for every number it reports. In both, engineers make the decisions. We bring eight published power-system benchmark families, previously scattered across separate papers, into one suite of 519 tasks, and we verify not only each answer but the work behind it, by replaying the agent's tool calls. The Grid Ontology cites the right regulatory evidence more often than a general coding agent or retrieval pipelines, leads on LegalBench-RAG and ranks first on the public leaderboards of the Enterprise RAG Challenge and ViDoRe V3. Grid Studio scores highest on the 519 power-system tasks and is the fastest of all the systems we compare, both by a statistically significant margin. With an optimiser in the loop, its reinforcement packages cost 33-67% less on average than those the agent designs alone.
evidence_items.title: An Agentic Framework for Automated Power System Studies and Grid Connection Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Skill extraction benchmarks score models against a few human-annotated positives and treat every other skill in the vocabulary as equally wrong. At the scale of ESCO (13,939 skills) this binary view can reward models that rank the annotated positive high for the wrong reason, and hides semantically nonsensical predictions. The WorkRB Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026 replaces it with graded relevance: every candidate skill in a model's ranking window carries a 0 to 4 grade, and the leaderboard scores nDCG@100 against these grades. Since ternary judgements proved too coarse for objective annotation, relevance is decomposed into a cascade of four binary questions (same domain, activity mentioned, right granularity, replacement of a gold positive) that a smaller LLM judge can answer reliably; the labels are validated with blind human and frontier-model re-annotation. This paper documents the annotation methodology, the construction of five benchmark datasets (four with vacancy sentences as queries, one with lexically distant skill surface forms), the validation of the LLM cascade, and insights from the submissions. The field converged on multi-stage retrieve-and-rerank pipelines, whose gains come from clearing nonsense out of the ranking window rather than finding more positives: at the top of the leaderboard, the graded ordering is uncorrelated with what binary evaluation would have said. Graded labels expose much bigger gaps between top submissions and baselines than binary evaluation does, and show that semantic-understanding skill recommendation is still wide open. The clear next direction is bringing efficiency back: every submitted system we could size uses at least 42x, typically several hundred times, more parameters than the baselines it beats.
evidence_items.title: Grading the Unannotated: Insights from the WorkRB Skill Extraction Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026

evidence_items.summary: Effective polyp segmentation in colonoscopy images is crucial for early detection of colorectal cancer, a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. While current deep learning models perform well on traditional Dice benchmarks, border segmentation remains difficult. Most methods use boundary information only as an additional loss signal during training, which prevents the network from explicitly learning border-guided feature selection or mask refinement. This paper introduces BGD-SF PolySegNet, a boundary-guided encoder-decoder architecture that controls three phases of the segmentation pipeline: dynamic multi-scale context aggregation, selective skip-feature fusion, and final mask refinement. The architecture comprises a pretrained EfficientNet-B4 backbone and three proposed modules: Boundary-Guided Dynamic Cascaded Multi-Scale Context Aggregation (BGD-CMSCA), Boundary-Guided Selective Attention Fusion (BG-SAGF), and a Multi-Level Boundary Guidance Head (MBGH). The model is trained on 3,535 annotated images from Kvasir-SEG, BKAI-IGH NeoPolyp-Small, and PolypGen, and evaluated on four held-out benchmark datasets. On the internal test set, BGD-SF achieves a Dice of 0.887, IoU of 0.839, mask-derived Boundary F1 of 0.531, HD95 of 30.32, and ASSD of 18.10, improving Boundary F1, HD95, and ASSD by 15.7%, 27.5%, and 34.6% over the strongest CNN baselines. External validation on CVC-ClinicDB, CVC-ColonDB, ETIS-Larib, and CVC-300 yielded Dice scores of 0.891, 0.776, 0.863, and 0.885, respectively. The model runs at 35 FPS with 22.51M parameters. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirm statistically significant mask-derived Boundary F1 improvements over six of seven ablation variants (p < 0.001; small-to-moderate effect sizes, r = 0.215-0.434), demonstrating that integrating boundary guidance as an active architectural component measurably advances polyp boundary delineation.
evidence_items.title: BGD-SF PolySegNet: boundary-guided dynamic selective fusion network for robust polyp segmentation in colonoscopy images

evidence_items.summary: This work presents an evaluation of large language models (LLMs) for English to dialectal Arabic machine translation on the MADAR dataset. We evaluate both translation directions (English to Arabic and vice-versa) on 16 Arabic dialects. Our experiments cover a diverse set of models, including specialized Arabic models (Jais, Nile), multilingual models (Gemma, Command-R, Mistral, Aya), and commercial APIs (GPT-4.1). We employ multiple evaluation metrics: BLEU, CHRF, COMET (both reference-based and reference-less variants) and GEMBA (LLM-as-a-judge), as well as a small-scale manual evaluation, to assess translation quality. We discuss the challenges of automatic MT evaluation, especially in the context of Arabic dialects. We also evaluate the ability of LLMs to classify the dialect used in a text. The study offers insights into the capabilities and limitations of current LLMs for dialectal Arabic machine translation, particularly highlighting the difficulty of handling dialectal diversity, although the results may be influenced by possible training data contamination, which is always a concern with LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Current state of LLMs for Arabic dialectal machine translation

evidence_items.summary: Inner-speech decoding from electroencephalography could support non-invasive communication for people with severe motor impairment, but comparison across studies is hindered by dataset- and protocol-specific evaluation. We present a controlled cross-dataset study using one preprocessing pipeline, one within-subject five-fold cross-validation protocol, and a compact dual-attention Transformer (VC-DATNet; approximately 131,000 parameters) across three public corpora: Thinking Out Loud (10 participants), BISpeech (4), and SyncSpeech (3). VC-DATNet achieved per-participant sensor/source hybrid accuracies of 39.48% on the four-class Thinking Out Loud task, 20.60% on the eight-word BISpeech task, and 25.53% on the eight-word SyncSpeech task, for which we report the first decoding result. Sensor-space and cortical source-space representations were complementary, with each performing better for different participants; this pattern replicated across all three corpora and nine architectures. Moreover, ten decoders spanning convolutional, recurrent, temporal-convolutional, hybrid Transformer, and pretrained foundation-model families converged within a narrow accuracy range on every dataset. These findings indicate that representation choice should be individualized and suggest that performance on these public corpora is constrained more by signal quality and dataset scale than by model capacity. The released pipeline provides a reproducible benchmark for future inner-speech decoding studies
evidence_items.title: Inner-Speech Decoding from EEG Across Three Corpora Under a Fixed Architecture and Protocol

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) enables the transfer of learned representations from a large teacher network to a small student network. In foundational KD, the student network uses the original training data of the teacher model to accomplish this task. However, due to privacy concerns, the original training data is often not available. To overcome this reliance on original training data, several data-free knowledge distillation methods have been developed. Some of these methods operate in the white-box setting, and a few methods generate synthetic data by training a generator network. White-box methods use the teacher model's parameters to obtain a synthetic dataset. To avoid relying on teacher parameters, some methods use computationally expensive generative approaches to obtain such a dataset. There also exist certain black-box methods that generate the synthetic data without accessing teacher parameters. These methods are also computationally intensive. We propose a data-free knowledge distillation method that utilizes just the teacher's output logits and does not require access to its architecture, parameters, or gradients. We generate synthetic data via Projected Gradient Ascent (PGA) starting from smooth random noise signals. Required gradients are obtained through zeroth-order gradient estimation rather than backpropagating through the teacher's parameters. The student is then trained on these synthetically generated samples. We evaluate the proposed method on several benchmark datasets and show that the distillation performance is comparable with approaches that have access to the teacher model parameters.
evidence_items.title: ZOPGA-KD: Zeroth Order PGA Guided Data Free Knowledge Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Amodal video object segmentation is fundamentally limited by the absence of datasets that combine real-world complexity with precise ground-truth annotations. To address this, we present Real Video Amodal Segmentation (Real-VAS), a new large-scale, zero-shot evaluation dataset built from composited real-image video. We introduce a novel data generation pipeline that enables the creation of programmatically consistent amodal ground truth for real-world footage, in which the object mask, occlusion boundary, and composited image are all derived from a single unoccluded source, without relying on human estimation or expensive 3D reconstruction. Our dataset is structured into two challenging scenarios: dynamic Occlusion, created by compositing two clips of moving objects, and a unique Container category featuring complex, physically constrained interactions. These container scenarios--On Surface Containment, Articulated Containment, and Mobile Containment--allow us to generate precise ground truth by simulating an object's motion based on its container's tracked transformation. As a result, Real-VAS provides a diverse and challenging benchmark for evaluating amodal segmentation models on realistic video with the precision of synthetic data. The dataset and our generation code will be made publicly available.
evidence_items.title: Real-VAS: a Real-World Video Amodal Segmentation Dataset

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Video Conferencing 1000 (VC-1K), an open-source test set comprising approximately 1,000 video sequences specifically designed for evaluating video processing and encoding pipelines in real-time communication (RTC) scenarios. Unlike existing test sets that primarily rely on studio-produced or screen content, VC-1K consists of user-generated video call content captured on consumer mobile devices under a wide variety of conditions. The dataset predominantly features talking-head sequences with distinct faces, but also includes a small subset of outward-facing, rear-camera videos without faces to reflect additional common RTC use cases. It spans a wide range of real-world variables including device type, lighting conditions, motion levels, indoor/outdoor environments, and demographic diversity. All video sequences are accompanied by synchronous audio to facilitate multimodal research. We detail the dataset's design methodology and statistical distribution, and demonstrate its utility through a comparative encoder evaluation of OpenH264, SVT-AV1, and libaom under constant bitrate (CBR) encoding at resolutions typical of RTC deployments. Furthermore, two super-resolution approaches, RealESRGAN and GFPGAN, are evaluated on VC-1K, highlighting the dataset as a useful benchmark for pre- and post-processing research. VC-1K is intended to serve as a publicly available dataset for the video RTC research community.
evidence_items.title: VC-1K: A Diverse Video Test Set for Real-Time Communication

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for technical tasks in the oil and gas industry. Well-log interpretation requires combining depth-indexed measurements, derived petrophysical properties, and quality-control information to characterize lithology, porosity, permeability, fluid saturation, and reservoir quality within intervals and across formations and wells. Reliable interpretation depends on cross-curve consistency, data quality, and the availability of complementary measurements. Recent work introduced WellLogBench and WellLog-LLM (Shikhar, S. et al., 2026) to provide such a reproducible evaluation setting. WellLogBench established an expert-validated benchmark based on public LAS data and structured petrophysical contexts. These contexts are constructed using Petrophys (Shikhar, S. et al., 2026), an open-source library for standardized well-log processing, normalization, derivation of petrophysical properties, and assembly of model-ready interpretation contexts. WellLog-LLM combines Dynamic Feature Selection with supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and Group Relative Context Optimization (GRCO). GRCO is a training-free, GRPO-inspired method that derives reusable guidance from relative comparisons of model rollouts and applies it during inference without updating model weights. Although the aforementioned work provides a reproducible setting for well-log reasoning, its scope does not cover the full conditions encountered in operational carbonate fields. Operational carbonate datasets contain operator-specific mnemonics, incomplete log suites, logs from different vintages and acquisition types (e.g., wireline and LWD), borehole and acquisition effects, legacy interpreted curves, and sparse core coverage. Models must distinguish direct measurements from derived properties and qualify their conclusions when the required evidence is absent.
evidence_items.title: Well-Log LLM Benchmark: The First ADNOC Domain-Expert Curated Benchmark for LLM Reasoning of Well Logs on Carbonate Reservoirs

evidence_items.summary: Data-driven mechanistic hypotheses are essential to scientific discovery because they explain how underlying processes produce observed phenomena. AI agents and AI scientists increasingly support scientific data analysis. However, their ability to turn empirical findings into mechanistic hypotheses remains insufficiently examined. To address this gap, we introduce MechHypoBench, the first benchmark for evaluating whether AI agents and AI scientists can generate such hypotheses from empirical data. It combines paper-derived mechanisms from 14 scientific fields with real-world datasets containing 17.98 million records. The construction retains the observational complexity of empirical data while providing a specified underlying mechanism. Agents analyze the observations and propose open-form hypotheses. We develop an evaluation framework that assesses open-form mechanistic hypotheses through their consequences under withheld conditions. Experiments with general agents and AI scientists reveal a substantial gap between generated hypotheses and the underlying mechanisms.
evidence_items.title: From Scientific Observations to Mechanisms: Benchmarking Hypothesis Generation by AI Scientists

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to support decisions by calling external tools. Existing work on LLM tool-calling assumes these tools are perfectly reliable. However, in many applications, the tools are statistical predictors with non-trivial errors. We introduce PredActBench, a benchmark for evaluating dialogue agents that work with imperfect predictive tools, using education as a testbed. First, we build a benchmark in which LLMs work with noisy predictors to guide users' decisions. Second, we extend two prior metrics for trust calibration, Relative AI-Reliance and Relative Self-Reliance, to multi-turn dialogue. Third, we evaluate 13 LLMs on OULAD and our released PredAct-CS dataset of 60 courses with real final grades and synthetic weekly scores, alongside a human study involving 13 instructors and teaching assistants. We find that when tools are noisy, SOTA models rarely make predictor uncertainty visible to users, with our strongest baseline GPT-5.5 achieving an F1 of 57.2. As a result, users over-rely on incorrect predictions and unsupported claims, showing that task accuracy alone is not enough for AI decision support and agents must communicate when their tools may be wrong. We release PredActBench to support the development of LLM agents that help users calibrate their reliance.
evidence_items.title: PredActBench: Benchmarking Tool-Augmented Dialogue under Controlled Tool Noise

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) perform strongly across vision-language tasks, yet remain insufficiently explored in UAV scenarios. Recent UAV-oriented benchmarks have begun to evaluate MLLMs in aerial scenarios, but typically focus on scene understanding, event recognition, or navigation completion, rather than jointly assessing the dual-cognition capability required for UAV agents: reasoning about the UAV's own position, behavior, and observation state alongside external landmark states under continuously changing viewpoints, supported by explicit spatio-temporal grounding. To address this gap, we present UAV-DualCog, the first benchmark to formulate UAV dual cognition as the coordinated evaluation of Agent-State Reasoning and World-State Reasoning across multi-view images and egocentric videos, with explicit spatial or temporal grounding. The State-aware UAV Simulation Platform (SUSP) and the DualCog-aware Capture System (DCCS) construct 4,096 image and 2,048 video samples from 12 scenes, pairing complementary state questions within shared Agent-Landmark contexts. Extensive evaluations on 45 models show that current MLLMs remain far from reliable in UAV dual cognition: Agent-State Reasoning is generally weaker than World-State Reasoning, semantic answers do not reliably coincide with spatial or temporal grounding, and coordinated abilities remain limited. Thinking-mode comparisons, open-ended analyses, and sim-to-real validation show that these limitations persist across inference settings, formats, and environments. We further construct UAV-DualCog-Train and improve UAV dual-cognition performance through a lightweight optimization probe. Supplementary website, code, and dataset: https://smartdianlab.github.io/UAV-DualCog/
evidence_items.title: UAV-DualCog: A Dual-Cognition Benchmark for Grounded UAV Agent-World Reasoning with MLLMs

evidence_items.summary: Language-conditioned goal navigation requires embodied agents to locate user-specified targets without step-by-step guidance. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on category-level goals or rely on instance descriptions generated by vision-language models, which often contain ambiguities and semantic errors, limiting systematic and reliable evaluation. We introduce HieraNav, an open-vocabulary navigation task with goals at four hierarchical semantic levels: scene, room, region, and instance. We present Language as a Map (LangMap), the first goal navigation benchmark to enrich real-world indoor 3D scans with human-verified semantic annotations supporting tasks across all four goal levels. Built on HM3D using a contrastive annotation protocol that compares same-scene regions and instances, LangMap provides region labels and discriminative region and instance descriptions covering 414 object categories and contains over 18K tasks. Each target has concise and detailed descriptions, enabling evaluation across instruction styles. Automated and human evaluations validate our annotation quality: our descriptions improve text-to-view matching accuracy over GOAT-Bench's by 23 points on all shared annotated instances, and an independent human audit yields 92.5% unique-and-correct matches. We also propose PlaNaVid, an RGB-only baseline that combines Bounded Diverse Memory with high-level planning to prime a reactive policy for multi-goal navigation, achieving top-tier success rates without depth, 3D scene representations, or object masks. Further analyses reveal that exploration and hierarchical disambiguation failures become more prominent at finer goal levels, while long-tail categories, small objects, distant targets, timely stopping, and multi-goal completion remain challenging. Benchmark and code: https://bo-miao.github.io/LangMap
evidence_items.title: LangMap: A Human-Verified Benchmark for Hierarchical Open-Vocabulary Goal Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Synthetic text generation with Differential Privacy (DP) guarantees emerges as a principled approach that can enable the sharing of sensitive datasets across institutional and regulatory boundaries, while bounding the risks of re-identification and membership inference. LLM-based methods deliver promising results; however, comparisons are exacerbated by differing evaluation setups and "private" datasets, potential pre-training contamination is not considered and guarantees are not verified with DP audits. To advance this field, we introduce a unified evaluation framework with standardised utility and fidelity metrics and privacy audits, encompassing nine curated datasets that capture domain-specific complexities such as technical jargon, long-context dependencies, and specialised document structures. In a large-scale empirical study, we benchmark LLM-based state-of-the-art DP text generators of varying sizes (between 1--8B). Our results indicate that DP synthetic text generation remains an unsolved challenge, with quality deteriorating more as the private datasets deviate further from the generators' pre-training corpora. Our analyses suggest that synthetic data quality may be overestimated when LLMs have been pre-trained---without DP---on portions of the "private" data to be generated, and our membership inference (MIA) auditing setup for synthetic text reveals measurable membership signals even under tight privacy budgets. Finally, we note that under the "public pre-training, private generation" paradigm, the nominal $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ guarantee does not account for exposure during pre-training, motivating contamination-aware evaluation of DP synthetic text generation. Code and data splits: https://github.com/ImperialGlobalSingapore/synbench
evidence_items.title: SynBench: A Benchmark for Differentially Private Text Generation
