evidence_items.summary: Law changes over time. A court decides a case under the law in force on that day, and legal QA benchmarks grade answers against today's law. We checked 156,650 decisions of four Thai courts. Up to 67% of them cite law that has since been amended or repealed. We introduce NitiBench+, the sequel of our NitiBench, a Thai legal QA benchmark with 1,670 items across 17 domains, built from decisions of three courts. For each cited section it holds both the text in force on the decision date and the current text, and its retrieval corpus holds every dated version of every Thai statute section. Answers are graded on the Thai Bar Council rubric, the Bar-standard score, and on the overlap between the cited sections and the court's. The report has two parts. Part I measures the cost of the wrong text on 13 open-weight models. Reading the current text of amended law drops the Bar-standard score by 0.25 and missing repealed law drops it by 0.79. The penalty comes from rule changes, 0.45 on the 428 rule-changed items and none on the 331 wording-only items, and Citation F1 does not see it. The text in force is the fair setting. Part II benchmarks today's models on that setting. A public leaderboard ranks 26 models on a held-out test split of 500 items stratified by domain, with a validation split of the same shape released for public use, from memory alone, with the court's sections provided, and as a retrieval agent over the law in force, with the cost per item and the hallucinated citations. The best model scores 7.78 out of 10 and the best open-weight model 6.39. Without a search tool only five open-weight models recall any Thai law, and with it twenty of the 26 models gain and six lose. Leaderboard will take new models as they are released. Legal benchmarks must track dates, and on the right text today's models still leave a wide gap on Thai law.
evidence_items.title: NitiBench+: A Temporal Thai Legal Question Answering Benchmark Across 17 Domains

evidence_items.summary: Every multimodal-LLM multiple-choice benchmark ends with a scoring rule that converts a model's response, often free-form text rather than a clean option letter, into a right/wrong verdict, buried in its code. Unlike the dataset, this rule is chosen without justification and left unexamined, yet it sets the published number. We reproduce the official scorers of eight peer-reviewed benchmarks on five open vision-language models (VLMs) that fit a single 16 GB GPU, and introduce a blinded human-plus-LLM-judge adjudication (Cohen's kappa=0.956) that recovers what the model actually answered. The scoring rule alone moves accuracy by up to 22 points on identical outputs, yet exactly 0 wherever a model emits clean option letters, so it hides on strong-model leaderboards. It is the fallback and not the rambling that does the damage: the benchmark with the highest non-compliance we measure has an artifact of exactly zero, because its scorer abstains instead of guessing; a reasoning model with non-compliance 0.000 still swings 9.5 points with which regex match of its trace the parser keeps. No standard rule is reliable: snapping a non-answer to its closest option credits answers never given yet buries correct ones, abstention discards answers stated in words, and likelihood scoring follows answer-token priors, so a single grade conflates capability with luck rather than measuring either. We release all code, labels, and the protocol, and argue benchmarks should report a non-compliance rate and at least two rules, not one unexamined grade.
evidence_items.title: Same Outputs, Different Scores: Auditing the Unchecked Graders of Multimodal LLM Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Recent language model (LM) safety failures have largely been studied as disparate phenomena. In agentic misalignment, a model blackmails an executive to avoid being replaced. In alignment faking, it complies with harmful requests during training to keep its values from being modified. We argue that these behaviours share a common decision structure: a model assigned a goal must either take a harmful action to preserve it or refuse and lose it. We formalize this as a goal-harm conflict and present the same conflict under various elicitation protocols that range from compact forced-choice prompts to simulated agentic environments. These protocols span two perspectives on LM decision-making, which we term (i) the logit view, reading preferences from answer-token probabilities, and (ii) the sampling view, classifying open-ended responses with an LM judge. Under the logit view, we show that goal importance and harm severity additively shape how a model resolves these value conflicts. Under the sampling view, we derive two factorizations of the harmful-action probability that safety evaluations commonly report. The first measures how well a preference read from answer tokens carries over into behaviour, such as making a harmful tool call. The second attributes a low harmful-action rate either to refusal or to responses that reach no resolution. We then show how fictional context changes a model's preference under the logit view, and how tool use and partial observability -- two features of agentic evaluations -- change its harmful-action rate under the sampling view. Our work offers a descriptive framework for studying how LMs resolve such value conflicts and for estimating low-probability harmful actions at a finer granularity than the aggregate harm rates commonly reported in safety evaluations.
evidence_items.title: Characterizing When Language Models Take Harmful Actions to Protect Their Assigned Goals

evidence_items.summary: The multi-turn checker of the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) evaluates final state correctness but ignores the effects of intermediate calls: extra calls are free, function documentation does not describe side effects, and the scripted user never responds to proposals. Consequently, models asking for confirmation before destructive actions are penalized; 260 of 734 reference turns in the base category perform destructive actions without confirmation. We make BFCL effect-aware without replacing it. We infer effect declarations for all 128 functions by executing them in BFCL simulators and comparing state changes, with destructive writes identified by three annotators. A judge-free replay scorer reproduces official results across all 800 reference trajectories while reporting unrequested destructive calls, duplicate writes, redundant reads, surplus steps, and their token costs. We also introduce a confirmation-aware protocol with a deterministic simulated user. Across 11 open models, effect-aware scoring preserves the official ranking but reveals substantial differences in execution quality: the leading model loses 14.0 points due to unrequested destructive calls, while surplus steps consume up to 28% of input tokens. Adding effect hints to function documentation has no impact on eight evaluated models. Allowing the simulated user to respond recovers up to four points for models that seek confirmation. However, the best model completes only six of 576 conversations requiring destructive actions with explicit confirmation. These results expose a key limitation of current function-calling benchmarks: they cannot distinguish between asking for clarification and obtaining permission before potentially destructive actions.
evidence_items.title: CAREFUL-Bench: Effect-Aware, Judge-Free Evaluation of Multi-Turn LLM Function Calling

evidence_items.summary: Low Tucker rank tensors provide compact representations of multidimensional dependencies, but standard learning pipelines can incur substantial computational and memory overhead from redundant intermediate quantities. We reduce this overhead without modifying the underlying representation objective or parameterization. Our approach combines three complementary components: (i) sequential extraction of only task-required spectral components, avoiding unnecessary full decompositions; (ii) factor-wise multilinear contractions without materializing large Kronecker operators; and (iii) compact latent-state updates without storing full ambient tensor iterates. These components preserve the algebraic operations and learning trajectories of the original algorithms while reducing their computational and memory footprints. Across five low Tucker rank tensor estimators, our implementations match the original trajectories to numerical precision (relative discrepancies of $10^{-16}$ to $10^{-13}$), while reducing per-iteration runtime by up to $3.12\times$ and resident memory by up to $616\times$ ($99.8\%$) on the main order-3 benchmark at $n=100$, with memory reductions exceeding $900\times$ across the full evaluation suite. These results show that substantial computational redundancy can be eliminated from Tucker representation learning without changing the underlying model or learned representation.
evidence_items.title: Lightweight Representation Learning for Low Tucker Rank Tensors

evidence_items.summary: Decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer typed questions about a text (yes/no, multiple choice, or an ordinal score) with calibrated probabilities in a single forward pass and without generating text, which makes them an inexpensive candidate for LLM-as-a-judge workloads. We evaluate 14 System-1 decision models, selected with a pre-stated protocol, against four generative judges (Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning, and Claude Opus 5.5 with thinking) on eleven established judge benchmarks. Five of the 14 are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning on all five pairwise and best-of-4 benchmarks, and the two strongest, DReX-Max and d1-ultra, are significantly more accurate than Haiku on JudgeBench, LLMBar and RewardBench 2. Conditioned on a reference answer generated once per prompt, eleven models reach 90.3-93.4% on JudgeBench, statistically indistinguishable from Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 with reasoning, and on PPE best-of-16 every reference-guided System-1 judge matches GPT-5.6 with reasoning at roughly one-sixteenth of its cost per prompt. Several System-1 judges are better calibrated than every generative judge and correlate more strongly with human helpfulness ratings. Robustness to instructions injected into the judged response is a property of the individual model rather than of the System-1 design: an appended note to the evaluator reverses 0-5% of the correct verdicts of five models but 17-49% for the other nine. Two general System-1 leaderboards that contain no judging tasks predict judging accuracy (Pearson r = 0.95-0.96), a well-calibrated System-1 first stage matches Opus on LLMBar while escalating 17% of items, and same-size controls show that the correctness deficit of a 4B decision model is a reasoning gap rather than a size gap.
evidence_items.title: To Jev or Not to Jev: When Can System-1 Decision Models Replace LLM Judges?

evidence_items.summary: Deaf inclusion across sub-Saharan society faces regional hurdles, with Nigeria as the core empirical focus. Existing recognition models demand heavy computational infrastructure. However, standard mobile phones used locally rarely exceed 1 GB to 4 GB of RAM. This study addresses constraints through a lightweight YOLO11n object-detection framework. The system provides real-time Nigerian Sign Language recognition for low-resource hardware. A benchmark dataset containing 11,208 raw gesture images was established. The data spans 33 static classes collected from five signers. Partitioning isolates signers S1 through S3 for training. Signer S4 provides validation data. Signer S5 is reserved for testing. Spatial augmentations are restricted strictly to the training set. This yields 23,509 training images. The validation and test sets each maintain 1,681 images across varied environments. The framework integrates a quantization-aware compression objective. Loss functions merge with squared Frobenius-norm penalties to govern weight distortion. A Spatial-Density Occlusion Index quantifies background complexity and self-occlusion. A latency-profiling equation relates floating-point operations and memory bandwidth to chipset clock speed. Performance testing on physical Android hardware utilizes unquantized FP32 weights. Mean inference latencies span 405.5 ms to 1,759.4 ms. Measured against test data, the algorithm attains a Precision of 0.9975. Recall reaches 0.9991. Mean Average Precision is 0.9942. Outcomes support offline functionality on constrained mobile devices. Practical deployment operates through a mobile utility using CameraX. The application captures gestures in real time. Recognized signs display as text instantly.
evidence_items.title: Edge-Optimized YOLOv11n Architecture for Offline Recognition of Nigerian Sign Language Alphanumeric Gestures

evidence_items.summary: Airborne tree monitoring using remotely sensed data, combined with the growth of computer vision models for object detection and segmentation, can facilitate broad scale assessment of tree health, ecology and ecosystem function. However, datasets for airborne tree detection have been largely limited to a single geography, resolution, or annotation approach, making it difficult to develop general models and benchmark their utility for broad applications. We compile existing and newly published annotation datasets to create a comprehensive dataset for training and evaluating airborne tree detection in RGB imagery. The MillionTrees dataset has over a million individual trees from a broad range of forest types, tree species, and geographic locations. In addition, it has six million weakly supervised annotations from a range of sources including airborne LiDAR and photogrammetry, arborist surveys, and simulated landscapes. An evaluation standard is provided to facilitate rapid model development. We benchmark several existing tree detection algorithms and demonstrate that while current open-source models do not generalize across the diverse datasets in the benchmark, training on MillionTrees improves both within-domain and out-of-domain performance. Held-out validation datasets using ground truth derived from terrestrial LiDAR paired with overhead RGB show that overfitting to test data is common and hyperparameter tuning is an underappreciated challenge towards a global zero shot tree detection method. We discuss the limitations of the currently available data for airborne RGB tree detection, how to create more robust evaluation data and the need for better understanding of the uncertainty and utility of tree detection from airborne remote sensing.
evidence_items.title: MillionTrees: A global benchmark for tree detection across geography, sensor, and annotation geometry

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Formation evaluation is an investigation, not a single calculation or chat response. A petrophysicist must establish data readiness, select methods that fit the rock and available logs, compare several measurements, record uncertain inputs, and revise the interpretation when evidence conflicts. This paper presents PetroHarness, a harness designed for human supervision and open-source release that organizes this work around deterministic petrophysical calculations and a retained review package. PetroHarness separates scientific calculation from language-model coordination. The existing Petrophys library performs the depth-wise calculations. PetroHarness resolves the formation, checks inputs, builds a dependency-ordered scientific state, and lets a bounded LLM investigator request task-specific evidence through registered operations. Candidate reports are checked against the scientific results available to the model. The selected report, operation trace, evidence contract, and selection record are retained for petrophysicist review. The system was compared with a Baseline Agent using the same well logs, formation context, language model, Petrophys library (Shikhar et al. 2026), questions, and evaluator. In an automated benchmark-development evaluation of 221 questions from 18 wells and 50 formations, a content-centered Answer Quality Score increased from 38.82 to 52.02. The paired gain was 13.20 points, with a well-level 95% bootstrap interval of 10.14 to 16.31, and scores increased in every task family, with 180 of 221 cases improving. PetroHarness retained a portable trace, evidence contract, and draft-selection record for every run. Among reports containing numbers, at least 95% of the reported values could be found in the saved calculations in 98.6% of PetroHarness reports, compared with 12.0% for the Baseline Agent. The contribution is a practical boundary for agentic subsurface work.
evidence_items.title: PetroHarness: An Open-Source Agentic Harness for Auditable Formation Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Traditional robot task planning struggles to recover from failures and changing requirements because it relies on predefined rules, labelled datasets, and limited state awareness. Digital twins provide real-time virtual representations of physical systems, while multi-agent systems support collaborative, stepwise reasoning. However, their integration for failure evaluation, requirement adaptation, and state-aware robot planning remains underexplored, particularly at the architectural level. This study proposes a multi-agentic digital twin framework for human-in-the-loop workflows, enabling bidirectional communication between machines, digital twins, and multi-agents. The framework is validated through robot task planning for an aerospace product-qualification metrology process. Results show that digital-twin integration adds 885-1,149 milliseconds to communication between robots and agents because continuous state updates are required. Multi-agent workflows need more human feedback than single-agent workflows to align outputs with predefined goals and mitigate hallucinations, highlighting the importance of human-in-the-loop orchestration. Datasets, logs, code, videos, results, and deployment instructions are available on GitHub 1 .
evidence_items.title: A Multi-Agentic Digital Twin Framework for Human-in-the-loop Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark runner, Morpheus agent skill, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, biological scoring criteria and analysis scripts used to test whether LLM-based coding agents can rebuild published multicellular models in the Morpheus simulator. The release contains the subject-facing setup of benchmark version 3, which produced the main results of the accompanying preprint. The folder figures/ rebuilds every figure and table of the preprint from the data it contains. The eleven benchmark papers published under a CC BY licence and two bioRxiv preprints (CC BY 4.0 and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) are included unchanged under their own licences, not under the Apache License (see NOTICE); benchmark papers/papers.csv lists all 15 papers with DOIs, licences and the SHA-256 checksums of the files used, and benchmark papers/README.md explains how to obtain the four that may not be redistributed.
evidence_items.title: Morpheus agent benchmark: code and scoring criteria for testing LLM agents that build multicellular models in Morpheus

evidence_items.summary: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace (Keepace.ai) is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.
evidence_items.title: Keepace.ai: A Technical Report on a Large Language Model for Sports and Health

evidence_items.summary: Industrial shampoo-bottle surface defect detection must operate across many stock keeping units (SKUs), where differences in bottle geometry, material, label layout, reflectance, and imaging conditions can substantially alter the appearance of the same defect. Existing industrial defect datasets rarely provide both instance-level defect annotations and product-variant identities, making it difficult to study SKU-aware detection under realistic manufacturing conditions. We introduce Bottle-SKU, a large-scale multi-SKU benchmark for shampoo bottle surface defect detection. Bottle-SKU contains 13,119 images, 20,419 instance-level bounding boxes, seven defect categories, and 48 bottle SKUs, enabling evaluation of both shared defect recognition and SKU-specific appearance variation. To address the challenge of SKU-specific appearance variation, we propose Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation (ProDMM). ProDMM constructs a visual prototype for each SKU from training images and predicts a soft SKU distribution for each input. The resulting prototype-conditioned representation dynamically generates low-rank Query/Value modulation for the visual backbone and residual conditioning for defect-text-to-visual attention, while preserving the pretrained Grounding DINO detection pathway. The model is trained jointly with detection, SKU-domain classification, and modulation-regularization objectives. Experiments on Bottle-SKU and the public GC10-DET-SKU metallic surface defect dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided domain conditioning for industrial surface defect detection. The source code and model will be released on https://github.com/Event-AHU/Industrial_Anomaly_Detection
evidence_items.title: Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation and a Large-Scale Multi-SKU Benchmark for Shampoo Bottle Surface Defect Detection

evidence_items.summary: Language models are increasingly expected to support users in stressful or uncertain situations, where warmth and empathy are desirable. While recent work associates warmer models with reduced reliability, we show that this conclusion is incomplete. Prior studies often train primarily on empathetic dialogue, making it difficult to separate tone effects from SFT-induced distribution shift. We revisit this issue at both the model and evaluation levels. We study prompting, SFT, and RL for inducing warm behavior, and comprehensively evaluate capability preservation using an 11-dataset benchmark suite and EMOFACT under emotional contexts. Across multiple model families, we find that warmth effects are task- and model-dependent, while task-aligned adaptive tone can improve empathy and targeted reliability, although some capability trade-offs remain. We further introduce human-validated empathy evaluators specifically developed to assess empathetic model responses. Our results suggest that models can be more supportive in social interactions while remaining reliable.
evidence_items.title: Empathy Is Not the Scapegoat for Declines in Factuality and Reliability

evidence_items.summary: Recent agent benchmarks increasingly ground evaluation in executable environments, from code repair to web navigation, app APIs, and function calling. Yet completing consequential work beyond code requires more than producing a plausible response or valid tool call: agents must gather missing information over multiple turns, follow domain policies, coordinate dependent tools, and realize the correct persistent state transition without collateral effects. In this paper, we introduce Thinkingbox, a sandbox for tool-agent-user interaction that provides isolated MCP-compatible tool sessions, complete execution traces, and outcome evaluation over terminal backend state. Built on this sandbox, Thinkingbox-bench contains 507 policy-conditioned workflows across business scenarios, including retail, hospitality, auto insurance, neobank internal IT, and consulting IT/HR support. Each attempt is evaluated by task-specific executable checks that accept valid trajectories while rejecting wrong, missing, or extra effects; designated tasks additionally check required properties of the final response. Our experiments reveal that even the strongest proprietary and open-weight models show steep reliability drops: Claude Opus 5 falls from 66.50% pass@1 to 47.53% pass^20, and Kimi-K3 from 57.37% pass@1 to 17.60% pass^20. Moreover, many failed trials terminate cleanly after valid state-changing actions, so response- or tool-call-level signals poorly proxy end-to-end completion. Thinkingbox-bench reveals a large gap between occasionally finding a successful trajectory and reliably completing stateful business tasks. We release Thinkingbox, Thinkingbox-Bench, and Thinkingbox-integrated reinforcement learning framework.
evidence_items.title: One Success Isn't Reliability: Thinkingbox, a Sandbox and Benchmark for Agents in Stateful Business Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge graph foundation models such as Ultra and Trix achieve strong inductive transfer by learning relation-graph representations that generalise to unseen entities and relations. Extending this transferability to temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) remains challenging: existing temporal models tie their parameters to dataset-specific entities, relations, or timestamps and are not designed to transfer to TKGs with disjoint vocabularies. We propose GRATE (Gated Rotary Attention for Temporal Encoding), an entity-side message function that adds no learnable parameters and encodes time through relative time differences by rotating each edge message according to its time gap to the query and applying a query-conditioned gate to select temporally relevant signals. GRATE integrates into NBFNet-style KG foundation models while preserving structural transferability. Existing TKG benchmarks evaluate within shared train/test vocabularies and cannot directly test cross-dataset temporal transfer; we therefore construct GDELTIndT and WIKIIndT, inductive transfer benchmark suites with disjoint entities, relations, and timestamps spanning both interpolation and extrapolation. Across these benchmarks and held-out forecasting datasets, a single jointly pretrained GRATE checkpoint improves over the static base model in most settings.
evidence_items.title: GRATE: Temporal Extensions for Inductive KG Foundation Models via Gated Rotary Attention

evidence_items.summary: Computer-use agents could automate repetitive screen-based clinical work, but their reliability in medical graphical user interfaces remains largely unvalidated. Existing benchmarks focus on general web or desktop tasks and underrepresent medical software, which requires domain knowledge, exhibits markedly different UI design from mainstream applications, lacks public testing environments, and demands safety validation beyond task completion. We introduce MedCUA-Bench, an interactive benchmark for clinical computer-use agents. It covers 18 clinical scenarios across 10 medical domains, reconstructed from real product manuals and open-source medical systems to capture authentic clinical interfaces while avoiding licensing and privacy constraints. Each task ships with paired intent- and step-level goals to disentangle clinical reasoning from UI execution, and is evaluated by a deterministic checker over task completion and five clinical safety dimensions. Across 23 agents, the best closed-source model reaches 54.2% strict success, while all models remain below 9% on the real OpenEMR. Open-source agents average only 2.5%, with the best reaching 16.2%. MedCUA-Bench exposes the gap between current agents and reliable clinical software use, providing a reproducible testbed for future research.
evidence_items.title: MedCUA-Bench: A Screenshot-Only Benchmark for Clinical Computer-Use Agents

evidence_items.summary: Estimating the 9D pose of everyday objects from a single real-world image remains challenging. This is largely due to the lack of large-scale supervision. Most existing datasets either rely heavily on synthetic renderings or provide limited coverage of real-world objects. We address this gap with Every9D-22M, a dataset of 9D pose annotations for 22.8M real-world images from 114K object-centric videos spanning 630 everyday object categories, making it nearly two orders of magnitude larger than any prior real-world 9D pose dataset in at least one of category, object, or image count. To achieve this scale, we leverage object-centric videos by reconstructing object-level point clouds via multi-view geometry and aligning similar instances into a shared canonical coordinate frame. Canonical poses are manually annotated for only a small set of reference objects (fewer than 0.01% of all images) and propagated to the remaining instances via cross-instance alignment. All propagated canonical poses are then verified from multiple viewpoints. We further introduce cross-category orientation rules that induce category-level symmetries, enabling symmetry-aware evaluation. Beyond establishing dedicated training and evaluation splits as a benchmark for 9D pose foundation models, we show that training on Every9D-22M generalizes better to other datasets than training on existing datasets, and outperforms prior foundation models in rotation accuracy on all benchmarks except the viewpoint-biased ImageNet3D, where joint training with ImageNet3D surpasses them as well. Data and code are available at https://github.com/GenIntel/Every9D.
evidence_items.title: Every9D-22M: Large-Scale Real-World 9D Canonicalization of Everyday Objects

evidence_items.summary: Robust optimization (RO) provides a principled framework for decision-making under uncertainty, but its practical use is often limited by the need to manually reformulate uncertain optimization models into tractable deterministic counterparts. Recent large language models (LLMs) have been shown promising for automating optimization formulation, yet RO reformulation remains challenging because it requires precise multi-step reasoning and mathematically consistent transformations. To facilitate systematic evaluation of LLM-based reformulation, for which no dedicated benchmark currently exists, we develop AutoRO-Bench, a benchmark featuring an automated data generation pipeline for the core RO reformulation task and a curated dataset for the RO application task. To address the reformulation challenge, we propose Automated Reformulation with Experience Memory (AutoREM), a tuning-free memory-augmented framework that autonomously builds a structured textual experience memory by reflecting on past failed trajectories through a tailored offline adaptation procedure. AutoREM requires neither domain-specific expert knowledge nor parameter updates, and the resulting memory readily transfers across different base LLMs. Experimental results show that AutoREM consistently improves the accuracy and efficiency of RO reformulation across in-distribution datasets, out-of-distribution datasets, and diverse base LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Automated Reformulation of Robust Optimization via Memory-Augmented Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: As 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) gains attention in immersive media and digital content creation, assessing the aesthetics of 3D scenes becomes important in helping creators build more visually compelling 3D content. However, existing evaluation methods for 3D scenes primarily emphasize reconstruction fidelity and perceptual realism, largely overlooking higher-level aesthetic attributes such as composition, harmony, and visual appeal. This limitation comes from two key challenges: (1) the absence of general 3DGS datasets with aesthetic annotations, and (2) the intrinsic nature of 3DGS as a low-level primitive representation, which makes it difficult to capture high-level aesthetic features. To address these challenges, we propose Aes3D, the first systematic framework for assessing the aesthetics of 3D neural rendering scenes. Aes3D includes Aesthetic3D, the first dataset dedicated to 3D scene aesthetic assessment, built on our proposed annotation strategy for 3D scene aesthetics. In addition, we present Aes3DGSNet, a lightweight model that directly predicts scene-level aesthetic scores from 3DGS representations. Notably, our model operates solely on 3D Gaussian primitives, eliminating the need for rendering multi-view images and thus reducing computational cost and hardware requirements. Through aesthetics-supervised learning on multi-view 3DGS scene representations, Aes3DGSNet effectively captures high-level aesthetic cues and accurately regresses aesthetic scores. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves strong performance while maintaining a lightweight design, establishing a new benchmark for 3D scene aesthetic assessment.
evidence_items.title: Aes3D: Aesthetic Assessment in 3D Gaussian Splatting

evidence_items.summary: Penetration testing is essential for assessing and strengthening system security against real-world threats, yet traditional workflows remain highly manual, expertise-intensive, and difficult to scale. Although recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities for automation, existing applications rely on simplistic prompting without task decomposition or domain adaptation, resulting in unreliable black-box behavior and limited insight into model capabilities across penetration testing stages. To address this gap, we introduce PentestEval, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLMs across six decomposed penetration testing stages: Information Collection, Weakness Gathering and Filtering, Attack Decision-Making, Exploit Generation and Revision. PentestEval integrates expert-annotated ground truth with a fully automated evaluation pipeline across 346 tasks covering all stages in 12 realistic vulnerable scenarios. Our stage-level evaluation of 9 widely used LLMs reveals generally weak performance and distinct limitations across the stages of penetration-testing workflow. End-to-end pipelines reach only 31% success rate, and existing LLM-powered systems such as PentestGPT, PentestAgent, and VulnBot exhibit similar limitations, with the evaluated autonomous agents showing particularly low success rates under our benchmark settings. These findings highlight that reliable autonomous penetration testing requires stronger structured reasoning and fine-grained stage-level diagnosis. PentestEval provides the foundational benchmark needed for future research on fine-grained, stage-level evaluation, paving the way toward more reliable LLM-based automation.
evidence_items.title: PentestEval: Benchmarking LLM-based Penetration Testing with Modular and Stage-Level Design

evidence_items.summary: Medical Image Quality Assessment (IQA) serves as a critical safety gate for clinical AI, yet existing approaches rely on scalar metrics that fail to capture the descriptive, expert-like evaluation process central to clinical practice. We introduce MedQ-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for language-based medical IQA evaluation with MLLMs, establishing a perception--description paradigm across 5 imaging modalities and over 40 quality attributes. The benchmark comprises two complementary tasks: MedQ-Perception probes low-level visual attribute discrimination via 2,600 expert-annotated perceptual queries; MedQ-Description covers both no-reference and comparison description sub-tasks with 708 expert-annotated samples, evaluated through a four-dimensional judging protocol. Comprehensive evaluation of 23 state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals that current models exhibit only preliminary and unstable capabilities, and highlights the urgent need for targeted optimization of MLLMs in medical IQA. Project & Dataset: https://github.com/liujiyaoFDU/MedQ-Bench
evidence_items.title: Can MLLMs Perceive and Describe Medical Image Quality Beyond Scores?

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.
evidence_items.title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified

evidence_items.summary: Theoretical limitations of transformers on state tracking---the ability to track information about entities or variables over long contexts---have motivated new recurrent language modeling (LM) architectures such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN). These architectures have, in particular, been benchmarked against the $S_5$ word problem, a theoretically hard state-tracking task that captures abilities such as code evaluation under arbitrary variable assignment. It, however, remains open whether other, simpler forms of state tracking might both be more relevant in practice and already explain observed differences between these architectures. We propose evaluating state tracking using a hierarchy of word problems with four increasing levels of difficulty: r-trivial, corresponding to immutable assignment to variables in programming; aperiodic, where assignments are mutable; soluble, where assignments are self-referential; and general finite state tracking. Theoretically, we show that the class of problems transformers are thought to length-generalize on does not even contain all aperiodic state tracking. On the other hand, we prove that GDN with positive eigenvalues expresses all aperiodic problems, and the regular languages recognized by certain transformers are precisely all soluble ones, thus providing a fine-grained picture of state tracking capabilities of various architectures. Taking these ideas to practice, we construct StateBench, a 4-tier long-horizon state-tracking benchmark. Our systematic direct training experiments across architectures largely align with theoretical expectation, albeit with interesting observations at very large scale length-generalization. Additionally, we also evaluate pretrained models---both open hybrid and closed frontier ones---on StateBench, finding that none of them robustly solves even soluble state tracking, suggesting a direction for future improvement.
evidence_items.title: A Fine-Grained Hierarchy and Benchmark for State Tracking in Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Real-world driving requires context-aware decision-making. Existing end-to-end driving benchmarks primarily assess trajectory quality through safety, compliance, comfort, and driving progress, leaving context-dependent decision-making insufficiently characterized. To fill this gap, we present PlanContext, a benchmark for evaluating in-context driving decision-making. PlanContext constructs paired evaluations by varying high-level driving intentions while keeping the observed scene fixed, enabling a natural and controllable assessment of context-dependent decision-making. We further define six representative driving contexts and jointly evaluate contextual decision correctness, road compliance, and dynamic safety with class-balanced metrics. Experiments on 9,561 scene-condition instances from NAVSIM and 23 public end-to-end driving models show that high conventional driving-quality scores do not consistently correspond to strong route-level in-context driving decision-making. Further analysis shows that model behavior varies with decision timing, road structure, and traffic interaction depending on the decision required by the current context. Our results highlight in-context driving decision-making as an important complementary dimension for evaluating end-to-end driving systems.
evidence_items.title: PlanContext: Benchmarking In-Context Driving Decision-Making

evidence_items.summary: This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Despite the remarkable progress, current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory due to inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our TRIO is to equip three well-designed agents with an iterative refinement paradigm by aligning their individual optimization objectives. Specifically, we first expand ambiguous queries with a query extension agent and quantify the reward based on the improved answer quality, which can be utilized to refine our agent for higher expansion efficiency. To enhance the retrieval quality, we include a unanimity voting to annotate the expanded query as insufficient or sufficient, and their generative outcomes are utilized as ground truth to optimize the judge agent. To further improve evidence utilization and answer accuracy, an answer agent is optimized with dynamic matching-based rewards with curriculum learning for final outputs. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed TRIO in comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingtaoren/TRIO.
evidence_items.title: TRIO: Task Refinement with Individual Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

evidence_items.summary: Long-form multi-shot video editing requires an intended edit to remain coherent across abrupt changes in scene, viewpoint, and subject appearance, while processing substantially longer visual context than conventional single-shot editors. We introduce MoviEdit, an end-to-end framework for scalable long-form multi-shot video editing that jointly addresses the challenges of data, modeling, and evaluation. To provide cross-shot supervision data at scale, we develop automatic data-generation pipelines spanning synchronized multi-view footage, real-world multi-shot videos, and generated multi-shot content, yielding 87K paired editing videos without manual annotation. Architecturally, MoviEdit employs a cascaded bidirectional-autoregressive design: a lightweight bidirectional stage first establishes a globally coherent editing draft over a spatiotemporally compressed representation, which is then autoregressively propagated and refined over the full video. We further introduce MoviEdit-Bench, a dedicated benchmark for systematic evaluation of long-form multi-shot video editing. Extensive experiments show that MoviEdit substantially outperforms existing open-source models and performs on par with industry frontier models across text-guided and image-guided editing. Visit our project page for complete results and to access the benchmark: https://multi-shot-edit.github.io/
evidence_items.title: MoviEdit: Long-form Multi-Shot Video Editing Made Easy

evidence_items.summary: An LLM judge assesses agent steps from text packets. A renderer converts recorded runs into these packets, while software checkers test records and packets against requirements. We ask what evidence shows a packet is what the evaluation requires and propose four input-assurance obligations: required content survives rendering, checkers cover their requirements, a failed check stops later use and the judge reads the bytes last checked. In one pipeline with 30 trajectories, matching hashes, passing checkers and successful staging (copying packets for the judge) coexisted with violations of all four obligations, the last two in integration tests. The renderer omitted every structured tool call, leaving 53 of 60 judged steps blank despite matching hashes. For one judge configuration, later context raised error flags by 13 more on error than on correct steps. Restoring every call reduced this contrast to 2, a reduction of 11 (0.37 per trajectory, 95% cluster-bootstrap interval 0.17 to 0.53). In packets ending at the judged step, that configuration abstained at least once on every blank step, while the other four sometimes abstained but also flagged blank error and correct steps. Both separately written checkers accepted an unmatched tool result. In integration tests, a stub replacing the judge read a failed build's packet and a copy changed after staging. Three added controls stopped 18 of 19 constructed fault cases before the stub read any packet. The remaining stale script never ran. We turn the obligations into four tests and plan to evaluate their transfer to independent pipelines.
evidence_items.title: Does the Judge See What the Evaluation Requires? Input Assurance for LLM Agent Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision.
evidence_items.title: PixelBench: Can LLMs Understand and Generate Images Pixel by Pixel?

evidence_items.summary: AI coding agents rely on repository-level instruction files to understand project conventions, development workflows, and constraints. However, different agents support different instruction formats, and limited empirical evidence exists about how these files are adopted, what information they contain, whether coexisting formats provide consistent guidance, and how they are maintained. We conduct an empirical study of 3,387 instruction files from 1,000 GitHub repositories across four formats: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GitHub Copilot instructions, and Cursor rules. We find that 42.2% of instruction-bearing repositories in the higher-popularity cohort maintain multiple formats. Among 386 manually examined pairs of corresponding sections, 16.1% provide divergent guidance. Our maintenance analysis further shows that 40.4% of the analyzed files have only one recorded modification event and that maintenance patterns differ across formats. Based on category prevalence and category addition ratios (CAR), we derive an evidence-based template containing ten Required, four Gap, and two Recommended categories. In an exploratory generation experiment, explicit template guidance increases structural category coverage from 18.7% to 82.8%. We further introduce AGIT-Instruct, a benchmark for evaluating instruction-file generation through structural coverage and content alignment. Across four generation configurations, retrieval-augmented generation achieves the highest full-file ROUGE-1 F1 of 0.459. A manual assessment of 278 generated category instances finds that 19.4% fully preserve and 61.2% partially preserve developer-written intent. Our findings provide empirical guidance for organizing and maintaining agent instruction
evidence_items.title: Toward an Evidence-Based Template for Agent Instruction Files: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Consistency, and Maintenance

evidence_items.summary: Social-media comments are interactions, yet they are often translated and evaluated as isolated text. This mismatch is especially problematic when meaning depends on surrounding discussion, community-specific slang, or culturally situated expressions. We introduce CULTURE-CMT, a Chinese-English benchmark for contextualized social-media comment translation that restores the post and conversational context naturally available to users. Its 572 manually verified examples are organized into Slang, Context, and Both, enabling diagnostic analysis of distinct and interacting sources of translation difficulty. To support scalable evaluation, we further develop a retrieval-augmented cultural-effectiveness Judger that combines a calibrated scoring model with dynamically retrieved cultural knowledge. CULTURE-CMT reveals several non-trivial patterns. Providing interaction context improves most model configurations, but does not eliminate culturally ineffective translations. Examples requiring both contextual grounding and culturally situated language remain substantially more difficult than either source of difficulty alone. Moreover, larger models are not consistently better, and thinking produces highly model-dependent gains, including occasional degradation. In contrast, a 27B model adapted on benchmark-disjoint social-media data achieves the lowest observed invalidity rate among the evaluated configurations under thinking inference with context. Together, these results suggest that realistic social-media translation is not simply a matter of scaling models or reasoning longer, but of learning to translate meaning as it is constructed within evolving online interactions.
evidence_items.title: CULTURE-CMT: Benchmarking Contextualized Social Media Translation

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement-learning (RL) benchmarks built on microscopic traffic simulators such as SUMO are increasingly used to compare agent architectures for electric vehicle (EV) charging assignment. Unlike crashes, defects in the reward function, the environment's stochastic model, or the state encoding often fail silently: the simulation completes, produces plausible numbers, and the comparison is biased. We report five such defects, found by auditing a five-agent benchmark on OpenStreetMap road networks, stated generically: a shared random generator that desynchronises seed-paired comparisons, an ablation-specific reward clip applied unconditionally, a normalisation mismatch that zeroes a reward term, a per-timestep penalty that should fire once per event, and a state dimensionality documented but never wired into the network. We quantify three: a rejection counter inflated up to 125x across agents/cities, a reward term bounded at about $10^{-4}$ of its intended scale, and a 16.6%/16.3% greedy-action divergence from a state-encoding mismatch. Re-analysing a historical ablation, no A1-A2 effect survives family-wise correction; a 56-run campaign confirms the RNG defect's mechanism directly while showing its correction does not change that conclusion. We provide an eight-item checklist as a low-cost first-pass audit; in a later regeneration, three checks caught two new defects while three further process/artefact defects fell outside its boundary.
evidence_items.title: Silent Reward and Environment Defects in EV Charging Simulation Benchmarks: A Diagnostic Checklist

evidence_items.summary: Recently, speech-driven facial and oral animation technologies have been used in various fields such as education, speech therapy, and healthcare. But methods to objectively evaluate the quality of generated results are still limited. Accordingly, we propose the Fr\'echet Oral Distance (FOD), which uses embeddings from an Oral Motion Encoder (OME) and a TIMIT-Vis reference distribution. In experiments, FOD reproduced model rankings similar to the coordinate-based metric, Lip Vertex Error (LVE), and showed trends consistent with user preference. Our framework provides objective and reproducible benchmarking without relying on expensive equipment or subjective evaluation, and it can be extended to compare a variety of 2D/3D models.
evidence_items.title: Fr\'echet Oral Distance: A Coordinate-Free Metric and Benchmark for Speech-Driven Oral Animation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external skill libraries to support complex task execution. However, determining which skills are needed remains challenging in long-horizon tasks. Existing methods typically select a fixed skill set before execution, implicitly assuming that a task's procedural requirements can be determined from its initial description. This assumption is restrictive for long-horizon interaction, where new requirements emerge from intermediate observations, execution outcomes, and newly revealed constraints. This motivates just-in-time skill retrieval, which dynamically selects skills as execution unfolds. Just-in-time skill retrieval is promising but challenging: the utility of a skill depends not only on the current context, but also on the evolving task state shaped by prior steps. To this end, we propose JitSkill, a state-grounded framework that addresses this challenge through continuous task-state tracking. By connecting emerging requirements with accumulated task progress, JitSkill provides procedural support throughout execution without treating each retrieval decision independently. Experiments across three agent benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness in improving long-horizon task completion. Our code is available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/JitSkill.git/.
evidence_items.title: Just-in-Time Skill Retrieval via Long-Horizon State Tracking

evidence_items.summary: Anticipating financial outcomes requires synthesizing evolving evidence and reasoning under uncertainty, making deep research systems promising tools for forecasting. Yet evaluating forecasting ability is challenging because historical backtests may reward memorized outcomes or information retrieved after the forecast date. Live forecasting avoids direct access to realized outcomes, but feedback arrives only after events resolve. To obtain timely feedback and assess historical scores, we introduce FinForesight, a diagnostic backtesting benchmark for financial deep research systems. Across the Chinese, U.S., and Hong Kong markets, the benchmark evaluates four forecasting tasks: valuation, return ranking, event direction, and future financial fundamentals. Two capability diagnostic tasks assess counterfactual reasoning and financial calculation, scored separately from forecasting performance. Our harness-compatible framework restricts retrieved evidence to information available at the forecast date. We compare pretraining-era, resolved post-cutoff, and live evaluations to test whether controlled backtests approximate future performance. Pretraining-era scores exceed post-cutoff scores in most temporal comparisons, and stronger retrieval controls narrow the gap between post-cutoff backtests and live results. Forecasting attribution and robustness analyses reveal how scores respond to retrieval policy and how predictions respond to prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations. The code and benchmark data are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: FinForesight: A Diagnostic Backtesting Benchmark for Deep Research Systems in Financial Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Harness engineering and self-evolving agents improve language-model agents quickly, yet their gains live outside the model. The harness is re-sent and re-paid on every call, and the standard route to internalization is a weight update that is costly to iterate and fixed once merged. We propose compiling the harness instead. Latent Harness distills an external condition into a rank-8 activation shift. The shift is applied at the output of every decoder block of a frozen backbone, at 0.03-0.05% of parameters. The condition is either an explicit process-level behavior instruction or the behavioral contract of an agentic harness. At inference the compiled bundle carries no harness text and adds no tokens. It exposes three runtime controls for injection strength, injection phase, and shift-space mixing. Compiled behaviors recover the source-harness gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings. Where the explicit source pays the heaviest per-call token tax, the compiled form exceeds it. The same bundles transfer zero-shot across tasks (5 of 7 pairs positive) and compose in shift space, while stacked text instructions interfere destructively. Used as a search space, they lift budget-matched harness search by 1.45 times. On three agentic benchmarks the operator aligns policy to the harness con- tract. Under matched data, capacity, and effective strength it outperforms same-capacity LoRA, which needs 11.1 times the parameters to reach the same band, and it regresses nothing where the base policy is already strong. Across 1B-to-8B models the method skeleton is invariant while gain locations move with the model-task pair, which delimits where compiled harnesses should be deployed.
evidence_items.title: Latent Harness: Compiling Agent Behaviors into Post-Block Activation Shifts

evidence_items.summary: Cloud-based software systems frequently release new versions, a fact further accelerated through agentic coding. Each new release, however, brings the risk of performance regressions which can irritate end users, increase infrastructure costs, and increase carbon footprints. Therefore, developers strive to catch such regressions in testing stages, usually through so-called continuous benchmarking. The standard way of doing this is using microbenchmark suites which, however, take notoriously long to execute. Optimizing the execution of microbenchmark suites is, hence, an active field of research. In this paper, we propose AdapBench, an online scheduling system for reducing the execution duration of microbenchmark suites. AdapBench is the first approach which dynamically makes at-runtime decisions for prioritizing the most informative benchmarks and early-stopping each one once enough evidence has accumulated to accept or reject a performance change hypothesis. We evaluate our prototype on eight popular Java projects, commonly used by microbenchmark research, and four additional Go projects. At matched 90% change detections and false-positive rate compared to an optimistic uniform run, AdapBench saves 42% of the aggregate execution duration on the Java projects, with negligible scheduling overhead (below 0.001% of the total runtime). On the Go projects, AdapBench finds every performance change with zero false positives while saving 85% of the full run.
evidence_items.title: AdapBench: Adaptive Early-Stopping and Prioritization for Efficient Microbenchmarking in Cloud-based CI/CD

evidence_items.summary: Semantic IDs (SIDs) have emerged as a promising approach for discriminative recommendation by encoding continuous item rep- resentations into compact discrete identifiers. However, existing SID-based methods face two fundamental limitations: semantic mis- match between content semantics and collaborative preferences, and objective mismatch between SID construction and downstream recommendation optimization. To address these challenges, we propose SIDRec, an end-to-end recommendation-aware SID learn- ing framework that jointly models content and collaborative in- formation while aligning SID construction with recommendation objectives. Specifically, SIDRec introduces a self-updating fusion mechanism that explicitly integrates pretrained content represen- tations with collaborative embeddings initialized from a trained recommendation model, enabling preference-aware semantic mod- eling. Furthermore, SIDRec employs an MMoE-inspired joint opti- mization mechanism with shared experts and task-specific gates, allowing recommendation supervision to directly guide differen- tiable quantization and produce task-adaptive discrete representa- tions. Extensive experiments on three public benchmark datasets demonstrate that SIDRec consistently outperforms all competing methods across both AUC and GAUC, achieving up to 5.15% relative improvements over the strongest baselines. Further ablation stud- ies validate the effectiveness and complementarity of collaborative semantic modeling and end-to-end SID optimization.
evidence_items.title: SIDRec: End-to-End Semantic ID Representation and Modeling for Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Transient thermal fields during solidification connect casting process conditions and cooling behaviour to the formation of defect-prone regions in aluminum cast ings. Repeatedly solving this thermal problem across geometries and process conditions is computationally expensive, motivating data-driven surrogate models. However, existing machine-learning studies on casting thermal behaviour rely on study-specific simulation databases that do not support reproducible geometry-level benchmarking. We introduce LM6-CastBench, an open simulation dataset for geometry-aware learning of transient thermal fields in LM6 aluminum sand casting, combining three geometry families, ten variants per family, five pouring tempera tures, and three mould temperatures (450 geometry-process cases in total). Each case retains CAD geometry, unstructured mesh connectivity, spatial descriptors, process metadata, and time-resolved nodal temperatures. We benchmark a point wise MLP against a spatially structured U-Net under geometry-level data splits; the U-Net reduces temperature-field errors by a large margin, with the biggest gains on geometries with localized features and abrupt section changes. LM6-CastBench gives researchers a reproducible dataset and benchmark for geometry-aware surro gate modelling of casting thermal behaviour.
evidence_items.title: LM6-CastBench: A Geometry-Aware Simulation Dataset for Transient Thermal Prediction in LM6 Sand Casting

evidence_items.summary: Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents \emph{X-World~1.6}, advancing X-World~1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.
evidence_items.title: X-World 1.6: Building Controllable Virtual Cities with World Models

evidence_items.summary: AI agents write and execute code, manipulate user interfaces, and transact on their users' behalf. We ask what forms failure takes in human-agent interaction, and how those forms change as agents act with greater autonomy. From 695 documented incidents in two public repositories, we developed 12 failure modes bottom-up within three interaction stages adapted from Amershi et al.'s guidelines, coding the autonomy at which each arose. What a person can do when an agent fails depends on how much the agent completes between points of user involvement--a property fixed at deployment. Therefore, the same model on the same task can fail differently under different configurations. All 12 modes appear at both low and high autonomy, and rising autonomy changes the form each failure takes. Users need controls between full delegation and full manual work, and neither incident records nor agent benchmarks reach the interaction where these failures occur.
evidence_items.title: When AI Agents Act on Our Behalf: A Taxonomy of Human-Agent Interaction Failure

evidence_items.summary: Medical imaging has served as primary proving ground for clinical AI, yet a decade of intense research has not translated into proportionate bedside impact. We argue that this gap is not primarily a product of insufficient algorithmic performance, inadequate regulation, or limited explainability. Rather, it reflects a structural misalignment, between how AI systems are designed and evaluated, and how clinical decisions are made. This work identifies 8 interconnected dimensions of this misalignment: 1) the dominance of pixel-only models in a multimodal clinical world; 2) the erosion of physician trust through opaque and inflexible systems; 3) the unfulfilled promise of foundation models in data-sparse medical domains; 4) the persistent bottleneck of non-shareable under-curated datasets; 5) the gap between validated algorithms and deployable clinical platforms; 6) the slow, unmonitored translation of evidence into routine practice; 7) the risk of AI displacing rather than extending physician judgment; and 8) the failure of prediction-centric AI to generate actionable, agentic clinical guidance. For each dimension, we reframe the problem and propose a path forward, culminating in a vision of physician-centered AI solutions with agentic reasoning that extend, rather than replace, clinical judgment.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking AI in Medical Imaging: Assumptions, Reality, and Reframing; Towards Physician-Centered Agentic Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Agentic systems have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for automated theorem proving in formal mathematics. To assess how far these capabilities extend to program verification and how reliably existing benchmarks can measure them, we audit CLEVER, a Lean 4 benchmark for verifiable code generation, using three independent agentic stacks based on Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, and Kimi K2.5. Our audit finds arguably erroneous reference specifications in 80 of 161 entries, each accepted by the benchmark's authors, distills a taxonomy of benchmark errors, and exposes structural limitations of isomorphism-based scoring, whose signal breaks down when generated and reference specifications formalize different yet defensible readings. In the process, the stacks generate arguably valid specifications for up to 98.8% of entries, certify implementations against sound reference specifications for up to 92.3%, and reach up to 96.2% end-to-end success over entries with sound premises, suggesting that CLEVER no longer stresses modern agentic provers as much as its design intended. Looking ahead, we translate our findings into recommendations for future work, with our error analysis doubling as a repair list for CLEVER and a heuristic checklist for the next generation of benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Isomorphism Is Not Enough: An Agentic Audit of Verified Code Generation in Lean

evidence_items.summary: Split Federated Learning (SFL) enables privacy-preserving collaborative training by partitioning models between clients and a server. However, under non-IID data distributions, SFL often suffers from biased optimization and unstable convergence, while existing solutions largely adapt techniques from conventional federated learning. In this work, we observe that the split architecture of SFL inherently alters how client information is represented and coordinated, opening opportunities for bias compensation beyond parameter-level aggregation. Based on this insight, we propose BESplit, an architecture-aware framework that exploits the intrinsic structure of SFL to mitigate non-IID effects. First, to prevent biased local data from dominating global updates, we introduce Evidential Aggregation (EA) to perform fine-grained reweighting of client contributions based on evidential uncertainty. Second, to further reduce distributional skew, we develop Bias-Compensated Collaboration (BCC) to align split-layer representations by pairing complementary clients. Finally, Dual-Teacher Distillation (DTD) is incorporated to synchronize knowledge between decoupled client and server models, enabling independent local inference. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that BESplit consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, convergence stability, and computational efficiency under diverse non-IID settings.
evidence_items.title: BESplit: Bias-Compensated Split Federated Learning with Evidential Aggregation

evidence_items.summary: Chirality is a fundamental molecular property that governs stereospecific behavior in chemistry and biology. Capturing chirality in machine learning models remains challenging due to the geometric complexity of stereochemical relationships and the limitations of traditional molecular representations that often lack explicit stereochemical encoding. Existing approaches to chiral molecular representation primarily focus on central chirality, relying on handcrafted stereochemical tags or limited 3D encodings, and thus fail to generalize to more complex forms such as axial chirality. In this work, we introduce ChiDeK (Chiral Determinant Kernels), a framework that systematically integrates stereogenic information into molecular representation learning. We propose the chiral determinant kernel to encode the SE(3)-invariant chirality product and employ cross-attention to integrate stereochemical information from local chiral centers into the global molecular representation. This design enables explicit modeling of chiral-related features within a unified architecture, capable of jointly encoding central and axial chirality. To support the evaluation of axial chirality, we construct a new benchmark for electronic circular dichroism (ECD) and optical rotation (OR) prediction. Across four tasks, including R/S configuration classification, enantiomer ranking, ECD spectrum prediction, and OR prediction, ChiDeK achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, most notably yielding over 7% higher accuracy on axially chiral tasks on average.
evidence_items.title: Learning Molecular Chirality via Chiral Determinant Kernels

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides a benchmark resource for AI-rewritten Bengali text detection. It contains 4,008 labeled Bengali text samples, comprising 2,004 original human-written texts and 2,004 corresponding AI-rewritten texts. The human-written texts were collected from authentic Bengali sources, including National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB) textbooks, Bengali literary works available through Wikisource, and Bengali Wikinews articles published before 2020. Each original text was rewritten using one of four widely used large language models, namely ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or DeepSeek, through a standardized prompt designed to preserve the original semantic meaning, writing style, and approximate text length. Each human-written text is paired with its corresponding AI-rewritten version through a unique Pair ID, enabling direct comparison between original and rewritten texts. The dataset includes metadata such as the text source or rewriting model, content category, word count, and class label. It covers multiple domains, including Education, Bengali Literature, and News, and is intended to support research on AI-rewritten text detection, stylometric analysis, authorship attribution, paraphrase identification, and other Bengali natural language processing tasks.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark Dataset for Human Vs. AI-Rewritten Bengali Text Detection

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains records from the local language-model data collection used in Multi-Source Prior Pooling for Recorded Hard-Drive Failures: An Evaluation of Local Language Models. The study evaluates whether elicited prior distributions improve predictions of recorded hard-drive failure counts beyond a historical covariate model using Backblaze Drive Stats. The collection covers six models accessed through LM Studio: Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b, Mistral Small 3.2, Gemma 3 27B, Phi-4, and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct. It comprises 73,800 planned response slots across 20 development cohorts and 21 evaluation cohorts, with ten batches of 30 responses per model and cohort. The repository includes: protocol.json: The recorded collection protocol and request configuration. responses.jsonl: The exported response records, stored as one JSON object per line. seed manifest.json: The request-to-seed assignments used to organize generation and response retries. summary.json: The collection summary, including completion counts, response-validation results, retries, and comparator fallbacks. These files document the collection underlying the reported analyses. They should be interpreted alongside the manuscript’s definitions of response validity, numerical fitting, and fallback handling. Model identifiers and random seeds alone do not guarantee identical outputs across inference environments. Reproducing the complete analysis also requires the cohort data, historical priors, analysis code, and relevant software configuration.

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents compact long histories to fit their context windows, but the compacted context must still carry the operating rules that govern later actions. Prior work shows that violations rise after compaction, but measures compliance outside a complete agent harness and does not identify where each violation comes from. We introduce ARCBench(Agent Rule Compliance Benchmark), a configurable benchmark built on the open-source pi agent harness. Its tool-calling agent loop lets us measure rule compliance from actions taken during execution, bringing the evaluation closer to deployed agent workflows. Using ARCBench, we examine where violations after compaction come from, and how different compaction configurations and adversarial settings change their sources. We find that compaction rarely deletes the rule: most violations after compaction occur while the rule is still in the compacted history, with the agent treating a later request as permission, ignoring the rule, and proceeding anyway. Where violations come from depends on the configuration: how the rule is delivered decides whether the agent would break it even without compaction, while the compaction strategy and budget decide whether the rule survives. The strongest compactor-targeted attack more than doubles violations by corrupting the rule in the summary and changing how the agents behave, whereas the strongest defense restores the rule in most summary but still violates. Finally, retaining a rule does not guarantee compliance: compacted runs that retain the rule violate more than twice as often as runs with the full history.
evidence_items.title: Do Agents Still Follow the Rules? Benchmarking Rule Compliance under Agent Context Compaction

evidence_items.summary: Preprint — critical narrative review; not peer reviewed. Machine learning studies report strong performance on fraudulent job advertisements, but benchmark scores alone provide limited evidence of reliable recruitment screening. This critical narrative review examines 13 purposively selected empirical studies published between 2017 and 2026, alongside dataset documentation and methodological literature. Ten core studies have explicitly identified ancestry in the Employment Scam Aegean Dataset; corpus cleaning, translation, and renaming therefore require provenance checks before being interpreted as independent validation. Reported results also differ in test populations, resampling boundaries, and metric averaging. A within-study resampling comparison illustrates how protocol changes alter the interpretation of accuracy, while recent cascades show that threshold adjustment and routing errors must be separated from the contribution of a second model. Contextual and human-input approaches broaden the available evidence, but subjective trust and predictive accuracy answer different questions. The review provides a study-level protocol audit and a reporting framework covering split independence, fraud-class performance, calibration, explanations, and operational outcomes. Priorities include independently collected multilingual advertisements, threshold-matched comparisons, and prospective assessment of human decisions. The resulting synthesis supports more informative evaluation rather than a ranking of architectures across incompatible experiments. Supporting materials: study-level evidence ledger, protocol audit, reference-verification record, search and evidence log, and LaTeX manuscript source. The core evidence includes 10 full-text appraisals and 3 appraisals limited to abstracts and publication records. AI assistance disclosure: This review develops an earlier university-project manuscript supplied by the author.
evidence_items.title: Learning to Detect Recruitment Fraud: A Critical Review of Dataset Lineage, Evaluation, and Decision Support
