evidence_items.summary: STARLI | F091–F100 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume I · Collective Microrobotic Autonomy, Swarm Safety and Mission Continuity Author: 33 | Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.3 | English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume collection closes the first hundred of the STARLI 300-theme research-design atlas. Research Unit I (F091–F095) examines autonomous sampling, local-to-global coordination, pheromone-like signaling, collision avoidance and collective energy allocation. Research Unit II (F096–F100) examines distributed planning, localization uncertainty, changing network topology, fault isolation and safe mission handoff. Each volume states prospective physical tests rather than completed experimental findings. The ten English working editions total 7,770 PDF pages: 300 candidate mathematical plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The v1.3 Gate-annotation pass contrasts mechanisms, physical witnesses, blinded falsifiers, rivals, stopping boundaries and successor interfaces. These editorial counts and text-screening results do not establish causal independence or scientific validation. The Ten Research Directions F091 Nanorobotic Collective Autonomy Sampling At The Limit — Proposes controlled tests of swarm sampling throughput and identity preservation. A concealed communication partition probes whether completion gains survive the loss of collective coordination, against a centralized full-state controller; collision events and consensus error remain explicit vetoes. F092 Microrobotic Local Collaboration And Global Mission At The Limit — Asks whether agent-to-agent collaboration improves global agreement when robots lack an unmetered global-state feed. Hidden adversarial-neighbor states test dependence on outside tracking; fixed behavior rules with matched energy provide the comparator.
evidence_items.title: STARLI | F091–F100 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume I · Collective Microrobotic Autonomy, Swarm Safety and Mission Continuity Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.3  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume collection closes the first hundred of the STARLI 300-theme research-design atlas. Research Unit I (F091–F095) examines autonomous sampling, local-to-global coordination, pheromone-like signaling, collision avoidance and collective energy allocation. Research Unit II (F096–F100) examines distributed planning, localization uncertainty, changing network topology, fault isolation and safe mission handoff. Each volume states prospective physical tests rather than completed experimental findings. The ten English working editions total 7,770 PDF pages: 300 candidate mathematical plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The v1.3 Gate-annotation pass contrasts mechanisms, physical witnesses, blinded falsifiers, rivals, stopping boundaries and successor interfaces. These editorial counts and text-screening results do not establish causal independence or scientific validation. The Ten Research Directions F091  Nanorobotic Collective Autonomy Sampling At The Limit — Proposes controlled tests of swarm sampling throughput and identity preservation. A concealed communication partition probes whether completion gains survive the loss of collective coordination, against a centralized full-state controller; collision events and consensus error remain explicit vetoes. F092  Microrobotic Local Collaboration And Global Mission At The Limit — Asks whether agent-to-agent collaboration improves global agreement when robots lack an unmetered global-state feed. Hidden adversarial-neighbor states test dependence on outside tracking; fixed behavior rules with matched energy provide the comparator. F093  Nanorobotic Collective Pheromone Communication At The Limit — Explores prospective chemical-trail or signal-mediated coordination with collision exposure as a primary outcome. Hidden actuator saturation and a matched-actuation single-agent baseline challenge claims that signaling, rather than redundancy or imposed motion, caused the improvement. F094  Microscale Robot Collective Collision Avoidance Control At The Limit — Examines collision-safe motion while monitoring spatial coverage, recovery time and communication burden. A blinded shared-localization bias tests whether apparent avoidance depends on erroneous common position estimates; safety-boundary crossings trigger rejection. F095  Nanorobotic Collective Energy Allocation At The Limit — Tests dynamic allocation of limited energy across agents during dropout and recovery. Hidden agent-loss clusters challenge energy accounting and recovery-time claims against fixed rules with an equal energy budget; persistent unsafe confidence is a stop condition. F096  Microrobotic Distributed Mission Planning At The Limit — Studies task planning without a central controller using communication load, work-per-task and selective abstention as prospective metrics. Hidden network partitions expose plans that depend on unavailable messages, while a matched-actuation single-agent system tests whether coordination adds value. F097  Nanorobotic Collective Localization Uncertainty At The Limit — Tests whether robots can act safely when position confidence is uncertain or neighbors provide deceptive state information. Energy per accepted task, abstention and completion are checked against a full-state centralized benchmark; unrecognized safety-boundary crossings invalidate the claim. F098  Microrobotic Collective Dynamic Topology Control At The Limit — Examines when changing neighbor connections should trigger reconfiguration or justified refusal to proceed. Hidden actuator saturation challenges topology decisions; fixed energy-matched rules and independent task and consensus measurements distinguish adaptive control from misleading internal agreement. F099  Nanorobotic Collective Fault Isolation At The Limit — Investigates recognition and containment of malfunctioning agents without allowing errors to propagate across the swarm. A blinded shared-localization bias tests whether fault labels confuse a common sensor defect with separate robot failures; recovery to a known-safe state is mandatory. F100  Microrobotic Collective Mission Handoff At The Limit — Designs a traceable transfer of task state and authority across agents after concealed dropout clusters. The study checks consensus error, collisions and coverage against centralized full-state control; an apparently successful handoff is rejected if safety invariants are violated. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries All ten volumes are prospective, nonclinical research-design working editions for traceable materials, authorized ex-vivo systems, synthetic phantoms and bench-scale microfluidic tests. Proposed comparisons require preregistered budgets, blinded perturbations, independent reference measurements, complete negative-trial denominators and explicit safety stops. No new experimental results, validated in-body autonomy or clinical benefit are claimed. Mathematical derivations, physical unit consistency, claim-level DOI linkage and substantive causal novelty still require specialist review; the automatic Gate-text distinctness audit cannot replace it. They are reference points for existing methods, not evidence that any STARLI-specific candidate device or proposed experimental advantage has been demonstrated. Independent source-to-claim verification remains necessary. evidence_items.summary: Study-level extraction of evaluation indicators, implementation weaknesses, and mitigation strategies from 128 health policy implementation studies published between 2015 and 2025. This dataset underpins a critical interpretive synthesis of health policy implementation research. For each of the 128 included studies it records the bibliographic details, the country of study and its World Bank income group (FY2024), the evaluation indicators reported and the dimensions they address (efficiency, equity, sustainability), the implementation weakness reported and its category (structural, institutional, or operational), flags for the co-occurrence of weakness types, and the mitigation strategy categories reported. Contents Sheet "128 studies" - the study-level extraction. Every analytical column was verified study by study against the source record, and a category was assigned only where the study itself reported it. Method Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed were searched for studies published between 2015 and 2025. Of 941 records screened, 128 were purposively sampled for interpretive analysis. Sampling was purposive rather than exhaustive, in line with the critical interpretive synthesis approach: the counts describe this body of evidence and do not estimate prevalence in the wider literature. No formal critical appraisal of methodological quality was undertaken.

evidence_items.summary: This repository provides reproducibility and audit evidence accompanying the study "Incremental Value of Changed-Code Context for Regression Test Prioritization in Continuous Integration: A Frozen-Protocol Empirical Study." The study investigates the incremental contribution of production-code change context to regression test prioritization across four open-source Java projects: Deeplearning4j, OkHttp, Graylog, and SonarQube. The evaluated change-context representation combines five CodeBERT-based similarity features with two change-availability features. The research archive documents selected preserved results from the original frozen R0/R3/R4 evaluations, post-freeze conventional-baseline comparisons, chronology sensitivity analyses, provenance audits, integrity manifests, and statistical verification procedures. The original frozen results are distinguished from subsequent exploratory and corrective analyses. The archived evidence supports verification of selected reported results and methodological decisions. It does not constitute a complete, independent end-to-end reproduction of the original experiment. Reconstructed models must not be interpreted as the original frozen model weights. Git commit timestamps and historical CI trigger timestamps are not independently verified test-result availability times. Accordingly, the chronology audits do not establish operationally leakage-free prioritization. The underlying public benchmark is RTPTorrent Version 1.1 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.4046180). This repository is intended to provide supporting research evidence for the associated manuscript. The precise scope of the deposited materials is determined by the included files and their accompanying documentation.

evidence_items.summary: Effective retrieval-augmented generation across bilingual Greek–English applications requires embedding models capable of capturing both domain-specific semantic relationships and cross-lingual semantic alignment. Existing multilingual embedding models distribute their representational capacity across numerous languages, limiting their optimization for Greek and failing to encode the morphological complexity and domain-specific terminological structures inherent in Greek text. In this work, we propose ORPHEAS, a specialized Greek–English embedding model for bilingual retrieval-augmented generation. ORPHEAS is trained with a high quality dataset generated by a knowledge graph-based fine-tuning methodology which is applied to a diverse multi-domain corpus, which enables language-agnostic semantic representations. The numerical experiments across monolingual and cross-lingual retrieval benchmarks reveal that ORPHEAS outperforms state-of-the-art multilingual embedding models, demonstrating that domain-specialized fine-tuning on morphologically complex languages does not compromise cross-lingual retrieval capability.
evidence_items.title: ORPHEAS: A Cross-Lingual Greek-English Embedding Model for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

evidence_items.summary: The performance of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems is heavily dependent on the quality of embedding models, which serve as the interface between knowledge repositories and generative models. Current fine-tuning approaches for embedding models rely predominantly on synthetic data generation and simple contrastive learning frameworks, which often lack semantic depth and fail to capture complex domain-specific relationships, particularly in morphologically rich languages such as Greek and in specialized domains such as legal text processing. In this paper, we introduce KG-Tune, a knowledge graph-driven fine-tuning methodology, which is specifically tailored for RAG applications. KG-Tune addresses the limitations of existing methodologies by leveraging structured knowledge extraction through a systematic two-phase training framework that incorporates (i) systematic extraction of entities, relationships and atomic facts from domainspecific knowledge graphs to generate semantically grounded training instances, and (ii) hard negative mining to enhance discriminative capabilities. Experimental evaluation on four heterogeneous Greek datasets demonstrates that the proposed methodology achieves considerable improvements, with top-3 accuracy gains ranging from 5.4% to 18.0% and an average performance improvement of 11.1% compared to traditional fine-tuning approaches. An ablation study further confirms the significance of these improvements.
evidence_items.title: KG-Tune: Improving embedding models for domain-specific RAG via knowledge graph-driven fine-tuning

evidence_items.summary: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness for constructing machine-checked proofs for real-world system specifications in TLA+ with agentic AI. Proving correctness of complex system specifications requires discovering inductive invariants, reasoning about intricate state transitions, and decomposing proofs into tractable obligations. TLAPS-Bench provides a proof harness that supports iterative proof development atop the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS), where agents are equipped with proof tools and libraries, with safeguards against reward hacking. Using the harness, we have employed AI agents to prove desired properties for important system specifications that were not proved before, spanning cache coherence, Byzantine consensus, and write-ahead logs. TLAPS-Bench contains 265 proof targets (each encodes a property to prove) from 95 TLA+ specifications of real-world systems. We evaluated frontier AI agents, represented by Codex with GPT models, on a subset of 70 proof targets across 12 specifications. The highest-scoring model, GPT-6.1 Sol (max), proved 31 (44.3%) proof targets. The results show challenges and opportunities in end-to-end proof development.
evidence_items.title: TLAPS-Bench: Formally Proving Correctness of Real-World System Specifications with TLA+ Proof System

evidence_items.summary: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.
evidence_items.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory

evidence_items.summary: Reaction data underpin machine learning for reaction prediction, condition recommendation, and retrosynthetic planning, yet extracting these data from literature figures still requires substantial manual effort. Many figures encode multiple experiments through shared templates, substituent tables, and product grids. Recovering concrete reaction records therefore requires molecular recognition, association of evidence with individual experimental entries, and reconstruction of indirectly specified participants. We present RxnMiner, a multimodal agent system that combines an expert-informed extraction procedure with a chemistry toolbox to coordinate these operations. The agent reads molecular structures, resolves shared and entry-specific evidence, and instantiates participants from templates to assemble source-linked reaction records. We also introduce ChemRxn-Bench, a benchmark of 603 reaction figures with 8,547 manually annotated and reviewed reaction records, evaluated under a common protocol for exact molecular identity and reactant-product pairing. On this benchmark, with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as the backbone, RxnMiner raises stereochemistry-aware reaction macro-F1 from 21.0% under direct prediction to 71.0%, compared with 25.0% for the strongest existing extraction system. Across five backbones, it also outperforms the same base agent without the extraction procedure and chemistry toolbox by 9.4 to 25.5 points. Applied without human intervention to 10,107 literature figures, RxnMiner produces a silver corpus of 88,202 source-linked reaction records.
evidence_items.title: RxnMiner: A Multimodal Agent for Structured Reaction Data Extraction from Chemistry Figures

evidence_items.summary: Code and cached agent answers for the paper "Where Is the Truth When AI Agents Disagree? Dependence-Aware Belief Propagation for Unsupervised Truth Discovery" by Laure Berti-Equille, accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (IEEE BigData 2026) as a short paper. LLM agents often give conflicting answers, and many deployed agents are variants of one base model, so their errors are correlated. BP-TD infers the true answers and each agent's reliability without labels, using mean-field variational inference on a one-coin Dawid–Skene model with per-agent decorrelation weights, derived from base-model provenance or from answer co-occurrence, so that agents sharing a base model count together as about one vote. The archive contains the BP-TD implementation, all baselines (majority vote, Dawid–Skene, LTM, TruthFinder, Investment, Sums, CRH, CATD, SSTF-IV/VI, ClusterVote, ACCU, DEPEN, correlation fusion, a mean-field Ising aggregator, and adapters for CARE, ISP and OW-I), the experiment scripts, the cached answers of 13 local LLM agents on MMLU, SciQ, TruthfulQA, ARC-Challenge and BoolQ (plus 5,000- and 10,000-question MMLU harvests), and the result CSVs behind every number in the paper. Every number recomputes on a CPU from the bundled answers, with no model queries. CARE is fetched separately by a script because its repository has no licence. Only derived agent answers and gold labels are redistributed, not the benchmark texts; they keep the licence of their source benchmark. Version 2.0.0 is the camera-ready release. Compared with v1.1.0 it adds the experiments of the final paper (label-free threshold selection, one-pass weighted vote, sub-pool and strong-bloc analyses, label budget, comparisons with CARE, ISP and OW-I, reliability over 40 test splits, full 5,000- and 10,000-question MMLU runs) and the ARC answers. It also loads all cached questions by default (previously 500) and breaks ties at random when selecting the best agent.
evidence_items.title: BP-TD: code and cached data for "Where Is the Truth When AI Agents Disagree? Dependence-Aware Belief Propagation for Unsupervised Truth Discovery" (IEEE BigData 2026)

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) extends conventional predictive and generative AI by enabling systems to pursue goals through reasoning, planning, information retrieval, memory, tool use, and interaction with clinical workflows. These capabilities create new opportunities for medicine but also a distinct evaluation problem: the reliability of an agent cannot be inferred from the accuracy of its underlying model or final answer alone. Errors may arise during information retrieval, tool use, state updates, inter-agent communication, or autonomous action and may propagate across a clinical workflow. This critical review examines approaches for evaluating and clinically validating agentic AI in medicine. Existing frameworks, including TRIPOD+AI, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, DECIDE-AI, STARD-AI, FUTURE-AI, and Good Machine Learning Practice, provide important foundations but were not primarily designed for systems with persistent state, repeated actions, tool use, and multi-agent interaction. Emerging agent benchmarks increasingly address interactive tasks, tool use, trajectory reliability, and adversarial testing. We propose a five-level evaluation framework spanning model, agent, trajectory, system, and clinical outcome, together with a clinical validation ladder progressing from component testing and simulation to retrospective evaluation, prospective silent deployment, supervised clinical use, bounded action, and post-deployment surveillance. Key gaps include standardized trajectory metrics, evaluation of correlated multi-agent errors, autonomy-aware validation, human–agent performance, and lifecycle monitoring. Radiotherapy is used as a high-stakes clinical exemplar. We argue that agentic AI should be evaluated as a dynamic sociotechnical system and that clinical evidence must extend beyond accuracy toward behavioral reliability, safety, and demonstrated clinical benefit.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Critical Review of Evaluation, Clinical Validation, and Safety Frameworks for Agentic AI in Medicine

evidence_items.summary: Producing an executable CAD script is not sufficient to establish that an agent has satisfied an engineering design request. Evaluation must also consider the resulting geometry, specified dimensions, and native CAD modeling history. We present Parametric CAD Bench v3, a 100-task benchmark comprising 30 text-to-CAD creation tasks, 30 text-to-CAD create-and-edit tasks, and 40 tasks that reconstruct mechanical parts from engineering drawings. Agents operate in a pinned FreeCAD environment and submit native CAD artifacts to a separate programmatic verifier. The primary metric is mean continuous task reward, combining geometry similarity and specification consistency rather than binary task success. A September 24, 2026 snapshot covers 13 model-agent systems; Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 achieves the highest overall point estimate, 61.03%, and an image-to-CAD mean reward of 84.66%. These measurements describe complete systems, not isolated model capabilities. We release versioned tasks, evaluation configurations, and inspectable result artifacts.
evidence_items.title: Parametric CAD Bench v3: Evaluating Agentic Parametric CAD Authoring from Text and Engineering Drawings

evidence_items.summary: Progress in AI is often measured by what a single model can do on its own. Yet teams of AI agents are starting to make breakthroughs and discoveries in science, medicine, mathematics and software engineering. As AI begins to work in teams of agents and people, the ability to collaborate becomes a core part of their intelligence. Research on human teams has measured this ability for decades. Inspired by this, we introduce the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark, which measures how well an AI agent works as a teammate. It contains 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of teamwork, from refusing an unsafe shortcut to checking the work that a weaker model leaves behind. Each task comes from a real record or an existing benchmark, from aviation accident reports and clinical cases to coding tasks and negotiations, and has a programmatically verifiable outcome. To isolate teamwork from individual capability, models are scored only on tasks that they can solve by themselves when they have full information. We evaluate 18 closed- and open-weight models and find that every model, across sizes and families, has clear weaknesses as a teammate, with the best model scoring only 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models almost always refuse unsafe shortcuts and report misconduct, yet they cave under interpersonal pressure, reaching the best overall deal in only 14% of conflicts, and their pass rate drops from 97% to 81% when they take over a task in which a weaker model has cheated. Crucially, general capability does not guarantee good teamwork, as models with nearly the same capability score differ by up to 11 points as teammates. The benchmark includes 160 public tasks with code and data, along with 80 held-out tasks for evaluation. As AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents and people, the ability to collaborate effectively is becoming a crucial capability to measure and develop.
evidence_items.title: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: The rapid growth of automated code generation has created a pressing need for automated code review. Yet code review resists full automation: it depends on context beyond the \textit{diff}, on the author's intent, and on judgments about design and maintainability on which even expert reviewers disagree. Existing code review benchmarks lack standardization and rely largely on noisy human review comments scored with text-similarity metrics, which reward surface overlap and fail to measure precision. We introduce \texttt{CR-Bench}, a defect-centric evaluation framework that recasts SWE-Bench issues as pull-request review tasks with full repository context. After filtering for review-detectable defects and grounding each to a single originating pull request, \texttt{CR-Bench} contains 584 instances, with a 174-instance \texttt{CR-Bench-Verified} subset derived from SWE-Bench Verified. Each instance pairs a pull request with a known defect, its ground-truth fix, and a taxonomy label for bug category, impact, and severity. We propose two complementary metrics: \emph{Known-Defect Detection Rate} (KDDR), which measures whether an agent identifies the labeled defect, and \emph{Usefulness Rate}, which measures the fraction of review comments that are actionable. We evaluate eight code review agents over four backbones, plus commercially available Gemini Code Assist, using three independent LLM judges. Even the strongest systems detect only about one-third of known defects (KDDR $\approx$ 33\%), and Gemini Code Assist detects 8.1\%.
evidence_items.title: CR-Bench-v2: Evaluating the Real-World Utility of AI Code Review Agents

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Background: Open tibial shaft fractures are challenging injuries because of soft-tissue compromise and the risk of fracture-related infection (FRI). Antibiotic-coated intramedullary devices have been investigated as a way to combine fracture stabilization with local antimicrobial delivery; the available evidence remains heterogeneous and does not establish superiority for every fracture pattern or device. Objective: To describe clinical and radiological outcomes in patients with open tibia–fibula fractures treated with the Versatile Antibiotic Intramedullary Interlocking (VAIL) system. Methods: This prospective observational study was reported as having enrolled 50 patients with Gustilo–Anderson grade II, IIIA, or IIIB open fractures between 2024 and 2026 . The nail was coated with polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cement containing vancomycin and gentamicin. Outcomes reported in the source manuscript included postoperative infection and radiographic union assessed using the Radiographic Union Scale for Tibial fractures (RUST). Results: The source dataset reports 11 postoperative infections among 50 enrolled patients (22%), including six superficial infections (12%) and five deep infections (10%). Infection was reported in 0/14 patients operated on within 12 hours, 5/27 operated on at 13–24 hours, and 6/9 operated on after 24 hours. Forty-eight patients completed the stated 9-month follow-up. At that time point, 39/48 had RUST scores of 10–12, five had scores of 7–9, and four had scores of 6 or less. Conclusion: The series describes the use of a PMMA antibiotic-coated interlocking nail in selected open tibial fractures.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Clinical and Radiological Outcomes in Open Tibial Shaft Fractures Managed with A Versatile Antibiotic Intramedullary Interlocking Nailing System

evidence_items.summary: STARLI | F101–F110 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · Distributed Microrobotic Coordination, Safety and Sample Integrity Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This collection presents ten prospective research-design monographs in micro/nanorobotic collective systems. Research Unit I (F101–F105) examines self-organizing sampling, load balancing, safe-stop behavior, local sensor fusion and asynchronous control. Research Unit II (F106–F110) investigates competing tasks, adaptive routing, contamination control, collaboration reliability and heterogeneous-agent coordination. The editorial aim is to define independently testable, resource-bounded questions, not to claim demonstrated autonomous performance or clinical efficacy. The ten English working editions comprise 7,770 PDF pages: 300 prospective mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study sections, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate has six annotation categories: causal mechanism, measurement witness, blind falsifier, rival explanation, stopping boundary and successor interface. Architecture counts are not evidence of experimental validation or independently certified scientific originality. The Ten Research Directions F101  Nanorobotic Collective Self-Organization Sampling At The Limit — Explores whether locally coordinated sampling can preserve sample identity while keeping collision exposure within a bounded envelope. The proposed witness is harmful collision frequency [events/(agent min)], alongside the atlas collision-rate outcome. Equal-energy fixed-rule behavior is the baseline; leaked global tracking is a rival explanation. Confidence maintained despite a concealed communication partition rejects the claim.
evidence_items.title: STARLI | F101–F110 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · Distributed Microrobotic Coordination, Safety and Sample Integrity Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This collection presents ten prospective research-design monographs in micro/nanorobotic collective systems. Research Unit I (F101–F105) examines self-organizing sampling, load balancing, safe-stop behavior, local sensor fusion and asynchronous control. Research Unit II (F106–F110) investigates competing tasks, adaptive routing, contamination control, collaboration reliability and heterogeneous-agent coordination. The editorial aim is to define independently testable, resource-bounded questions, not to claim demonstrated autonomous performance or clinical efficacy. The ten English working editions comprise 7,770 PDF pages: 300 prospective mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study sections, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate has six annotation categories: causal mechanism, measurement witness, blind falsifier, rival explanation, stopping boundary and successor interface. Architecture counts are not evidence of experimental validation or independently certified scientific originality. The Ten Research Directions F101  Nanorobotic Collective Self-Organization Sampling At The Limit — Explores whether locally coordinated sampling can preserve sample identity while keeping collision exposure within a bounded envelope. The proposed witness is harmful collision frequency [events/(agent*min)], alongside the atlas collision-rate outcome. Equal-energy fixed-rule behavior is the baseline; leaked global tracking is a rival explanation. Confidence maintained despite a concealed communication partition rejects the claim. F102  Microrobotic Collective Load Balancing At The Limit — Studies how task redistribution changes spatial coverage without relying on unmetered additional actuation. Coverage spatial entropy [nat] is the proposed endpoint, linked to the original coverage-entropy outcome. A single-agent controller with matched total actuation tests whether the apparent gain comes merely from redundancy. Failure to recover a known-safe state ends the trial. F103  Nanorobotic Collective Safe Stop At The Limit — Defines a test of independently observed transition to a safe state after a collective disturbance. The witness is time to demonstrably safe state [s], preserving the atlas recovery-time field. A fully observing centralized controller provides the comparator; increased agent count is an alternative cause of faster recovery. Crossing any registered safety invariant terminates evaluation. F104  Microrobotic Collective Local Sensor Fusion At The Limit — Examines whether local sensor exchange improves accepted mission decisions under limited communication. Communication traffic per accepted task [bytes/task] is a proposed measurement, with the original communication-load outcome retained. Equal-energy fixed rules challenge the fusion benefit; unacknowledged global state tracking is a competing explanation. Hidden partitions test whether confidence remains appropriately bounded. F105  Nanorobotic Collective Asynchronous Control At The Limit — Investigates decision timing when individual robots update at different rates rather than using a single synchronized command. Total metered energy per completed task [J/task] is the proposed observable, preserving the atlas energy-per-task field. The control comparison matches total actuation to a single-agent system; redundancy without true adaptation is the alternative. Failure to regain a known-safe state requires stopping. F106  Microrobotic Collective Task Competition And Coordination At The Limit — Proposes experiments in which agents must choose between competing tasks under bounded control authority. Selective abstention and service coverage [fraction] is the candidate measurement, anchored to the atlas abstention outcome. A fully observing centralized controller is the strong comparator, with simple agent-number advantage as a rival. Breach of registered safety invariants invalidates any coordination gain. F107  Nanorobotic Collective Adaptive Path Planning At The Limit — Tests whether locally coordinated route changes improve mission completion when obstacles or task geometry vary. Task-success fraction under equal energy [fraction] is the proposed endpoint, linked to the original task-completion measure. Fixed behavior at the same energy budget is the baseline; leaked external tracking may falsely suggest adaptation. Concealed network partitions probe erroneous collective confidence. F108  Microrobotic Collective Contamination Control At The Limit — Addresses a different physical constraint: preserving sample separation during repeated collective handling. The new proposed endpoint is cross-sample chemical carryover [mass fraction], while the source atlas retains consensus error. A matched-actuation single-agent control tests claimed collective benefit; redundancy alone may explain task performance. Inability to return to a known-safe state is a mandatory stop. F109  Nanorobotic Collective Collaboration Reliability At The Limit — Examines whether distributed cooperation can remain safe and reproducible across adverse trials. Hazardful collision frequency [events/(agent*min)] is the candidate observable alongside the original collision-rate outcome. A fully observing centralized controller is the baseline, and additional robots are a rival source of apparent performance. Safety-invariant crossing overrides aggregate success statistics. F110  Microrobotic Collective Heterogeneous Agents Coordination At The Limit — Studies coordination across agents with different sensing, mobility or task roles, while preserving traceable collective outcomes. Coverage entropy under heterogeneous roles [nat] is the proposed witness. Equal-energy fixed behavior is the baseline; outside tracking that silently supplies global state is a competing explanation. Unjustified high confidence during a concealed partition rejects the proposal. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries These are prospective nonclinical research designs restricted to authorized bench-scale, ex-vivo or synthetic reference settings with traceable sample identity, calibrated measurement and bounded actuation. Proposed endpoints are editorial additions and do not replace original atlas outcomes. No laboratory experiments or clinical results are reported. Matched energy and actuation, blinded disturbances, full negative-trial records and noncompensable safety stops are needed before any advantage claim. PDF structure and archive integrity can be checked automatically, but derivation-level physics, causal independence, source-to-claim DOI alignment and specialist review remain incomplete. Selected Established Methodological References Yang & Zhang (2021) · Motion Control in Magnetic Microrobotics: From Individual and Multiple Robots to Swarms · DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-032720-104318   |   Farivarnejad & Berman (2022) · Multirobot Control Strategies for Collective Transport · DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-042920-095844   |   Seo, Paik & Yim (2019) · Modular Reconfigurable Robotics · DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-053018-023834 These existing methodological citations are reproduced from the source archive evidence register; they do not validate the STARLI-specific proposed systems. Identity-to-claim mapping for each flagship, including additional source DOI candidates, has not been exhaustively verified. evidence_items.summary: Tracing illicit funds on public blockchains remains largely manual. As funds move across accounts and undergo asset conversions, they become mixed with other inflows, requiring repeated queries and expert judgment to trace. Large language model (LLM) agents offer a way to automate this process, but their ability to reconstruct case-related transfer networks from limited clues remains unclear. To bridge this gap, we present AMLBench, an anti-money laundering (AML) benchmark built from 24 real-world cases and 5.05 million Ethereum transfer records. For each case, agents start from limited clues and explore these transfer records through composable transaction-query and fund-flow analysis tools, deciding which accounts and branches to pursue. The final tracing results are evaluated against case annotations, while tool interaction logs reveal how agents discover and select relevant transfers and at what resource cost. We also develop AMLAgent, which integrates fund-tracing guidance and query feedback to dynamically guide investigative decisions. With GPT-6 Astra, AMLAgent achieves macro averages of 80.82% transfer-level precision and 84.73% query coverage across 24 real-world cases. Further analysis of the large-scale Bybit case reveals substantial differences in transfer retention and token usage across models, even with similar submission precision. AMLBench establishes a reproducible benchmark for evaluating both tracing outcomes and investigative processes, laying the groundwork for more reliable and efficient autonomous AML investigations.
evidence_items.title: AMLBench: A Real-Incident Benchmark for Agentic Blockchain Anti-Money Laundering

evidence_items.summary: A feedback controller is tuned to be robust against noise and bounded disturbances. An adversary who can write to its set-point or to one of its sensors is neither, and the margins a control engineer reads off a noise analysis say little about how far such an adversary can push the physical process. We study this gap on a benchmark nonlinear loop with seven classical control laws, run at a realistic 1 kHz rate with measurement noise, model error and a quantised sensor, and on ArduPilot, an open-source autopilot, in software-in-the-loop flight. On the benchmark the two attack channels behave in opposite ways. A reference attack never appears in the tracking error, yet the derivative feedforward that most designs use makes the reference channel cost about 75 times more actuation than the same injection on the sensor channel. A sensor bias destabilises the loop beyond a critical value that we derive in closed form, and across six hundred tunings of the linear laws that value is proportional to the actuator noise the law admits, so noise rejection is bought with attack margin and the quietest law is the most fragile. A residual detector tuned to avoid false alarms under a realistic model error leaves a patient attacker a bias window of up to four set-point amplitudes, and a model-consistent covert attack defeats any single-sensor test on an unstable plant. On ArduPilot the feedforward fields of a set-point message turn a 1m command into an excursion of up to 74m with every health signal nominal, navigation ramps up to 2m/s displace the vehicle by over 100m per minute without an alarm, and a second receiver helps only when the two are compared. We measure the autopilot's stealth window against its own detector tuning, evaluate a protocol-boundary rate gate and a receiver cross-check, and release all code.
evidence_items.title: Reference and Sensor Attacks on Classical Control Laws and an Open-Source Autopilot

evidence_items.summary: Highway work zones are critical edge cases for autonomous vehicles (AVs), combining atypical geometries and jurisdiction-specific regulations that existing benchmarks fail to capture: real-world datasets lack 360° multi-modal, full-scene 3D work zone annotation, and no single recorded site can span the layouts and regulatory variants needed for generalizable models. We present WorkIng, a dual-domain benchmark and training resource. WorkIng-Highway provides a 360° multi-modal work zone benchmark with synchronized 128-channel LiDAR, six RGB cameras, and RTK-GPS across 32 km, yielding 12,000+ annotated frames and 227,399 tracked 3D bounding boxes. WorkIng-CARLA complements this with procedural simulation spanning 24 regulation-aware scenarios across six canonical topologies and six international traffic standards, populated by 100+ custom 3D assets. Benchmarking representative 3D detection and end-to-end planning architectures shows that real-world data remains the primary performance driver, and that scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves architectures across 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning. Resources: https://github.com/cvims/WorkIng
evidence_items.title: WorkIng: A Real-World and Synthetic Highway Work-Zone Benchmark Dataset for Autonomous Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Long-range detection of small drones is complicated by their visual similarity to birds and by the limited detail available from ground-based cameras. Combining visible and infrared observations offers complementary information, but their usefulness depends on target size, cross-modal alignment, and image quality. We present AVID, a benchmark for studying these factors using real RGB-infrared bird-drone surveillance footage originating from the Drone Detection Dataset and curated for the IEEE ICIP 2025 Video and Image Processing Cup. AVID comprises 32,040 corresponding frame pairs from 115 videos, with 35,952 existing bird and drone annotations at $320\times256$ resolution. Targets occupy an unusually narrow size range: 68.1\% have a geometric-mean bounding-box side of 8--16 pixels, and 99.0\% meet the COCO small-object criterion. To characterize the geometric difficulty of combining the modalities, we introduce an object-relative alignment ratio and an alignment burden curve. In a sample of 300 frame pairs, 32.3\% have estimated global translations greater than 5 pixels; among the 264 pairs with matching annotations, 16.3\% exceed one median target side. We further introduce AVID-C, which simulates seven families of image degradation at five severity levels independently in RGB, infrared, or both. A fixed-feature analysis examines how scale, degradation, and added cross-modal shifts affect fitted bird-drone class overlap. At 12--16 pixels, the Bhattacharyya error bounds are 0.148 for RGB, 0.198 for infrared, and 0.046 for their combined features. These values describe separation in the specified feature and density models, not detector accuracy. Together, AVID and AVID-C support scale-aware, alignment-aware, and sensor-specific studies of tiny aerial targets.
evidence_items.title: AVID: A Weakly Aligned RGB-Infrared Dataset and Perturbation Benchmark for Tiny Aerial Targets

evidence_items.summary: Language models' abilities to interpret tasks and generate programs offer a promising basis for 3D spatial reasoning. Yet following spatial instructions in 3D scenes requires programs to construct geometric references that language leaves implicit. In this work, we introduce VoxProg, which formulates 3D object placement through voxel programming: a language model translates task interpretations into executable programs over local voxel views of scene surfaces. Because these views index surface geometry on regular grids with explicit coordinates and neighborhood relations, an evidence program can isolate task-relevant regions and boundaries directly from scene meshes, and a downstream pose program can measure the resulting geometry to compute a target $SE(3)$ pose. Visual and numerical feedback from execution lets the model inspect intermediate selections and candidate placements to iteratively revise its code. To evaluate open-ended placement across functional use, geometric fit, and contextual arrangements, we introduce the 71-task VoxProg-Bench benchmark along with an evaluation suite pairing perceptual Intent Alignment and 3D Physical Validity. Across VoxProg-Bench and external benchmarks, VoxProg consistently outperforms relation-based, keypoint-based, and mesh-based baselines.
evidence_items.title: VoxProg: 3D Spatial Reasoning through Voxel Programming

evidence_items.summary: Agentic tasks require a large language model to interact with the world, navigating information and gathering evidence across multiple steps with restricted resources. Due to this complexity, agentic task failures arise from various sources, and pinpointing these failure causes is essential to diagnose and improve agentic systems. Existing benchmarks, however, tend to focus on a single leaderboard score, leaving the underlying failure modes opaque. To fill this gap, we introduce AgentHop, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,011 multiple-choice questions paired with a controlled seven-tool sandbox under fixed token, turn, and tool-call constraints. AgentHop reveals model vulnerabilities by dissecting a single accuracy score along four axes of agent operation: retrieval, synthesis, tool-call, and resource management. Across 19 models, we find that behavior clusters by model family, with tool-call signatures revealing distinct family fingerprints: GPT models commit early, Anthropic and GLM checkpoints verify before committing, DeepSeek and Kimi over-search, and Gemini-3 Pro stays balanced. Decomposed axes further expose within-family structure: Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 land within one accuracy point yet diverge on retrieval-versus-synthesis emphasis, with Opus retrieving more and Sonnet synthesizing better. We release the full benchmark set and the harness to support diagnostic agent benchmarking.
evidence_items.title: AgentHop: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agentic Multi-Hop Question Answering over Scientific Citation Graphs

evidence_items.summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) introduce new opportunities for safety monitoring through their Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, CoT is not always faithful to the model's final output, undermining its reliability as a monitoring tool. To address this, we investigate the hidden representations of LRMs to determine whether future behavior can be predicted from prompt and CoT representations. By evaluating a probe at each generated token, we construct a probe trajectory, the continuous evolution of a concept's probability across the reasoning process. To characterize these temporal dynamics, we extract signal-processing features that capture volatility, trend, and steady-state behavior. We find that trajectory features help precisely where the static probe is weakest, adding 21.7 AUROC points on average, and improving in every such case where that probe falls below 70. We also present two methodological insights. First, template-based training data achieves near-parity with dynamically generated model responses, eliminating the need for a costly initial inference and labeling. Second, the use of a pooling operation is necessary: last-token methods achieve poor performance, whereas average and max pooling achieve 78.5% to 97.4% AUROC and yield stable probe trajectories. Across seven reasoning models from three families and six evaluation datasets, we find probe trajectories to be a promising signal for monitoring model behavior. Warning: This article contains potentially harmful content.
evidence_items.title: Monitoring the Internal Monologue: Probe Trajectories Reveal Reasoning Dynamics

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping financial decision-making by enhancing analytical accuracy, speed, and strategic insight across corporate finance and financial services. The primary objective of the study is to evaluate how AI applications support strategic and operational financial decisions, while also assessing associated risks related to transparency, accountability, and decision control. A qualitative case study methodology is adopted, drawing on secondary data sources including corporate reports, financial disclosures, technology implementation documents, and industry publications. The findings indicate that AI significantly improves forecasting accuracy, real-time financial monitoring, and scenario analysis, leading to more informed and timely financial decisions. The study offers original value by providing practical, case-based evidence on how AI transforms financial decision-making processes beyond theoretical models. The implications are relevant for stakeholders seeking to leverage sustainable financial performance.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Decision-Making

evidence_items.summary: This study explores the impact of integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into a flipped classroom in higher education. Using a quantitative approach with complementary qualitative data, the research involved 136 management students, yielding 77 valid responses. Data were analysed via IBM SPSS 29.0, employing descriptive, inferential, and Exploratory Factorial Analysis. Findings indicate that GenAI integration enhances student engagement and promotes a deeper understanding of AI tools. Students reported increased awareness of GenAI's capabilities and limitations, and improved critical evaluation skills. Class size emerged as a significant factor influencing participation and organizational effectiveness. Overall, results provide empirical evidence of the educational benefits of GenAI in flipped settings, supporting teaching and learning. The study contributes to discussions on fostering critical GenAI use and offers practical implications for AI-driven pedagogical strategies.
evidence_items.title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence in Flipped Classrooms

evidence_items.summary: Financial decision-making is being revolutionized by the use of artificial intelligence (AI). Whereas traditional statistical methods may be limited by the scope and complexity of contemporary financial datasets, AI technologies such as machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) permit companies to analyze not only structured but unstructured datasets efficiently. As such, there have been significant improvements in financial decision-making processes related to portfolio management, risk analysis, fraud detection, and algorithmic trading. evidence_items.summary: This paper describes a leaf classification framework based on machine learning methodologies. The dataset included 36 leaf species with 340 instances and 16 features. Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, XGBoost, AdaBoost, and Random Forest were applied initially on the raw dataset. It was found that Decision Tree, XGBoost and Random Forest performed well, with accuracy scores of 53%, 60% and 85% respectively. After feature reduction based on Information Gain and correlation matrix analysis, four highly correlated features were removed. This led to a marginal improvement in accuracy to 60% for Decision Tree and to 65% percentage for XG Boost, while the accuracy of Random Forest dropped to 74%. We also applied SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) to balance the raw dataset. This enhanced the accuracy of Random Forest and XGBoost to 91% and 81% respectively. With Computer Vision, we achieved an accuracy of 66% for SVM, 61% for Random Forest, 43% for K-NN and 37% for the Decision Tree classifier on the image dataset. The pre-trained VGG16 model achieved an impressive 90.47% accuracy, outperforming the custom CNN model and conventional models like Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) and KNN with various K-values from the literature
evidence_items.title: Smart Leaf Identification and Analysis using Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Are the orbital scales of planetary systems continuously variable, or discretized into a quantum-like ladder? Following the semiclassical procedure of Bohr's quantum theory, in which quantization is postulated before the dynamics is derived, we introduce the quantum number n as a postulate and propose a benchmark equation that fixes the reference orbital radius of a celestial body directly from its radius and density, then use it as an empirical ruler for a decisive large-sample test. Applied to a large exoplanet sample from the NASA archive (2026-02-26 snapshot, cross-checked against a 2026-10-25 re-retrieval), the quantum-number indicators decompose into integer and fractional parts: the integer parts form a clear ladder for Solar-System and Kuiper-belt bodies (four Kuiper-belt dwarfs within 0.03% of the nearest integer; the remaining nine bodies deviate by 0.25–5.2%, with Venus at 18.6% as the benchmark-inner boundary case), while no significant integer clustering is detected in the exoplanet sample at current precision (the fractional part is statistically indistinguishable from uniform, χ² = 4.29, df = 9, p ≈ 0.89); within the Solar System, the same ladder extends from Mercury (n ≈ 1.04) and Earth (n ≈ 1.02) through Ceres (n ≈ 96.6) to the Kuiper-belt dwarfs Pluto (n ≈ 640), Eris (n ≈ 826), Haumea (n ≈ 1.02×10³) and Makemake (n ≈ 1.29×10³), spanning three orders of magnitude. When an orbit occupies the n ≠ 1 rung, the inversion from the orbital radius yields the equivalent value of that rung rather than the true value, which is the normal state of ladder occupation. The derived relations allow the radius, density and mass of a celestial body to be retrieved from its orbital radius.
evidence_items.title: The Benchmark Equation for Celestial Orbital Quantization: Verification and Applications

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Ultracool dwarf (UCD) stars are a common source of contamination in high-redshift galaxy searches because both populations have red colors, and these early-forming galaxies can have sizes that are difficult to resolve even with space telescopes. We have developed the Foreground Contamination Evaluator of Nearby dwarf stars in high- Z photometrically selected Objects ( FC-ENZO ), a code that predicts magnitude-dependent UCD contamination for a given survey setup and galaxy selection method. FC-ENZO combines UCD number density models, synthetic spectral libraries, and photometric selection criteria to estimate contaminant populations. We find that the predicted contamination is sensitive to the adopted UCD spectral model, stellar metallicity, and Galactic distribution models, with the Galactic distribution model producing variations of up to several factors. The Elf Owl models predict higher contamination than the Bobcat models, primarily because of their broader coverage of T and Y dwarf spectra. The dominant contaminants are late L to early Y-type UCDs, which are most commonly misclassified as galaxies at z ∼ 8. For surveys with similar areas, broad-band observations from different space telescopes produce comparable numbers of contaminants at a given redshift, but contaminants are concentrated near the survey limiting magnitude, resulting in higher bright-end contamination fractions for shallower surveys. Adding medium-band filters can reduce the UCD contamination rate at z ∼ 8 by a factor of a few. At z ≳ 30, F356W dropout selections can suffer substantial contamination from Y dwarfs. FC-ENZO provides a practical tool for survey design and for identifying fields suitable for spectroscopic follow-up.
evidence_items.title: Assessing Ultracool Dwarf Contamination in Photometrically Selected High-redshift Galaxy Samples

evidence_items.summary: Higher education institutions are increasingly transitioning from traditional rule-based automation toward autonomous, goal-directed agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems within administrative environments. Unlike conventional automation tools, agentic AI systems can interpret context, plan actions, utilize external tools, and adapt dynamically to changing conditions. This chapter examines the opportunities and risks associated with these systems in student support services. It discusses benefits such as improved responsiveness, continuous service availability, and reduced administrative workload, while also evaluating risks including algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, decision opacity, and the potential reduction of human-centered support. The chapter further proposes a governance framework based on Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) oversight models to support responsible and transparent AI deployment in higher education administration
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI in Higher Education Administration

evidence_items.summary: Advances in scientific AI have accelerated hypothesis generation, prediction, and experimental design, but translating these capabilities into reliable physical experimentation remains a major bottleneck in scientific discovery. Although automation, high-throughput experimentation, foundation models, and cloud infrastructure have accelerated individual stages of the scientific workflow, they have not unified the discovery process. Scientists must still coordinate between computational models and physical laboratory systems to translate scientific designs into executable experiments and ensure their results are reliable. We argue that the next generation of laboratories will be agentic: environments in which scientists, AI systems, equipment and robotic platforms operate as collaborative discovery partners. We propose an architecture built around two complementary components: an agentic foundation that translates scientific designs into coordinated execution plans, and an evolving laboratory world model that represents physical state, predicts action outcomes, and incorporates experimental feedback. Together, they connect computational reasoning to observable and verifiable physical execution. Multimodal perception, robotics, and human–AI interfaces can make laboratory actions and evolving experimental conditions accessible to these systems, supporting adaptive execution and learning. We further propose an evaluation framework centered on physical grounding, execution fidelity, scientific validity, and adaptive coordination under human oversight, rather than autonomy alone. This Perspective outlines how agentic laboratories could connect scientific reasoning, physical experimentation, and trustworthy evidence within a human-in-the-lead discovery loop.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Laboratories of the Future: Towards World Models for Scientific Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Research taste, the judgment of what to read, which problems to pursue, and which methods to try, increasingly shapes the work of AI scientists, yet it remains far less understood than their ability to execute research. We introduce IdeaTaste, a benchmark that scores an LLM by how closely the research proposals it writes from a literature snapshot frozen at 2025 match the work the same communities published in 2026. Our experiments span six contemporary language models and four research areas from established to emerging fields, covering more than 90{,}000 proposals in total. LLM agents fall well short of human communities in both the literature they cite and the ideas they state, reaching about 26\% of the human level on citation matching and only 18\% on idea matching. Their populations can cite as diversely as a community and take up its tasks and methods, yet rarely arrive at the concrete approaches and research plans it pursues. Neither richer field context nor larger populations substantially close this gap. In blinded expert review, AI proposals trail the 2026 papers least in presentation and most in expected success, echoing their gap in concrete approaches, and those whose ideas no human paper shares fare worst, suggesting weaker directions rather than overlooked opportunities. These results indicate that the main bottleneck in AI research taste lies less in finding the directions a community works on than in turning them into the concrete approaches it goes on to pursue. We release IdeaTaste as an open, continuously updated leaderboard (https://cxcscmu.github.io/IdeaTaste) that benchmarks contemporary AI proposals against future publication cycles.
evidence_items.title: IdeaTaste: Do LLMs Share the Research Taste of Human Researchers?

evidence_items.summary: Malware detection remains a critical challenge in computer science and cybersecurity due to the continuous evolution of malicious software, concept drift, and the declining generalization capability of machine learning models over time. This study investigates the temporal performance of hybrid artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models for static malware detection using the EMBER dataset. A quantitative experimental design is employed to compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) classifiers with a hybrid ensemble approach. The methodology incorporates feature preprocessing, chronological data partitioning, supervised model training, and temporal performance evaluation using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). Comparative analysis examined differences in classification performance and temporal degradation across the evaluated models. Confusion-matrix analysis and false-negative rates were also considered to assess classification reliability and identify potential detection errors. The hybrid framework combined tree-based learning and neural network predictions to investigate classification performance and detection consistency across temporally distinct malware samples. The significance of this research lies in addressing the limitations of conventional random-split evaluation and providing a more realistic framework for assessing the temporal generalization of intelligent malware detection systems. The findings are intended to inform the development of adaptive, scalable, and robust cybersecurity solutions capable of responding to evolving malware threats.
evidence_items.title: Temporal Evaluation of Hybrid Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Models for Malware Detection using The EMBER Dataset

organizations: Henan University of Economic and Law
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) faces a hard constraint in public-facing nutri-tion QA: answers must be faithful to official sources. Yet Chinese official nutrition data lacks an auditable evaluation benchmark —numeric faithfulness, refusal bound-aries, and hallucination suppression remain unquantified. We present NutriQA, a traceable RAG question-answering benchmark on official Chinese nutrition data: 200 items in a four-category taxonomy (composition 60 / guideline 50 / special 50 / re-fusal 40), a three-level gold-provenance system (official food-composition values, ver-batim guideline excerpts, gold-free refusal items), and fully auditable deterministic judgment rules (numeric ±1 tolerance + key-point coverage + fabrication detection). Full-scale experiments on three commercial models (qwen-plus, deepseek-chat, glm-5.3-flash) show: (1) hybrid retrieval (BM25 character-bigram + vector RRF, top k=8) achieves a 160/160 hit rate, with retrieval method choice outweighing chunking gran-ularity; (2) retrieval optimization lifts RAG gain from ~0.15–0.17 to 0.20–0.225, de-coupling retrieval hit from the generator; (3) a novel boundary subclass (out-of-KB foods × numeric baits) quantifies 100% numeric fabrication by bare LLMs over out-of-KB objects with mutually exclusive cross-model intervals (3–4× apart), which RAG compresses to ~0–2.5% via“retrieved-not-covered → refuse”; (4) deterministic rules agree with human annotation at 0.949, outperforming a generic LLM judge at 0.846. Data, code, and full evidence are pinned at git tag v1.0.0 for independent verification and reproduction.
evidence_items.title: NutriQA: A Traceable RAG Question-Answering Benchmark and Empirical Study on Official Chinese Nutrition Data

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The drilling industry continues to pursue technologies that improve operational efficiency while reducing environmental impact and health, safety, and environmental risks. Conventional logging-while-drilling (LWD), measurement-while-drilling (MWD), and rotary steerable system (RSS) bottomhole assemblies (BHAs) rely on lithium batteries to power downhole electronics, introducing limitations associated with battery capacity, transportation, handling, replacement, and disposal. This paper presents the first successful global deployment of a fully battery-less triple-combo RSS BHA in a horizontal carbonate reservoir in North Oman. The system replaced conventional lithium battery modules with a mud-driven turbine-generator architecture capable of continuously supplying electrical power to the RSS, MWD telemetry, and triple-combo LWD sensors. The BHA acquired real-time azimuthal gamma ray, resistivity, density, neutron porosity, and directional measurements while maintaining continuous steering performance throughout the drilling interval. The field deployment demonstrated uninterrupted power generation, stable telemetry performance, continuous high-quality formation evaluation, and successful trajectory control without battery replacement or power interruption. The elimination of lithium batteries reduced operational complexity, hazardous material handling, logistics requirements, and environmental footprint while maintaining drilling performance comparable to conventional battery-powered systems. The successful implementation establishes a new benchmark for sustainable downhole power management and demonstrates the technical readiness of battery-less drilling systems for future global deployment.
evidence_items.title: New Benchmark for Battery-Less Drilling Technologies: First Trial in North Oman

organizations: School of Computer Engineering and Technology, Dr. Vishwanath Karad MIT World Peace University, Pune, Maharashtra, India
evidence_items.summary: Sports video analysis has evolved from niche methodologies to expansive technological frameworks that integrate multiple sports disciplines. This research provides a comprehensive comparative analysis of four deep learning architectures: ConvLSTM, Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCNN), Optical Flow with LSTM, and C3D-Lite, specifically for detailed tennis action recognition using the Three dimEnsional TennIs Shots THETIS dataset. The experiments were performed over five random seeds and three stratifications of data into three skill sets: S1 Mixed (all players), BS2 Beginner-Only (Players 1–31), and BS3 Expert-Only (Players 32–55), using common train-validation-test splits to ensure the reproducibility of results over different architectures. The LRCNN provided the best performance (Verified with results in Table 55 65%) and a generalization gap of 14 percentage points due to the use of pretrained features of the InceptionV3 architecture. The C3D-Lite architecture demonstrated the most accurate-efficiency trade-off in terms of mean test accuracy 55.25% ± 3.5% for S1. The Optical Flow + LSTM combination provided validation accuracy of 57.8% (S1), 58.2% (BS2), and 63.8% (BS3), whereas training accuracy was 100% for each seed and strategy, which implies full memorization of the training set. ConvLSTM suffered severe overfitting (∼40% training-to-test gap) and is not recommended for limited-scale video datasets. Cross-seed McNemar analysis confirmed result reproducibility across all strategies. Performance remained consistent across skill-stratified partitions, indicating that mixed-skill datasets are sufficient for deployment. This work establishes the first multi-architecture benchmark on the THETIS dataset with full computational profiling, cross-sport applicability analysis, and deployment guidance for racquet sports analytics.
evidence_items.title: Deep learning architectures for tennis action recognition: Benchmark for cross-sport video analysis

evidence_items.summary: We examine whether daily green bond exchange-traded fund (ETF) returns can be forecast more accurately than the zero-return benchmark. Using four ETFs with data through 17 April 2026, we compare linear, penalized, boosting, feedforward, recurrent, and combination forecasts in historical out-of-sample experiments. The contribution is empirical and evaluative, not a new algorithm. Combinations occasionally reduce squared error by less than 0.3%; the gains are statistically insignificant and heterogeneous across funds. An adjusted-price comparison with four conventional bond ETFs on identical dates finds no significant difference in combination-loss gains between the groups. Hyperparameter and dependence checks do not reverse these findings. Hypothetical close-to-close trading payoffs are sensitive to transaction costs, but are not executable backtests. Overall, the tested models provide limited incremental predictive information, without establishing market efficiency or a forecasting difficulty unique to green bonds.
evidence_items.title: Applied Mathematical Forecast Evaluation of Green Bond ETF Returns Under the Random Walk Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Building surrogate models for production system simulators is a recurring engineering task that remains manual, expert-dependent, and inconsistent across teams. Each update cycle requires a specialist to select input parameters, run simulations, choose ML architectures, tune hyperparameters, validate results, and package the model, spanning days to weeks. Conventional AutoML partially automates model selection but wastes resources on architectures more complex than necessary. This paper presents a multi-agent framework, powered by large language models (LLMs), that automates the full surrogate modelling lifecycle for multiphase production systems in two operating modes: conversational (expert-in-the-loop) and autonomous (self-optimizing until convergence). The framework makes four contributions. First, an autonomous Dataset Generation pipeline, which consists of a three-agent DAG (Sampling Designer, Simulation Runner, Data Reporter) that infers the relevant input parameters, their physically bounded ranges, and an appropriate Latin Hypercube sample size directly from a natural-language description of the well, dispatches the resulting design to the simulator, and returns an audited, reported dataset, removing the manual setup and scripting that otherwise precede every development cycle. Second, a complexity-aware experiment planning strategy in which every autonomous round starts from a default roster of fast, classical regressors spanning a linear, a kernel, and an ensemble-tree family, and escalates to deep-learning or gradient-boosted architectures only through the refinement loop, when a round's best result has failed to meet the stopping criterion. This eliminates the principal inefficiency of conventional AutoML, which is unnecessary evaluation of heavy models.
evidence_items.title: Production Surrogate Modelling Auto-Research Multi-Agentic System

organizations: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Kyungnam University, Changwon 51767, Republic of Korea
Artificial Intelligence Convergence and Open Sharing System, Kyungpook National University, Daegu 41566, Republic of Korea
Department of Artificial Intelligence, Kyungpook National University, Daegu 41566, Republic of Korea
evidence_items.summary: Key information extraction (KIE) models are increasingly used in high-stakes document workflows, where each extracted value must be accompanied by evidence a reviewer can verify. Evaluating their explanations is difficult: human rationale annotation is costly, and in agglutinative Korean, subword tokens misalign with the units humans read. We present KoDocXAI, an evaluation framework and pilot benchmark for the explanations of KIE models on Korean administrative form documents. It derives a value-region rationale reference from existing KIE bounding-box annotations and scores value-region plausibility, whether or not an explanation localizes the extracted value; re-aggregates subword attributions to morphemes and eojeols (Korean spacing units); and measures faithfulness by modality-wise perturbation with the pretraining [MASK] token while protecting the ground-truth span. The pilot benchmark v1.0 covers five fields over 300 permit-and-authorization dispatch documents, 20% of which are doubly annotated. With a fine-tuned LayoutXLM, Integrated Gradients exceeds a random baseline on both axes, whereas attention rollout stays at baseline level under both a first-token and a span-level target. Span protection removes inflated faithfulness scores and a spurious aggregation-level effect. The modality interventions differed in strength, but under them the image channel contributed practically nothing, confining the validated scope to text and layout. These results hold for this document type and model; they support validating the measurement protocol itself and reporting explainability separately by axis and modality.
evidence_items.title: KoDocXAI: A Quantitative Evaluation Framework and Benchmark for Explainability in Key Information Extraction from Korean Administrative Form Documents

organizations: PTT Exploration and Production Public Company Limited, Bangkok, Thailand
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Offshore maintenance strategies for reciprocating engine-driven Booster Compressor (BC) packages rely heavily on static calendar intervals. This approach stems from fragmented technician logs, non-standardized field descriptions, and sparse failure records that hinder classical Weibull analysis. We addressed these data gaps across 51 satellite Wellhead Platforms (WHPs) in the Gulf of Thailand by deploying a digital reliability pipeline that combines Large Language Model (LLM) field log parsing, CMMS major overhaul synchronization, and hybrid Weibull-Exponential failure modeling. The framework was evaluated across 51 offshore Wellhead Platforms (WHPs) operating in the Gulf of Thailand, ingesting 711 historical shutdown records and mapping them against 114 predefined engineering risk categories using Large Language Models. To achieve high semantic precision, a domain-specific prompt architecture was engineered incorporating a field-jargon-to-engineering translation dictionary, exact predefined failure list injection, strict output constraints, zero-temperature generation control, and Python-level validation. Time-Between-Failures (TBF) datasets were systematically constructed by establishing platform-specific "Day 0" baselines from CMMS 48,000-hour major overhaul completion dates. Probabilistic failure behavior was quantified using a hybrid modeling structure: sparse failure modes (n = 2) were assigned a forced Exponential model (β=1.0), while modes with were fitted using Weibull Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). Lifecycle cost-rate optimization based on Nakagawa's age-replacement formulation was applied to 31 eligible failure modes with valid cost data. Time-based preventive maintenance (PM) proved cost-effective only for clear wear-out mechanisms (β &gt; 1), reducing lifecycle cost rates by up to 99.6% against run-to-failure (RTF). For random failure mechanisms (β ≈ 1) and sparse n=2 modes, calendar replacement yielded zero financial benefit.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Decision-Loop Asset Strategy Optimization Using Hybrid Probabilistic Failure Modeling

organizations: Institute for Advanced Study in Physics
evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents can coordinate computational drug discovery, but adapting a campaign to new evidence requires scientific software that supports flexible workflows, consistent modeling, and continuity across research sessions. Here we present ETALON, a harness that equips a general-purpose coding agent with an integrated environment for computer-aided drug design. Three independently usable systems supply its scientific operations: MolQuarry for chemical and biological evidence, MolCascade for molecular preparation, screening, and docking, and PRISM for molecular generation and physical modeling. Each exposes configurable procedures with explicit scientific requirements, so the host can revise its research strategy while retaining consistent preparation and evaluation practices. Operations registered with a common execution layer are checked before dispatch, and their outputs carry separate records of completion, verification, and admission, so that an incomplete computation is not recorded as an unfavorable molecular result. A persistent research graph links evidence, judgments, experiments, and results across sessions, and candidate method revisions are compared with frozen baselines under criteria declared in advance.
evidence_items.title: ETALON: Verified Execution and Persistent Research Memory for Agentic Computer-Aided Drug Design
