evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate detailed video captions, yet they may overemphasize minor details while overlooking essential context and key events. We argue that not all visual evidence deserves equal attention, as the importance of visual information depends on the content of each video. Motivated by this observation, we propose Reviso, an agentic video captioning framework that learns what to observe and how to gather relevant visual evidence. From a low-frame-rate global preview, Reviso constructs a hierarchical Context--Focus--Points (CFP) observation plan that identifies the video context, prioritizes key aspects, and defines concrete observation targets and corresponding tools. Guided by this plan, Reviso performs goal-directed active perception by selectively revisiting temporal segments and combining tools for fine-grained inspection. It interprets the acquired evidence, updates its plan as needed, and integrates global and local information to generate the final caption. To learn this observation strategy, we develop a verification-guided pipeline that constructs high-quality training trajectories through factual verification and teacher-guided refinement. We further train Reviso using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), incorporating a key-fact reward for caption quality, a Plan Alignment Reward (PAR) for identifying important observation targets, and an Unproductive Tool-Call Penalty (UTCP) that adjusts observation-cost penalties based on caption quality. Experiments across four video captioning benchmarks show that Reviso outperforms the evaluated open-source baselines, while its generated captions better support downstream video question answering. These findings highlight the effectiveness and potential of priority-guided active observation for video captioning.
evidence_items.title: Reviso: Not All Visual Evidence Deserves Equal Attention in Video Captioning

evidence_items.summary: The term "linear representation hypothesis" (LRH) has appeared across diverse subfields of artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and cognitive science. But previous works have not consistently treated the LRH as a falsifiable scientific hypothesis; we analyze these inconsistencies and examine their implications for how prior theoretical and methodological results should be interpreted. Based on this analysis, we argue that claims regarding linear representations become well-defined only through careful examination of the model, representation location, feature definition, and evaluation dataset. We therefore propose a more rigorous formalization of the LRH that makes these dependencies explicit and allows the hypothesis to be evaluated as a falsifiable scientific claim. Finally, we identify some non-trivial open problems that warrant further attention from the research community.
evidence_items.title: A Survey on the Linear Representation Hypothesis

evidence_items.summary: Large video models have exhibited impressive performance on a wide range of visual question answering tasks, owing to the rise of powerful, pretrained text and vision encoders. The usefulness of such models have also been demonstrated on a wide range of benchmarks, with an important caveat - the dominant approach in these benchmarks evaluates multiple choice reasoning via text options. This is a natural way to test text-based reasoning in these models, and has led to significant insights regarding model behavior in the community. In this work, we ask a different question - what happens when the evaluation modality is visual, rather than text? We introduce three new vision-centric evaluation benchmarks in temporal frame retrieval, video future prediction, and causal memory distortion, all designed around evaluating visual understanding capabilities in large video models. Our approach complements the existing approaches to evaluate video understanding in frontier models. We show that current frontier models exhibit significant weakness when attempting to reason through visual queries, rather than text. We conclude with an extended analysis section that provides pointers for future improvements in visual understanding for large video models.
evidence_items.title: Not Another Text Benchmark: Putting the "Visual" Back in Visual Question Answering for Large Video Models

evidence_items.summary: Single image super-resolution aims to reconstruct high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs. This paper proposes FreeTransformSR, a novel lightweight super-resolution network based on a channel-wise free low-rank learnable transform. The transform learns task-adaptive basis functions in a data-driven manner, enabling adaptive feature modulation with minimal parameter overhead. To further enhance high-frequency detail recovery, we in-troduce a local feature modulation branch that complements transform-domain processing with depthwise convolu-tion. In addition, a soft complexity adaptive module dynamically fuses the outputs of local convolution and window self-attention branches through a lightweight gating network, adaptively adjusting the fusion ratio based on regional texture characteristics. An adaptive intensity modulation strategy is also incorporated to adjust transform-domain response strength at the sample level, enabling the network to dynamically adjust processing intensity according to input features. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that FreeTransformSR achieves competitive PSNR/SSIM performance with significantly fewer parameters and FLOPs. Specifically, FreeTransformSR achieves 32.41 dB on BSD100 (X2, 634K parameters) and 27.00 dB on Urban100 (X4, 653K parameters), while delivering faster inference speed than competing methods, making it well-suited for deployment in resource-constrained scenarios.
evidence_items.title: FreeTransformSR: Efficient Lightweight Image Super-Resolution via Free Low-Rank Learnable Transform

evidence_items.summary: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) for code generation can recognize a programming request that cannot be satisfied. Coding assistants are widely deployed, yet they are evaluated almost exclusively on solvable tasks where a test suite can score the output. A request may instead name a package that does not exist or ask for an algorithm that is mathematically impossible, and the appropriate response is to refuse. Models nevertheless respond with plausible code, and such fabrications are also a security concern because attackers can register the package names that models invent. We define code hallucination as ungrounded code generation, distinguish it from ordinary programming errors, and introduce a taxonomy of these failures together with a benchmark of 270 adversarial requests and 91 matched solvable controls across six languages and 24 subcategories. We evaluate 17 open-weight models with 6.7B to 671B parameters, collecting 6,137 responses. Models hallucinate on 54% of the adversarial requests and correctly refuse 31%. Larger models do better on algorithmic impossibilities and conflicting requirements, where hallucination falls from 84% for models at or below 7B parameters to 32% for those at or above 80B. For plausible but nonexistent dependencies and features, the rates are 88% and 61%, and even the largest model hallucinates on all 22 requests for nonexistent JavaScript and Rust packages. Two-thirds of hallucinations are confident fabrications without caveats, and some reasoning models fail to return an answer on solvable tasks. Scale teaches models to recognize what is impossible but not what does not exist, so grounding code generation in the real software ecosystem, for example by checking package names against registries, remains necessary regardless of model size.
evidence_items.title: Refusing the Impossible: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Code Hallucination in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Point-supervised change detection (PS-CD) aims to identify pixel-level changes between bi-temporal images using only sparsely annotated points. Although point annotations substantially reduce labeling costs, their limited spatial coverage often results in incomplete and noisy pseudo-labels. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage framework that introduces SAM2 priors into PS-CD and progressively adapts them to the target task. In Stage I, SAM2 generates object-aware candidate masks from point annotations on the bi-temporal images, and a bi-temporal mask selection strategy is designed to convert generic segmentation responses into more reliable change pseudo-labels. Subsequently, a lightweight CNN refinement module with an uncertainty-aware loss is employed to improve boundary quality and local structural consistency. In Stage II, we construct a teacher-student self-training framework in which the teacher is updated by exponential moving average and periodically refreshes the pseudo-labels. This design establishes a closed-loop optimization process that alternates between pseudo-label refinement and model re-optimization. Experiments on three benchmark datasets, including WHU-CD, LEVIR-CD, and SYSU-CD, demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms previous weakly supervised approaches on most benchmarks and remains competitive with several fully supervised methods.
evidence_items.title: Progressive Pseudo-Label Optimization for Point-Supervised Change Detection

evidence_items.summary: Unlike explicit attacks with obvious profanity, implicit hate speech hides malice within seemingly compliant expressions through metaphors and contextual hints, making its detection in online content review challenging. Many PLM- or LLM-based methods apply the same processing pipeline across samples, which may overlook differences in information requirements and introduce unnecessary computation. We observe that online hate speech is not monolithic but manifests in varied forms. We therefore define three fine-grained categories: Shallow, Targeted, and Context-Dependent. Accordingly, we propose Fine-grained Adaptive Implicit Hate speech Detection (FAID), a novel framework that first performs fine-grained classification and then adapts to specific categories. Specifically, for Shallow samples with surface-identifiable intents, the framework adopts lightweight Prompt-Tuning for rapid classification; for Targeted comments that bind malicious intent to concealed targets, we design knowledge augmentation to iteratively refine the model and reveal hidden targets; for Context-Dependent comments lacking background information, we utilize an agentic framework that automatically generates prompts to evolve context, infer missing background information and identify ambiguous malicious intents. This adaptive architecture focuses computational resources on complex implicit samples while avoiding redundant reasoning for shallow samples. Experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that FAID significantly outperforms SOTA baselines.
evidence_items.title: Sledgehammer or Scalpel? A Fine-grained Adaptive Framework for Implicit Hate Speech Detection

evidence_items.summary: Software performance optimization is a notoriously complex and manual task. Despite the growing use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for code refinement, we still lack benchmarks that capture how optimization actually happens in real-world codebases. Existing frameworks often oversimplify the problem by focusing on isolated functions or a single performance metric, missing the critical trade-offs between execution time and memory footprint, the inherent noise of the measurement environment, and the variability introduced by different input data and execution conditions. We address this by introducing SWE-Opt, a repository-level benchmark derived from 102 expert-written optimizations from open-source projects. Unlike previous benchmarks, SWE-Opt pairs each task with parameterized tests to evaluate runtime, peak memory, and Time-Weighted Memory Usage (TWMU) across varying input data and execution conditions under noise-aware measurement conditions. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs struggle significantly: runtime gains are sparse and inconsistent, and memory optimizations are nearly non-existent. An agentic setting with iterative repository exploration improves patch correctness substantially but does not translate into performance gains. This stands in sharp contrast to expert implementations, which achieve an aggregate speedup of 15.5x and peak memory reduction of 171.3x over benchmark tasks. Expert-written improvements are observed in 93.1% of tasks for runtime and 70.6% for peak memory. Our findings expose a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the demands of expert-level engineering.
evidence_items.title: SWE-Opt: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Performance-Oriented Repository-Level Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Image Difference Captioning (IDC) generates natural language descriptions that precisely identify differences between two images, serving as a key benchmark for fine-grained change perception, cross-modal reasoning, and image editing data construction. However, existing benchmarks lack diversity and compositional complexity, and standard lexical-overlap metrics (e.g., BLEU, METEOR) fail to capture semantic consistency or penalize hallucinations, which together prevent a comprehensive and robust evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on IDC. To address these gaps, we introduce DiffCap-Bench, a comprehensive IDC benchmark covering ten distinct difference categories to ensure diversity and compositional complexity. Furthermore, we propose an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol grounded in human-validated Difference Lists, enabling a robust assessment of models' ability to both capture and describe visual changes. Through extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art MLLMs, we reveal significant performance gaps between proprietary and open-source models, highlight the critical importance of reasoning capability, and identify clear limitations in model scaling. Our framework also demonstrates strong alignment with human expert judgments and strong correlation with downstream image editing data construction quality. These findings establish DiffCap-Bench as both a reliable IDC evaluation framework and a practical predictor of downstream utility. The benchmark and code will be made publicly available to support further research.
evidence_items.title: DiffCap-Bench: A Comprehensive, Challenging, Robust Benchmark for Image Difference Captioning

evidence_items.summary: Commonsense knowledge is widely used to support multimodal reasoning and generation, yet existing resources are predominantly text-only and lack grounding in visual context. This limitation often leads to the retrieval of semantically related but visually misaligned knowledge, and can degrade downstream performance. We introduce MMCOMET, a large-scale multimodal commonsense knowledge graph that integrates physical, social, and eventive knowledge with visual grounding. MMCOMET extends ATOMIC2020 by associating each commonsense triple with representative images through a hybrid alignment pipeline, resulting in over 900K multimodal tuples spanning 19 relation types. We further establish a unified evaluation framework across diverse vision-language tasks, including visual commonsense reasoning, visual question answering, visual storytelling, image editing, and image captioning. Our analysis shows that multimodal grounding provides more contextually aligned and reliable knowledge compared to both text-only knowledge graphs and LLM-based knowledge generation, particularly in reasoning-intensive scenarios. At the same time, we observe that the effectiveness of external knowledge is task-dependent, and naive knowledge integration can introduce noise in perception-dominated settings. To mitigate this, we propose an adaptive knowledge router that dynamically selects optimal paths or bypass knowledge in harmful settings. MMCOMET provides a scalable multimodal commonsense resource and a benchmark for studying the role of grounded knowledge in multimodal systems.
evidence_items.title: MMCOMET: A Large-Scale Multimodal Commonsense Knowledge Graph for Visual Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance in long-horizon agentic tasks through multi-step interaction and reasoning at test time. However, repeatedly invoking these models incurs substantial inference cost over an episode. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost, but using a fixed low precision throughout an episode can sharply lower task success. We observe that interaction steps differ sharply in their sensitivity to quantization: given the same context, decoding a step at low precision turns a success into a failure at only about 1% of the steps, which we call critical steps. Based on this observation, we propose Dynamic Mixed-Precision Routing (DMR), a framework that adaptively selects between high-precision and low-precision versions of the same LLM at each decision step. Leveraging an entire-space factorization to jointly predict a step's divergence and its effect on the outcome, DMR learns to recognize these critical steps by training only a lightweight router on the model's hidden state. By reusing a shared high-precision KV cache and the hidden states, DMR avoids redundant context prefill and a separate text encoder, enabling precision switching with less than 1 ms of overhead per step and adding less than 0.11% to step latency for routing. This mixed-precision design also enables nested quantization, reducing the memory footprint by 39% on average compared with FP16. Across three long-horizon agentic benchmarks with nested quantization, DMR achieves an average 2.44x decode speedup over FP16 at comparable task success rates, without fine-tuning the underlying model. On ALFWorld with GPTQ, DMR achieves a 1.71x decode speedup with 86.9% success, compared with 87.2% for FP16.
evidence_items.title: Dynamic Mixed-Precision Routing for Efficient Multi-step LLM Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used in sensitive domains such as medical AI, where privacy regulations, including HIPAA and GDPR, require the removal of specific individuals' or institutions' data. This motivates machine unlearning, which aims to remove the influence of target data from a trained model. However, existing unlearning benchmarks fail to reflect the hierarchical and multimodal structure of real-world medical data, limiting their ability to properly evaluate unlearning in practice. Therefore, we introduce MedForget, a hierarchy-aware multimodal unlearning benchmark that models data from medical institutions as a nested structure, enabling fine-grained evaluation across retain and forget splits. Experiments show that current unlearning methods struggle to achieve effective hierarchy-aware forgetting without degrading retained utility, measured by performance on clinically relevant prediction tasks. To address this limitation, we propose Cross-modal Hierarchy-Informed Projection for unlearning (CHIP), a training-free, hierarchy-aware multimodal unlearning method that deletes information by selectively removing target-specific weight subspaces while preserving sibling-shared information. Our results show that CHIP achieves the highest forget-retain performance gap across all hierarchy levels while maintaining competitive downstream utility compared to existing methods. Overall, MedForget provides a practical benchmark for evaluating hierarchy-aware multimodal unlearning for medical data, while CHIP offers an effective solution that generalizes across architectures and balances deletion with utility.
evidence_items.title: Hierarchy-Aware Multimodal Unlearning for Medical AI

evidence_items.summary: Generative large language models (LLMs) have been shown to exhibit harmful biases and stereotypes. While safety fine-tuning typically takes place in English, if at all, these models are being used by speakers of many different languages. There is existing evidence that the performance of these models is inconsistent across languages and that they discriminate based on demographic factors of the user. Motivated by this, we investigate whether the social stereotypes exhibited by LLMs differ as a function of the language used to prompt them, while controlling for cultural differences and task accuracy. To this end, we present MBBQ (Multilingual Bias Benchmark for Question-answering), a carefully curated version of the English BBQ dataset extended to Dutch, Spanish, and Turkish, which measures stereotypes commonly held across these languages. We further complement MBBQ with a parallel control dataset to measure task performance on the question-answering task independently of bias. Our results based on several open-source and proprietary LLMs confirm that some non-English languages suffer from bias more than English, even when controlling for cultural shifts. Moreover, we observe significant cross-lingual differences in bias behaviour for all except the most accurate models. With the release of MBBQ, we hope to encourage further research on bias in multilingual settings. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Veranep/MBBQ.
evidence_items.title: MBBQ: A Dataset for Cross-Lingual Comparison of Stereotypes in Generative LLMs

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents pyglenn 0.3.0, an open-source Python package for the   computation of thermochemical properties — heat capacity ($C p$), enthalpy   ($H^\circ$), and entropy ($S^\circ$) — from NASA-7 polynomial coefficients.   The package parses legacy FORTRAN thermo.inp files into a normalized SQLite database, exposes a typed, object-oriented Python API, and ships a command-line interface. The bundled dataset covers 2,035 chemical species   and 3,779 temperature intervals and is  enormalized with the dataset's original NASA Glenn/CEA reference gas constant ($R = 8.314510$ J/(mol·K),   CODATA 1986), which eliminates a systematic ~5.7 ppm bias that arises when the modern CODATA universal value is used instead. Cross-validation against NIST-JANAF reference data demonstrates sub-percent agreement for heat capacity and entropy across seven reference species. pyglenn has a single runtime dependency (NumPy), is installable from PyPI, and is suitable for researchers and engineers in combustion science, chemical thermodynamics, and related fields.
evidence_items.title: pyglenn: A Python Toolkit for Thermochemical Properties Calculation from NASA Polynomials

evidence_items.summary: Repairing obsolete tests in response to source code evolution is critical for test suite reliability and software quality assurance. While large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising tools for automating many software development tasks, the effective supply of context and the orchestration of repair pipelines in this source--test co-evolution scenario remain poorly understood. Moreover, although reasoning is found helpful for LLMs on some complex coding tasks, it remains unclear which reasoning steps actually contribute to effective test repairs and how the insights learned from LLMs' behaviors benefit coding agents. In this paper, we present a systematic empirical study of test repair for source-test co-evolution empowered by LLMs, investigating the effective setups and typical LLM behaviors. To support this study, we construct a new benchmark of 500 real-world source-test co-evolution cases from commits submitted between May 2024 and April 2026 across 15 highly-starred open-source Java projects. Our experimental results reveal several key insights for effective LLM-based test repair: the complementary benefits of combining test failure symptoms, source code changes, and supportive code context, as well as the effectiveness of self-repair rounds. We further derive a common reasoning action taxonomy from LLMs' reasoning traces, which proves instrumental in guiding LLMs to repair tests more effectively while at a lower financial cost. Applying our findings to the Codex agent further improves its repair success rate on challenging cases by 66.7%.
evidence_items.title: Finding the Pivots to Repair Broken Source-Test Evolution Using LLMs

evidence_items.summary: On July 1, 2025, Vietnam reduced its 63 provinces to 34, abolished its 696 districts, and replaced its 10,035 commune-level units (wards) with 3,321. ViAdminShift, a Vietnamese language resource about this event, consists of 7,995 benchmark items, 2,281 retrieval passages from pre- and post-reform Wikipedia revisions and dated templates, and old-to-new tables that a released script rebuilds from the official conversion table (not redistributed). Changed items store the pre-reform answer (except 121 address items), a $2\times2$ design uses untouched units as controls, and 400 addresses appear without diacritics. The tables agree with an independent lineage on 10,564 of 10,565 official pairs, disagreements were settled against the resolutions, and the probing-track scorer agrees with both authors' blind labels (Cohen's $\kappa=0.91$ and $0.89$). Data, outputs, code, and a datasheet are released. In the probing track, at least 20 of 67 models know the reform. Fourteen of them give the new province alone for at most 11% of plain questions about old addresses (old province only: 14-100%); a bare date recovers up to 100%. Post hoc (80 province-free addresses, single runs), with reasoning off, today's date in the system prompt leaves 68-100% old-province-only answers for 10 of 12 models; with reasoning, an "as of" prefix in the question leaves none for seven of eight. On the 1,262-item benchmark subset, with same-source old and new passages, small models unaware of the reform give 14-30% outdated answers and the five benchmark-track knowers (also differing in size or provider) 0-5%.
evidence_items.title: ViAdminShift: A Vietnamese Benchmark for Event-Level Knowledge Updates Built from the 2025 Administrative Reform

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly large-scale deep learning, have been driven by monolithic or offline training on massive curated datasets. While successful, these approaches face structural limitations: escalating data and computational demands, limited online adaptability, and a lack of system-level intelligence in open, non-stationary environments. This paper presents Networked AI - a networked intelligent system composed of interacting, heterogeneous, and continuously evolving AI agents. We establish a hierarchical layered architecture comprising an Agent Layer for heterogeneous capability construction, an Interaction Layer for signal-processing-guided online data extraction, and a Regulation Layer for stability-constrained collective evolution. Foundations in data science, signal processing, and system control are hereby synthesized into a unified theoretical framework of Networked AI, providing superior data efficiency, intelligence efficiency, interpretability, and scalability. Theoretical and experimental analysis demonstrates that Networked AI can approach near-linear scaling in resource demand, in contrast to the exponential increase in standalone end-to-end systems. It provides not only online adaptation to out-of-distribution environmental novelties, but also the autonomous evolution towards application-specific intelligence. Application frontiers are discussed for IoT spaces, embodied, spatial, and industrial intelligences, as well as the cellular infrastructure and beyond. Key open challenges are identified towards realizing locally autonomous, collectively intelligent, continuously evolving, globally regulated Networked AI.
evidence_items.title: Networked AI: Architecture, Theory, and Applications

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in medical question answering (QA) systems. While recent works aim at incrementally improving the downstream task accuracy, an empirical estimation of the models' energy consumption and the associated carbon footprints is often overlooked. In this study, we demonstrate how practitioners can estimate energy consumption and arrive at reliable emission estimates for medical QA tasks available in the OpenMedical-LLM leaderboard by investigating 13 LLMs from 3 model families ranging from 270M to 14B parameters. We discuss how one can critically interpret energy versus accuracy trade-offs for a set of models for a given task. With this work, we underline that reporting disjoint energy and accuracy metrics alone does not suffice for careful trade-off assessments, but it also demands systematic construction and interpretation of joint trade-off metrics. We envisage such studies aiding practitioners in adopting better and more efficient models for their task and helping them become active participants in building sustainable LLM pipelines.
evidence_items.title: Tug of Watts: A study on the Energy - Accuracy Trade-off of Large Language Models on Medical Question Answering Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.
evidence_items.title: Blueprint2CAD: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Engineering Drawing-to-CAD Render Correspondence

evidence_items.summary: Surgical video understanding is essential for intraoperative assistance such as workflow monitoring, instrument preparation and procedural documentation. Delivering such assistance in real time requires a model to jointly perceive the ongoing scene, remember past surgical events, and respond before clinically relevant moments pass. Existing approaches provide limited support for jointly retaining procedural evidence and deciding when to respond in streaming surgical video. In this work, we propose SurgStream, a workflow-anchored proactive streaming framework for real-time surgical video understanding. We first introduce Workflow-Anchored Memory (WAM) to record structured instrument-action-target observations and fold them into phase-level summaries, providing compact and queryable surgical memory. Deadline-aware Transition Learning (DTL) is then devised to supervise response states within clinical windows, enabling timely responses before procedural deadlines. We further introduce SurgStream-Bench, comprising 11.7K streaming interactions across various tasks covering real-time perception, backward memory queries, forward proactive QA, proactive alerts and caption memory. Experiments on SurgStream-Bench show gains over state-of-the-art methods, especially in memory and forward proactive QA. The source code will be available.
evidence_items.title: SurgStream: A Workflow-Anchored Proactive Streaming Framework and Benchmark for Real-Time Surgical Video Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Gait assessment supports the diagnosis, monitoring, and prognosis of diverse movement-related conditions, such as neurological and musculoskeletal disorders. Recent advances in deep learning using everyday wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) offer an accessible and low-cost approach to automated gait assessment. However, IMU measurements vary substantially across individuals, body locations, and device configurations, while existing deep learning models are typically developed using small, homogeneous datasets for specific clinical tasks, limiting their robustness and generalizability in diverse real-world contexts. Here we present GaitFM, a cross-modal foundation model for gait assessment using IMU sensors. GaitFM improves the generalizability of gait assessment by transferring knowledge from large vision models and pretraining on unlabeled IMU sensor data. We pretrain GaitFM on a large curated dataset comprising about 4,000 participants and 1.23 million gait windows across diverse clinical and daily conditions, sensor modalities, and body locations. GaitFM demonstrates strong performance across 18 gait-related tasks, including 3 gait parameter estimation tasks, 14 disease and gait abnormality detection tasks, and 1 clinical outcome prediction task. Furthermore, GaitFM generalizes across different sensor configurations and body locations, including those commonly used in clinical settings and everyday wearable devices. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of transferring visual knowledge in improving sensor-based gait assessment performance, offering a new promising pathway for addressing data scarcity in the sensor and medical domains.
evidence_items.title: GaitFM: A Cross-Modal Foundation Model for Wearable Gait Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to localize a target in a satellite image from an observation captured under another viewpoint. Existing methods typically specify the query with a click point or bounding box, marking the target region but underusing the semantic attributes and relations conveyed by natural language. Moreover, referring expressions are often viewpoint-dependent, making query-view descriptions difficult to ground directly in the satellite image. In this paper, we formulate cross-view visual grounding (CVVG), extending conventional point- or box-prompted CVOGL to instance grounding jointly guided by a referring expression and a visual exemplar. We present GAV (Grounding Across Views), a view-aware framework for selectively transferring visual and linguistic evidence across views. Its core is view-aware referring reasoning: target-centered descriptions are derived from the marked query image, checked for target-category consistency, and augmented with a direction-free role cue. Exemplar prompting, cross-view alignment, and scene-level discrimination ground this semantic evidence in a satellite instance. GAV achieves a new state of the art on MoP-UAV with 62.55% Acc@0.5. We also introduce CVOGL-Text, a benchmark for text-guided grounding from street- and drone-view queries to satellite images. GAV outperforms the click-point baseline by 7.09 and 6.79 Acc@0.25 points on the street- and drone-view splits, respectively, demonstrating robustness to larger viewpoint gaps. The code and annotations will be publicly released.
evidence_items.title: Grounding Across Views: Cross-View Referring Reasoning for Visual Grounding

evidence_items.summary: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%). An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in fact-dense U.S. federal agency text, but reworded 67-78% of the quoted spans, against its own prompt. Unit retention and detector evasion were not clearly related across tools (Spearman rho = -0.46, 95% CI -0.65 to 0.08), and the open model's four released files (two of them quantization-aware low-bit files) did not show the pre-registered monotone trade-off. On federal texts with matched human, AI-styled and humanized versions, a general-purpose decision model, Jev, asked a single zero-shot question, separated human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864 (0.827-0.902), 0.18-0.22 higher than Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and the adversarially trained RADAR, while calling 24% of the human originals AI at a 0.5 threshold. On the AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors scored below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39), also with line breaks removed. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs; two earlier data contacts are disclosed. We release the checker and the per-item results.
evidence_items.title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers

evidence_items.summary: Robots deployed in dynamic environments execute changing directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workloads under limited compute and timing budgets. This article presents MERIS, a framework for model scheduling under real-time constraints that combines proportional intermediate deadlines, MIMONet-aware graph refinement, and event-driven synchronization for multi-task inference on resource-constrained robotic platforms. We distinguish three representations: the application DAG, each MIMONet's internal encoder/decoder graph, and the refined scheduling DAG, and make the scope of the timing argument explicit. If the profiled execution bounds, release assumptions, precedence barriers, and per-level capacity premises hold, satisfaction of the assigned sub-deadlines composes to the end-to-end deadline. For non-partitionable tasks, we define a profile-bounded admission rule; before interpreting that rule as empirical timing evidence, we require direct per-task completion checks. We report run-level QoE alongside the offered-node deadline missing rate, making explicit that run completion and successful service of every node are different outcomes. We propose a comprehensive minibenchmark for evaluating the performance of schedulers under various DNN-driven autonomous driving scenarios. Extensive experiments on Nano Orin, AGX Orin, and M3 Max demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.
evidence_items.title: MERIS: Adaptive Real-Time Scheduling of Refined Inference DAGs in Dynamic Robotic Environments

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents are judged by what they deliver, and in professional work what gets delivered is a project, not a task. A project pays off only if the whole package holds, and one weak part can limit the value of the rest. Yet existing benchmarks mostly test agents on one task at a time, leaving a gap between the capability we measure and the outcome that makes agents useful. To address this gap, we introduce DeliverBench, which tests whether agents can carry a project from brief to final delivery. Its 11 projects, spanning financial due diligence, legal contract drafting, and drug safety reporting, are reconstructed with 13 domain experts from real materials and chain 150 subtasks through 2-15 rounds of new materials and client feedback. Because no reference outputs are injected, agents inherit their own errors from one task to the next. Expert rubrics then score every checkpoint as well as the final package. Across seven model-harness systems, even the best system scores only 65.0 out of 100 on final delivery and passes 50.0% of subtasks at a 90-point threshold. The failures are often failures of carrying work forward: in one audit project, all seven systems addressed the review findings, but only one preserved traceability. Together, these results suggest that task-level capability does not simply compose into delivery, which also depends on keeping the work coherent as it evolves.
evidence_items.title: DeliverBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Delivering Realistic Multi-Stage Professional Projects

evidence_items.summary: Despite recent advances in CUAs, their development remains constrained by the limited diversity, controllability, and reliability of interaction data. Moreover, conventional optimization pipelines lack iterative feedback, while existing recursive improvement approaches often rely on self-generated experiences, limiting ability expansion and yielding diminishing returns. To address these challenges, we introduce CUA-Master, a nested double-loop recursive improvement framework. At the system level, an outer world-data-model flywheel continuously incorporates open-world corpus and leverages evolving model weaknesses to guide subsequent data construction and optimization iterations. At the data level, an inner flywheel couples open-world seeding and autocatalytic propagation. The former mines authentic workflows as seed tasks from instructional videos, and employs visual-semantic dual-path trajectory reconstruction; The latter transforms these seeds into reusable primitives for controllable synthesis of diverse, complex, and verifiable tasks. To enable efficient and reliable trajectory collection, we further introduce a feedback-guided snapshot-rollback retry mechanism in various real environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUA-Master-27B achieves competitive performance across GUI-only and GUI-CLI hybrid benchmarks, scoring 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0, 43.9 on WeaveBench, and 25.0 on Agents' Last Exam. Our framework also substantially improves the quality and efficiency of data synthesis, and exhibits continuous gains across recursive iterations.
evidence_items.title: CUA-Master: Scaling Computer-use Agents through Open-World Recursive Improvements

evidence_items.summary: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
evidence_items.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Embodied agents need physical intelligence to understand their surroundings through physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning. These capabilities must work together to interpret events and make quantitative judgments. Existing benchmarks advance physical understanding and general-purpose tool use, yet the coordination of these capabilities in physical scenarios remains insufficiently characterized. Inspired by Popper's Three Worlds, we introduce TriPhysBench, a benchmark of 410 questions from 200 videos that brings physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning into a shared evaluation setting. Its measurement-grounded and knowledge-grounded subtasks impose complementary demands on obtaining observations and acquiring external specifications, then applying them to quantitative problems. Among six representative vision-language models, the best achieves an answer accuracy of only 50.38%, revealing limited performance on tasks that require these capabilities to work together. We further introduce TriPhys, a framework that learns a unified policy for physical perception, knowledge retrieval, and quantitative reasoning from complete tool-integrated trajectories. The policy uses intermediate reasoning to guide retrieval and computation, then incorporates tool feedback into subsequent physical inference. On 110 questions from videos excluded from training, TriPhys improves answer and solution scores across three Qwen configurations, with a 17.7% relative gain in answer accuracy for TriPhys-27B over its Qwen3.6-27B backbone. This work provides a benchmark and a learning pathway toward embodied agents that move beyond recognizing events to understanding and reasoning about the physical processes behind them.
evidence_items.title: TriPhysBench: Evaluating Physical Intelligence for Embodied Agents

evidence_items.summary: Science experiment videos demonstrate how experiments are performed, but offer no direct interaction for learners. Turning them into virtual experiments requires not only reproducing the observed apparatus and state changes, but also enforcing the preconditions governing each operation. We introduce Lab2Sim, a benchmark of 218 science experiment videos with evidence-grounded specifications and 11,881 rubric items. To address this task, we propose EduVideo2Code, which extracts experimental procedures hierarchically, encodes them as explicit state machines to guide code generation, and refines the resulting pages through execution-based verification. Experiments show that existing multimodal models readily generate runnable pages but struggle to faithfully reconstruct experimental apparatus. EduVideo2Code consistently improves all four evaluation dimensions across two backbone models, with apparatus fidelity gains of 24.15 points.
evidence_items.title: Lab2Sim: Turning Real-World Experiment Videos into Interactive Virtual Experiments

evidence_items.summary: This record contains a small, single-shot benchmark that tests how well largelanguage models write scientific machine-learning code. Each of [N] anonymizedmodels was asked once, with no follow-up or correction round, to write acomplete Google Colab script that trains a physics-informed neural network(PINN) for 1D quantum tunneling: a Gaussian wave packet hitting a finiterectangular barrier, governed by the time-dependent Schrodinger equation(hbar = m = 1; E = 2 < V0 = 3; domain [-30, 30]; T = 10). Each script was run unmodified in FULL mode with a fixed 2400-second trainingbudget. Every model chose its own architecture, numerical precision andtraining strategy; none of these were changed. All trained networks were thenscored against one shared Crank-Nicolson finite-difference reference. Thereference was validated by probability conservation, an analytic free-packettest and grid refinement. Five acceptance checks were fixed before looking atany results: relative L2 error of the wavefunction below 0.05 (fixed grid and1000 random points), reflection and transmission probabilities each within0.02 of the reference, and probability-norm drift below 0.02. Results: [X of N] scripts ran without modification. [Y of those] met all fiveacceptance checks. [One sentence on the main finding, using only what theresults show.] Limitations: one attempt per model, so results describe single-shot behaviorand not the best achievable outcome; models used different numerical precision(float32 or float64) and therefore completed different numbers of iterationswithin the same time budget; the models did not run their code beforesubmitting it. Author contributions: The author designed the study and the evaluationprotocol, fixed the test case and acceptance thresholds in advance, ran allexperiments and analyzed the results, with support from a university physicsprofessor. AI assistance: The evaluated models generated the PINN code.
evidence_items.title: Single-Shot Benchmark of LLM-Generated Physics-Informed Neural Networks for 1D Quantum Tunneling

evidence_items.summary: SAIFA aims to become Serbia's national hub for AI development, acting as an AI Factory Antenna linked to the Pharos AI Factory (Greece) and IT4LIA AI Factory (Italy). It provides a one-stop shop for computing access, AI tools, datasets, and consulting for academia, public administration, startups, and SMEs, built on national and partner computing resources (IPB's PARADOX and ITE's National AI Platform). Infrastructure resources and the access and use framework are described in the current draft of Deliverable D3.2, Report on infrastructure resources, access and use policies. The purpose of the Data Management Plan (DMP) is to contribute to good data handling through describing what data the project expects to generate and which parts of the data can be shared with the public. Furthermore, it gives instructions on naming conventions, metadata structure, storing of the project data and procedures to make public data available. The FAIR data management principles are described and their application in the case of SAIFA project, as well as a review of the resource allocation, data security and ethical aspects of data collection and usage. During the 36 active months of the project, Google Drive will be used for consortium administrative and management collaboration, including the output-tracking register. A partner-hosted Nextcloud-based solution is planned for controlled shared working and staging storage of research datasets and materials. Partner and HPC systems retain their processing and dataset-specific storage roles. Data will be handled in accordance with national and European rules on data protection and privacy. SAIFA will use an output-specific repository strategy to support its open-access and FAIR objectives. Zenodo remains the designated repository for public project deliverables, scientific publications, white papers and comparable public documents.
evidence_items.title: D1.2 Data Management Plan

evidence_items.summary: SWC-LibDeep: A Cross-Lingual Audio Deepfake Dataset for English and German SWC-LibDeep is a dataset for research on audio deepfake detection. It contains  22,500 synthetically generated speech samples  in English and German, created with six state-of-the-art voice conversion (VC) and text-to-speech (TTS) methods. The dataset comprises three equally sized subsets: LibriSpeech (English): 7,500 samples   Spoken Wikipedia Corpora English: 7,500 samples   Spoken Wikipedia Corpora German: 7,500 samples   The included deepfakes were generated using Seed-VC, Diff-HierVC, OpenVoice v2, kNN-VC, Zonos v0.1 Transformer, and XTTS v2. SWC-LibDeep supports research on cross-lingual and cross-dataset audio deepfake detection, method generalisation, language and accent effects, and synthetic-speech artefact analysis. This release contains synthetic deepfake audio only. The original bona-fide recordings are not redistributed and must be obtained from the respective source corpora (LibriSpeech and Spoken Wikipedia Corpora). The dataset was introduced in: Does Content Matter? Introducing SWC-LibDeep for Cross-Lingual Audio Deepfake Detection in English and German, accepted at the IEEE International Conference on Big Data 2026. Please consult the included README.md file for dataset structure, usage conditions, source-corpus attribution, and citation instructions. This restricted-access dataset is provided exclusively for non-commercial academic research purposes; access requests are subject to review and approval by the dataset authors.
evidence_items.title: Does Content Matter? Introducing SWC-LibDeep for Cross-Lingual Audio Deepfake Detection in English and German

evidence_items.summary: Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, proposes minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents' first choices match the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run remains limited. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste.
evidence_items.title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone. Code and dataset are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/BedBench
evidence_items.title: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning?

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for reproducible comparisons of legal release constraints at fixed work. Task-linked measurements connect these workloads to serving execution and GPU/NPU hardware behavior, revealing why serving efficiency does not always translate into timely task completion. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/ShengxuanQiu/MAServeBench.
evidence_items.title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads

evidence_items.summary: Proactive agents must decide whether, when, and how far to assist without an explicit request. Existing evaluations often rely on automated scores or binary verdicts, offering limited human diagnosis of evidence use and intervention quality. To address these gaps, we introduce HALO, Human-Grounded GrAnular EvaLuation of PrOactive Agents. HALO-Arena covers 4 proactive need types, Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity, across 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments. Scenarios require agents to retrieve evidence from structured databases or unstructured documents before judging whether assistance is warranted and choosing its scope. On HALO-Arena, we construct HALO-8K, a dataset of 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts for action level, acceptability verdicts, and human diagnosis. For rejected responses, human diagnosis covers timing, intensity, and other issues. Recorded reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds measure the effort behind these responses. The best proprietary and open-source models achieve 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability, respectively. Our central finding is that over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode, with Premature timing or Excessive intensity accounting for 61.20% of rejected responses. Further analyses yield complementary findings on the balance between intervention and restraint, evidence acquisition, and the calibration of timing and intensity.
evidence_items.title: HALO: Human-Grounded Granular Evaluation of Proactive Agents

evidence_items.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly used for scientific discovery. However, existing benchmarks mix law inference with programming, score data fitting instead of prediction on unseen inputs, and do not separate empirical evidence from pretrained priors. We introduce SciGame, a controlled benchmark that converts scientific literature into structured scientific cards. Each card yields a pair of Original and dimensionally consistent Counterfactual environments with the same task interface. SciGame contains a Historical collection of canonical laws and a live Temporal collection curated from papers published after model knowledge cutoffs. It evaluates agents in candidate-guided Identification and open-ended Discovery settings. Each setting runs under Prior-only, Fixed, and Adaptive protocols. Experiments on five frontier models yield three findings. First, familiar priors hurt performance once the governing relation is altered. Second, adaptive experimentation helps the strongest models but harms weaker ones under limited budgets. Third, good explanations can hide quantitative failures. Recovering the exact symbolic form remains the main bottleneck, even when agents interpret evidence correctly. Current agents can investigate systems actively, but inducing exact laws in unfamiliar settings remains an open challenge.
evidence_items.title: SciGame: Let Agents Play the Scientific Discovery Games in the Real and Counterfactual World

evidence_items.summary: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) aims to recover well-exposed and perceptually faithful images from severely degraded observations. Recent diffusion-based generative methods achieve strong perceptual quality by leveraging powerful image priors, but their iterative sampling incurs substantial computational cost, limiting practical deployment. Despite recent efficiency gains in generative LLIE, high-quality enhancement with a single function evaluation and low overall computation remains challenging, particularly under diverse real-world low-light conditions. We introduce GLOW-FM, a one-step latent flow-matching framework for efficient generative LLIE. GLOW-FM performs conditional transport in the latent space of a frozen Tiny-VAE and leverages Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) to enable enhancement with a single function evaluation. Matched comparisons with alternative one-step objectives support TVM as an effective design choice, and, to the best of our knowledge, this is its first adaptation to image restoration and specifically to LLIE. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world benchmarks demonstrate that GLOW-FM achieves competitive image quality and state-of-the-art cross-dataset generalization while requiring only a single function evaluation and 34 GFLOPs for the small variant. These findings highlight the potential of GLOW-FM to bring generative LLIE closer to practical deployment through single-step inference and compact latent modeling. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.
evidence_items.title: GLOW-FM: Efficient Generative Low-Light Image Enhancement with One-Step Latent Flow Matching

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer-use agents. We formalize Transition-Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer-use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer-use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.
evidence_items.title: Lost in Recovery: Demystifying Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents via Goal-Oriented Action Replay

evidence_items.summary: Recursively self-improving (RSI) systems are increasingly viewed as a promising means of accelerating progress toward artificial general intelligence. They aim to autonomously improve their capabilities by refining their working pipelines and recursively improving the strategies that guide subsequent refinements, with gains generalizing to unseen scenarios.However, existing evaluations lack reliable metrics to distinguish capability gains from scenario fitting, sustainable and extensible protocols for unseen tasks and difficulties, and fine-grained attribution of improvement to evolution traces. To this end, we propose SelfImprove-Bench,an RSI evaluation framework that organizes tasks into three primary capabilities (i.e., Exploring, Planning, Reasoning) as scenarios for guiding model evolution. We instantiated the tasks on games for controllability and reproducibility, and pairs them with scalable generation and orchestration driven by task templates and difficulty coefficients. Beyond task-level scores, SelfImprove-Bench organizes evaluation into generalization ladder levels G0 to G4 that measure how far gains transfer from training conditions. Experiments reveal that the evolutionary gains of existing RSI methods are inconsistent across generalization levels.
evidence_items.title: SelfImprove-Bench: Evaluating Generalization in Self-Improving Agents

evidence_items.summary: Multi-hop question answering (MHQA) requires recovering a complete set of supporting documents, yet most retrieval-augmented pipelines apply one evidence budget and one selection strategy to every question. This paper studies benchmark-defined adaptive candidate reranking for Indonesian MHQA in a closed setting in which each question is paired with ten candidate documents. A routing classifier assigns each question to a two-gold-document branch (HotpotQA), processed by two-stage sequential reranking, or to a four-gold-document branch (a bridge-comparison subset of 2WikiMultihopQA), processed by parallel ranking-based reranking, using lightweight XLM-RoBERTa cross-encoders. All components are trained without stemming and selected on a held-out validation split. On 8,000 Indonesian-translated evaluation questions, the framework recovers the complete supporting-document set for 95.40% of questions with 3.00 documents per question and 97.69% document precision. In evidence recovery, it significantly outperforms a single-model fixed-K=4 reranker (+2.60 points; McNemar's exact test p < 10−17); relative to top-4 selection with the same branch-specific scorers, it trades 0.89 points of containment for 23.55 points higher document precision and one document fewer per question. Ablations attribute the largest effect to sequential conditioning (+14.00 points at an equal budget of two documents) and show that routing errors cost 0.03 points within the benchmark, that transfer initialization mainly accelerates convergence, and that Sastrawi stemming degrades the scorers. Class-wise probes and a cross-source test show that the routing classifier relies on a film-topic shortcut and misroutes 10.78% of unseen two-document questions; it is therefore a benchmark-defined controller, not a detector of reasoning complexity, and the results do not establish generalization beyond the evaluated benchmark.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-Defined Adaptive Candidate Reranking for Indonesian Multi-Hop Question Answering

evidence_items.summary: Deliverable D3.2 offers the initial overview of available computing infrastructure resources that support AI application development and execution within SAIFA. It also establishes a common framework for accessing and using these resources. During the first implementation phase, data was gathered on national HPC and AI resources supporting SAIFA activities, including their technical specifications, capacity, access procedures, and resources allocated to the project. At the same time, the team collected and reviewed the national resource providers' existing access and usage policies. To facilitate early-stage development, SAIFA researchers now have direct access to national computing resources managed by the Office for Information Technologies and eGovernment (ITE), the Institute of Physics Belgrade (IPB), and the Innovation Center at the School of Electrical Engineering, University of Belgrade (ICEF). Currently, each resource provider grants access directly, with the project providing support and coordination. Users must adhere to the policies and conditions governing each resource. This setup is temporary until access is unified via the SAIFA AI Gateway. Based on the analysis of the policies applied by the national resource providers, SAIFA has developed a common set of use policies covering the principal requirements related to resource use, user responsibilities, security, data management, privacy and compliance. The objective is to establish a consistent policy framework applicable across resources accessed through SAIFA, while allowing individual providers to impose additional resource-specific conditions where necessary. This common framework will be further evaluated and aligned with the policies of the collaborating European AI Factories (Pharos and IT4LIA) as their resources become available to SAIFA users. In parallel, we have developed a common procedure for requesting and allocating computing resources.
evidence_items.title: D3.2 Report on infrastructure resources, access and use policies, v1

evidence_items.summary: This study examined the relationship between lavish lifestyle and the socioeconomic lives of youths in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria. The study sought to determine whether lavish lifestyle is significantly related to the socioeconomic lives of youths in the study area. Extant literature on lavish lifestyle, conspicuous consumption, youth consumer behaviour, and socioeconomic wellbeing was reviewed. The study was anchored on Thorstein Veblen's Theory of Conspicuous Consumption. A survey research design was adopted for the study. Because the exact population of youths aged 18–45 years residing in Calabar Metropolis was not available, Cochran's formula for an unknown or large population was used to obtain a minimum sample size of 384 respondents, which was rounded upward to 400 respondents to improve coverage and accommodate possible non-response. A multistage sampling technique involving purposive, cluster, and simple random sampling procedures was used. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire whose validity was established by experts in Sociology and Measurement and Evaluation, while reliability was determined using Cronbach's Alpha. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations, while the hypothesis was tested using the Pearson Product Moment Correlation Coefficient (PPMC) at the .05 level of significance. The findings revealed a significant relationship between lavish lifestyle and the socioeconomic lives of youths, with the correlation result indicating that higher levels of lavish lifestyle were associated with the socioeconomic outcome measured in the study. The study concluded that patterns of conspicuous consumption and excessive luxury spending have important implications for the socioeconomic wellbeing of youths.
evidence_items.title: Lavish lifestyle and socioeconomic lives of youths in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State Nigeria

evidence_items.summary: This paper looks into the topic of language attrition and shift among bilingual Nigerian children between the ages of 3 and 6 and the effect of early exposure to the English language in educational institutions in Nigeria on the preservation of native languages including Igbo, Yoruba and Hausa. Using the sociocultural theory presented by Vygotsky as the theory of child language acquisition, the study examines how the existing theories of child language acquisition are applicable to the realities of multilingual Nigeria and how the concept of bilingualism can be cognitively and culturally interpreted. The participants were two children in Enugu and Lagos, who were monitored in terms of longitudinal observations, audio recordings, and vocabulary tests over a period of six months. The results indicate moderate to high L1 attrition (40-70% lexical loss) as a result of urban schooling and weak L1 scaffolding of children with children showing code-switching patterns to favour English. The bilingual advantages were demonstrated on the cognitive flexibility tasks (75-88 percent accuracy), but unequal language exposure prevented complete retention of L1. Social mediation as seen by Vygotsky is very consistent (70-80%), but the cognitivism of Piaget and nativism of Chomsky are poorly fitting (20-40%), because they ignore cultural prestige and multilingualism processes. The research concludes that policies of additive bilingual education that involve the use of indigenous languages in the school curriculum are necessary to maintain lingual heritage without jeopardising cognitive growth in the multilingual Nigeria.
evidence_items.title: The Nigerian Bilingual Context A Re Evaluation Of Child Language Acquisition Models

evidence_items.summary: Supporting data, frozen models, analysis code and figures for a paired evaluation of a frozen VIIRS–ABI aerosol optical depth fusion procedure. The archive includes the complete input table of 259 April–June 2022 development pairs; archived inputs and predictions for 152 observations on additional dates in 2024, including 90 records with qualified AERONET references; stored evaluation and sensitivity-analysis outputs; the frozen model bundle; prediction and model-fitting modules; and figure sources. The primary observations originate from publicly available NOAA VIIRS and GOES-16 ABI products and NASA AERONET Version 3 Level 2.0. This archive starts from derived inputs and does not contain a complete raw-satellite-granule collection. Earlier-panel summaries are included, but complete earlier-panel record-level inputs are outside its scope. Numerical reproduction reports are archived evidence; raw-granule processing and model refitting were not performed as part of this packaging step. evidence_items.summary: Federated higher-education ecosystems rely on heterogeneous services, catalogues, workflow artefacts, and communication records governed by different data models and access policies. In such settings, intelligent search is not a conventional retrieval feature, because relevance must be reconciled with controlled visibility across institutions, alliances, and collaboration processes. Using Agora as the reference case, this paper examines access-aware intelligent search as a rights-preserving search and decision-support problem. It contributes three connected results: an analytical discoverability model linking shared identity, provider-aligned authorization, policy-bearing metadata, and workflow context; a governance model for AI-assisted search centered on traceability, fairness, auditability, and legal compliance; and an evaluation model combining retrieval effectiveness with access correctness, usability, and audit-oriented logging. Taken together, these results frame intelligent search as trustworthy AI-supported discovery in a federated environment. They also show that long-term viability depends on metadata quality, API stability, permission-aware reindexing, and integration with surrounding service workflows.
evidence_items.title: Access-AwareIntelligentSearchforFederatedServiceEcosystems: InsightsfromHigherEducationAlliances

evidence_items.summary: This article documents a participatory community service program on digital safety, fraudulent investments, and online gambling at Al Madinatuddiniyah Babul Huda Dayah, Padang Sakti, Lhokseumawe, Aceh, on 21 September 2026. The program aimed to strengthen students’ exposure to responsible smartphone use, financial risk awareness, and Islamic ethical principles. Its activities comprised institutional coordination, two interactive educational sessions, case-based explanations, discussion, and questions and answers. The first session discussed constructive digital practices and personal data protection; the second addressed warning signs of deceptive investment offers and the risks of online gambling. A descriptive qualitative account was developed from implementation narratives, learning materials, and activity photographs. The records document delivery of the planned content and opportunities for participant interaction, but do not include standardized baseline assessments, post-tests, or behavioral follow-up. Therefore, increases in knowledge or changes in behavior cannot be established quantitatively. The program illustrates a context-sensitive approach to integrating digital literacy, financial consumer protection, and Islamic values in dayah-based education, while highlighting the need for structured evaluation and continuing institutional support.
