evidence_items.summary: Herbal candies are functional confectionery preparations that incorporate plant-derived ingredients into a convenient oral dosage or consumer-friendly format. They may provide a practical means of delivering phytochemicals associated with oral hygiene, antioxidant activity and general nutritional support. Medicinal plants such as Azadirachta indica (neem), Syzygium aromaticum (clove), Ocimum tenuiflorum (tulsi), Phyllanthus emblica (amla) and Zingiber officinale (ginger) contain diverse bioactive constituents, including polyphenols, flavonoids, tannins, essential-oil components and vitamin C. Depending on the plant, extraction method and formulation, these constituents may contribute to antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory or sensory properties. However, their activity and stability can be affected by heat exposure, pH, moisture, ingredient interactions and storage conditions. The development of herbal candy therefore requires careful selection of plant materials, standardisation of extracts, optimisation of the candy base and systematic evaluation of physical, chemical, microbiological and stability characteristics. This review discusses the potential role of selected medicinal plants in oral-health-oriented confectionery, outlines a general approach to formulation and quality evaluation, and identifies research needs concerning bioavailability, safety, clinical effectiveness and product standardisation. Herbal candy should be regarded as a complementary product under investigation rather than a substitute for toothbrushing, fluoride use, a balanced diet or professional dental care. Likewise, claims of immune enhancement require specific scientific evidence and should not be inferred solely from antioxidant activity.
evidence_items.title: Review on Herbal Candy for Oral Health and Immune Support: Plant Bioactives, Formulation, Evaluation and Future Perspectives

evidence_items.summary: STARLI | F111–F120 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · Collective Microrobotics, Fault Resilience and Trustworthy Autonomy Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This collection presents ten prospective research-design monographs on distributed micro/nanorobotic collectives. Research Unit I (F111–F115) addresses limited communication, collaborative quantum sensing, consensus breakdown, dynamic task reassignment and joint human-machine authority. Research Unit II (F116–F120) examines misinformation propagation, graceful degradation, custody and mission integrity, cross-platform coordination and trustworthy autonomy. The ten studies propose falsifiable bench-scale experiments; none asserts demonstrated swarm intelligence, clinical efficacy or certified autonomous safety. The ten English working editions comprise 7,770 PDF pages in total: 300 prospective mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study sections, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate proposes six annotated research dimensions: causal mechanism, measurable witness, blinded falsifier, rival explanation, stopping boundary and successor interface. The counts describe publication architecture, not experimentally verified results or independently certified scientific originality. The Ten Research Directions F111  Nanorobotic Collective Limited Communication Control At The Limit — Investigates safe collective recovery when peer-to-peer messages are delayed, lost or limited. The proposed endpoint is time to independently confirmed safe recovery after communication loss, measured in seconds. Tests compare matched-actuation single-agent control against local coordination; task redundancy is a rival explanation. Failure to regain a known-safe state is a stopping condition.
evidence_items.title: STARLI | F111–F120 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · Collective Microrobotics, Fault Resilience and Trustworthy Autonomy Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This collection presents ten prospective research-design monographs on distributed micro/nanorobotic collectives. Research Unit I (F111–F115) addresses limited communication, collaborative quantum sensing, consensus breakdown, dynamic task reassignment and joint human-machine authority. Research Unit II (F116–F120) examines misinformation propagation, graceful degradation, custody and mission integrity, cross-platform coordination and trustworthy autonomy. The ten studies propose falsifiable bench-scale experiments; none asserts demonstrated swarm intelligence, clinical efficacy or certified autonomous safety. The ten English working editions comprise 7,770 PDF pages in total: 300 prospective mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study sections, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate proposes six annotated research dimensions: causal mechanism, measurable witness, blinded falsifier, rival explanation, stopping boundary and successor interface. The counts describe publication architecture, not experimentally verified results or independently certified scientific originality. The Ten Research Directions F111  Nanorobotic Collective Limited Communication Control At The Limit — Investigates safe collective recovery when peer-to-peer messages are delayed, lost or limited. The proposed endpoint is time to independently confirmed safe recovery after communication loss, measured in seconds. Tests compare matched-actuation single-agent control against local coordination; task redundancy is a rival explanation. Failure to regain a known-safe state is a stopping condition. F112  Microrobotic Collective Quantum Sensing Collaboration At The Limit — Proposes cooperative field sensing against independent calibrated reference measurements. Its candidate endpoint is normalized field-estimation error; the atlas also tracks communication load. A fully observed centralized controller is the comparator, and additional agent count may explain apparent improvement. Violation of registered safety invariants rejects the proposed collaborative sensing benefit. F113  Nanorobotic Collective Consensus Failure At The Limit — Examines whether distributed agreement remains justified when hidden partitions or corrupted information change the swarm's evidence. The candidate endpoint is the false-consensus acceptance fraction, with energy per task retained from the atlas. Fixed rules under equal energy challenge the proposal; leaked global tracking is a rival. Confidence maintained during a hidden partition triggers rejection. F114  Microrobotic Collective Dynamic Mission Reconfiguration At The Limit — Studies bounded mission reassignment following changing tasks, link loss or unavailable agents. The proposed witness is independently verified mission-reassignment success fraction, while selective abstention remains an atlas outcome. Matched total actuation controls for redundancy masquerading as adaptation. Failed return to a registered safe state is the hard stop. F115  Nanorobotic Collective Joint Human-Machine Oversight At The Limit — Tests whether collective task completion remains inside explicit human authorization and machine safety constraints. Authority-compliant task success fraction is the proposed endpoint, complemented by atlas task-completion records. A centralized full-state controller is the comparator; larger teams alone may explain any gain. Crossing a safety invariant overrides apparent task efficiency. F116  Microrobotic Collective Misinformation Propagation At The Limit — Addresses the spread of incorrect shared state estimates through a microrobotic collective. Its candidate observable is false-belief propagation rate, accompanied by the atlas consensus-error outcome. Equal-energy fixed behavior challenges the claimed mechanism, while hidden external state tracking may bias comparisons. Persistent confident agreement under concealed network partition is a rejection condition. F117  Nanorobotic Collective Graceful Degradation At The Limit — Evaluates whether a damaged or partially disconnected swarm retains bounded task capability rather than failing abruptly. Completion fraction under preregistered fault severity is the proposed witness; the atlas also records collision rate. Single-agent operation with matched total actuation tests whether redundancy alone explains resilience. Inability to return to a known-safe state stops the trial. F118  Microrobotic Collective Mission Integrity At The Limit — Proposes end-to-end custody and task-state audits for collective sampling missions. The measurable candidate is the valid sample-and-mission custody fraction, with coverage entropy retained from the original atlas. A centralized full-state controller anchors comparison; increased agent number can mimic benefits. Any violation of physical safety invariants invalidates the release claim. F119  Nanorobotic Collective Cross-Platform Collaboration At The Limit — Studies verified recovery and coordination across dissimilar robotic platforms with distinct sensing and control interfaces. Recovery latency in seconds is the proposed measurement and atlas recovery time is preserved. Matched-energy fixed rules are the baseline; external tracking that reveals global state is a rival. Confident consensus during a hidden communication partition is a stop condition. F120  Intelligent Nanorobotic Collective Trustworthy Autonomy At The Limit — Investigates whether autonomous collective decisions remain within defined authority and physical safety envelopes. The candidate witness is unsafe autonomous release fraction, alongside atlas communication load. A matched-actuation single-agent baseline tests purported benefits of collective intelligence versus redundancy. Failure to recover a known-safe state disqualifies the autonomy claim. The publication title follows the corrected source-introduction identity. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries These nonclinical research-design working editions are limited to traceable materials, calibrated sensing, physically bounded actuation, authorized reference systems and laboratory or simulated validation. Proposed endpoints supplement, rather than silently replace, the original atlas outcome fields. No laboratory results are reported. Equal-resource baselines, blinded disturbance tests, preservation of failed runs, raw evidence provenance and mandatory stop rules are required before claims of superiority. The source batch passes scripted PDF-structure checks; derivation-level physics, causal distinctness, individual DOI-to-claim relevance, exhaustive visual review and specialist peer review remain incomplete. evidence_items.summary: The current study focused on creating, improving, and assessing a herbal hydrogel that contains Manilkara zapota leaf extract for topical use. The leaves of Manilkara zapota underwent Soxhlet extraction using a hydroethanolic solvent. We then screened the extract for various plant compounds. Preliminary phytochemical analysis confirmed the presence of flavonoids, tannins, phenolics, terpenoids, glycosides, alkaloids, and saponins, which suggests the plant extract has antioxidant properties. We prepared herbal hydrogel formulations using Carbopol 940 as a gelling agent. Propylene glycol served as both a co-solvent and a penetration enhancer. We optimized the formulations using Design-Expert® software, considering Carbopol 940 and propylene glycol concentrations as independent variables. We chose viscosity, spreadability, and pH as dependent responses. The prepared formulations were assessed for physicochemical properties such as appearance, pH, viscosity, spreadability, extrudability, washability, homogeneity, and stability. The formulations showed satisfactory physical traits, including smooth consistency, good homogeneity, acceptable pH, and suitable spreadability for topical application. The viscosity increased with higher concentrations of Carbopol 940, while spreadability decreased accordingly. The optimized formulation had a viscosity of 20150 cP, a spreadability of 6.7 g·cm/sec, and a pH of 6.1. This formulation demonstrated favorable physicochemical properties and maintained stability throughout the study. The close match between predicted and experimental values confirmed the reliability of the optimization. The study suggests that Manilkara zapota leaf extract can be effectively included in a Carbopol-based hydrogel system. It may represent a promising herbal topical formulation for antioxidant uses. However, additional pharmacological and clinical research is necessary to confirm its therapeutic effectiveness and long-term stability.
evidence_items.title: Formulation, Optimization and Evaluation of Herbal Hydrogel Containing Manilkara zapota Leaf Extract

evidence_items.summary: A document-level knowledge graph has one node per entity, with all of its mentions, an entity type, and typed relations to other entities. End-to-end extractors build such graphs by fine-tuning encoders pretrained on 512-token contexts and extend them to longer documents with segments or added positions, while the prompted generative baselines we test obtain low strict scores. We present FREGE (Frozen REpresentations for Graph Extraction), which reads coreference clusters, entity types and relations from the hidden states and attention of a frozen decoder-only language model with lightweight probes; only a small span detector (125M parameters) is fine-tuned, and the language model is never updated. On DWIE, a benchmark of long documents with complete graphs, FREGE with Qwen2.5-7B reaches 67.8 F1 on relations with entity types, 15.5 points above the strongest fine-tuned system we trained on the same split, and its advantage over TaG and our position-extended JEREX baseline grows with document length. On SciREX, whose test documents average 6876 tokens, it reaches 18.3 binary relation F1 under the original benchmark's soft cluster-matching protocol, against 9.6 for the original SciREX baseline; on Re-DocRED it is on par with the strongest baseline.
evidence_items.title: FREGE: Coreference-Aware Document-Level Knowledge Graph Extraction

evidence_items.summary: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.
evidence_items.title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents

evidence_items.summary:
Recently, harness self-evolution has emerged as an important paradigm for improving agent performance. Prior studies show that evolving the agent harness can effectively enhance agent capabilities without modifying the foundation model's parameters. We find that existing approaches largely study agent evolution on a single task. In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. Whether an agent harness can continuously evolve across multiple tasks without suffering from catastrophic forgetting remains an important open question.
  In this paper, we investigate this open question through a comprehensive empirical study of continual harness self-evolution. We organize three software engineering task datasets into six different evolution directions and apply two representative harness evolution methods to perform continual evolution along these directions. Our experimental results show that evolution on a subsequent dataset can substantially undermine the performance on previously seen datasets. For example, with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, Meta-Harness improves its performance on SWE-Bench to 94.0% after evolution. However, after further evolution on FeatureBench, its performance on SWE-Bench drops to 32.0% by the fifth round, corresponding to a 66% relative decrease. Finally, based on our experimental findings, we identify several insights, providing directions for the continual self-evolution of agent harnesses. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/continual-harness-evolution.
evidence_items.title: Can Coding Agents Sustain Continual Evolution without Forgetting?

evidence_items.summary: Personal AI agents are increasingly capable of handling long-horizon tasks across applications, yet users often need to invest substantial effort in specifying goals, resolving ambiguity, and verifying outcomes. We argue that progress should be measured by how effectively agents amplify human agency: enabling people to pursue their goals with less routine supervision while retaining control over consequential decisions. We advocate Avatar Intelligence, a paradigm of persistent personal agents that represent users' goals, values, and constraints through sustained decision delegation across contexts and time. We describe a maturity roadmap from human-directed execution to autonomous operation within delegated domains, and introduce the Agentic Oversight Index (AOI) as a framework for evaluating delivered value against agent-side operational cost and human oversight burden. We identify three core research challenges: identity-continuous personalization that carries user preferences across tasks, user-situated evolution through Rehearsal Engineering, and safety mechanisms that combine technical control with accountability and recourse. These directions define a research agenda for reliable decision delegation to personal agents across tasks and over time.
evidence_items.title: Avatar Intelligence: Amplifying Human Agency Through Persistent Personal Agents

evidence_items.summary: As large language model (LLM) services expand toward distributed environments characterized by latency sensitivity, heterogeneous resources, and stringent privacy constraints, neither end-only nor cloud-only deployment can simultaneously balance generation quality, response latency, resource cost, and energy consumption. This survey systematically reviews optimization techniques for end-edge-cloud collaborative LLM inference services and establishes a four-layer taxonomy encompassing the algorithm, model, system, and chip levels. This taxonomy captures the end-to-end execution chain from collaborative decision-making to physical execution. The algorithm layer determines inference paths and task partitioning; the model layer provides deployable and collaborative model forms; the system layer manages resource mapping and pipeline execution; and the chip layer supplies the underlying computing, storage, and interconnect capabilities. These four layers are mutually dependent and collectively determine the end-to-end benefits of a collaborative solution. Furthermore, this survey defines representative collaboration paradigms and evaluation metrics, compares the performance gains, resource overheads, and applicability boundaries of different methods, and summarizes promising future directions, including cross-layer collaboration, dynamic adaptation, state-centric runtimes, and service-aware hardware.
evidence_items.title: End-Edge-Cloud Collaborative Inference for Efficient Large Language Model Services: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models are increasingly used to evaluate arguments, responses, and decisions, yet their judgments may be influenced by contextual information about who produced the content. This study examined how source expertise relevance and argument strength affect LLM evaluation and whether source effects differ across judgment dimensions. Twenty arguments spanning 10 topics were constructed as strong–weak pairs and presented under four source conditions: relevant expert, irrelevant expert, non-expert, and no source. Four large language models evaluated each argument on logical quality, credibility, persuasiveness, and agreement. Five repetitions were collected for each model-by-argument-by-source-by-dimension combination and averaged before inferential testing. Human validation assessed the intended argument-strength manipulation but showed negligible overall strong–weak separation in the second validation round, including two reversed topic pairs. Separate manipulation checks indicated that the models rated topic-relevant expertise and general professional expertise differently across source conditions. Source attribution most consistently affected credibility. Topic-level robustness analyses showed significant source-condition effects on credibility across all four models, while persuasiveness remained significant only for GPT-5.6 Sol. Relevant-expert attribution did not produce a universal advantage: credibility was significantly higher for relevant than irrelevant experts for Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek Flash, and Claude Opus 5.5 also showed significantly higher persuasiveness for relevant than irrelevant experts. Exploratory analyses suggested that this pattern may reflect an irrelevant-expertise penalty more than a universal bonus for relevant expertise. No robust evidence showed that relevant expertise disproportionately improved weak arguments.
evidence_items.title: Source Expertise, Argument Strength, and Multidimensional Source Sensitivity in Large Language Model Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Rare earth elements (REEs) are designated as critical materials due to their urgent need and supply uncertainties. The scarcity of REE supply is exacerbated by environmentally damaging extraction practices, necessitating more efficient, sustainable extraction and separation methods. Traditional techniques such as solvent extraction are often constrained by their extensive organic solvent consumption and limited extraction efficiency, especially for e-waste feedstocks containing heterogeneous compositions. As an alternative to traditional methods, solid-phase extraction (SPE) technique streamlines REE extraction and separation by providing high chelating selectivity, fewer operational stages, and minimal secondary waste generation. This review explores recent advances in ligand design for REE recovery, especially carbonyl amide-based, phosphorus-containing, β-diketone- and acylpyrazolone-based, macrocyclic, and biologically derived ligands. Enhancing the surface density of more REE-selective ligands on solid-phase matrices provides a viable pathway to overcome the thermodynamic constraints of separating adjacent, chemically homologous REEs in urban mining processes. Direct applications of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), to experimentally validated REE recovery remain limited and are mainly focused on narrowly defined tasks, including metal–ligand stability-constant prediction, ligand ranking, extraction-equilibrium modeling, and process simulation. Rather than treating AI-assisted REE recovery as a mature field, this review critically distinguishes demonstrated REE-specific applications from transferable computational frameworks that remain to be validated. Particular attention is given to molecular descriptors, coordination geometry, thermodynamic properties, data quality, and validation requirements for predictive ligand design.
evidence_items.title:
Ligand Design
for REE Recovery Using Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Underwater radiated noise (URN) poses a significant threat to the well-being of marine life from commercial vessels and it is crucial for naval vessels to maintain their stealth capabilities. Hence, the reduction of noise is an actively researched area in the marine sector. The marine propeller, especially when operating in cavitating conditions, contributes 80-85% of the overall URN of the vessel. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) coupled with acoustic analogies can predict the propeller noise characteristics in a shorter turnaround time than most other methods. However, an extensive validation is of paramount importance to gain confidence in the simulations. In this work, the propeller from the research vessel Princess Royal is simulated to predict the hydrodynamic (KT, KQ) and hydroacoustic characteristics under cavitating conditions. Extensive test data available from the research work at the University of Newcastle is used to validate the simulation model. Wall modelled large eddy simulation (WMLES) model coupled with the Ffowcs Williams-Hawkings (FWH) acoustics analogy is used for the prediction using the commercial CFD code Simerics-MP. These two simulation techniques were run simultaneously on a 26 million cell mesh. Cavitation was also included in the model using an equilibrium dissolved gas model which captures the evaporation and condensation of the working fluid due to local changes in pressure. These simulations took around 3 hours per complete revolution to run on 192 cores. The binary adaptive meshing technique in Simerics-MP helped to set-up the model in 30 minutes. The CFD results were compared against the test data from a cavitation tunnel experiment[7]. There are also hydrophone measurements available from the tests that were compared with the Computational Hydro-acoustics (CHA) results. Good agreement was found between the test data and simulation results.
evidence_items.title: CFD-Based Hydroacoustic Analysis of a Benchmark Marine Propeller

evidence_items.summary: Aim: To evaluate the occurrence and distribution of microplastics (MPs) in non-edible tissues (gills and digestive tract) and edible tissue (muscle) of Labeo rohita, Cyprinus carpio and Wallago attu. Methodology: Fish specimens were collected bimonthly from October 2024 to March 2025 from the Phillaur and Walipur Kalan stretches of Sutlej River. The collected samples were subsequently processed and analyzed by following the standardized protocol of National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Results: Majority of MPs were detected in the intestine (48.0%) and gills (40.4%), whereas lower proportion was found in the muscle tissues (11.6%). The highest level of MP contamination was recorded in W. attu collected from Wallipur Kalan, followed by L. rohita and C. carpio which exhibited moderate levels of contamination. Among different MP shape, fibers were most abundant (58.36%), followed by films (24.21%) and fragments (13.2%). Regarding size distribution, 0.1-0.5 mm MPs were the most prevalent (30.87%), followed by 0.5-1 mm size category (25.18%). In terms of colour, blue MPs were the most abundant (35.48%), followed by transparent (26.33%) and red particles (15.01%). Surface morphological analysis of MPs using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) revealed characteristic weathering features including pits, grooves and cracks. Interpretation: Present findings confirm that widespread occurrence of MPs in commercially important freshwater fish species from the Sutlej River, indicating contamination arising due to anthropogenic activities include direct discharge of plastic waste from industries and domestic source. This highlights the need for improved plastic waste management practices and reduced plastic utilization to mitigate MP pollution in fresh water ecosystems. Key words: Bioaccumulation, Fresh water fishes, Microplastics, Non-edible tissues, River Sutlej
evidence_items.title: Assessment of microplastic contamination in fish from the Sutlej River, India

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Seismic interpretation is rarely a single-task exercise. In practice, an interpreter moves back and forth between data quality, reflector continuity, fault expression, stratigraphic organization, seismic attributes, well control, and geological judgment. A fault cube, a horizon volume, or a conditioned seismic section may each be useful on its own, but none of them is sufficient if the outputs are disconnected from the rest of the interpretation workflow. This paper presents SeismicGen, a framework developed to make seismic AI more reusable and more consistent across interpretation tasks. The workflow is built around a Seismic Foundation Model, or SFM, that provides a shared seismic representation for several specialized interpretation agents. These agents support seismic conditioning, fault characterization, relative geological time estimation, relative acoustic impedance generation, fault and horizon extraction, seismic-to-well tie, and geobody detection. The purpose is not to replace the interpreter with a black-box system, but to provide a common technical layer that helps different AI outputs remain consistent with one another. The workflow starts with seismic preparation, normalization, and quality control. Depending on the interpretation objective, the seismic volume is then passed through selected agents. The outputs are not treated as isolated products. For example, fault probability and displacement indicators can guide fault-surface extraction, while relative geological time can support horizon organization. Results are checked through section-by-section review, geological consistency checks, residual and amplitude analysis, comparison with available well information, and interpreter-led validation. The main practical issue addressed in this paper is the lack of continuity between many existing seismic AI tools. A model may detect faults or pick horizons, but the output often remains separate from the broader interpretation process.
evidence_items.title: Scaling Subsurface Interpretation with Seismic Foundation Models and Agentic Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal models can predict progression from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but most evaluations assume that every modality is immediately available. We developed a retrospective framework using only the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) that separates statistical risk estimation, sequential evidence acquisition, language-model explanation, and deterministic verification. Participants with baseline MCI were assigned state-specific landmarks using information visible within a +/−90-day window. The primary simulation cohort included 425 participants with clinical/cognitive, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evidence; 153 converted to AD within 36 months after the landmark. Calibrated elastic-net models were evaluated with 10 repeated nested five-fold cross-validation. In the common-landmark cohort, adding MRI-derived and CSF features improved the Brier score from 0.158 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.141–0.175) to 0.138 (0.122–0.155) and the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from 0.837 (0.802–0.871) to 0.878 (0.847–0.908). A sequential policy used cross-fitted estimates of individual Brier-score gain to decide whether to request MRI or CSF. The fixed-threshold exploratory analysis requested 40.6% fewer simulated tests than an all-tests policy while meeting the prespecified Brier and AUROC noninferiority margins. Under fully nested threshold selection, the policy requested 46.9% fewer tests and met the AUROC criterion, while narrowly missing the Brier criterion (difference 0.00546, 95% CI 0.00090–0.01003; margin +0.01). In a 40-card-per-model engineering audit, local Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B models copied probabilities and cited supplied evidence correctly in 40/40 cards but matched the deterministic action in 16/40 and 15/40 cards, respectively. Execution authority therefore remained with the deterministic policy.
evidence_items.title: A Verifiable Agentic Framework for Sequential Multimodal Prediction of Mild Cognitive Impairment Progression

evidence_items.summary: Human working memory lets people maintain and update information. Large language models (LLMs) face a related demand when tracking updates within a single prompt without writing out intermediate states, yet existing tests differ in their constraints on written steps. We introduce a working-memory-inspired probe of cumulative state tracking with program-computed answers, 3 to 100 updates, and final-state, intermediate-state, or multi-target queries. It compares protocols on identical items. Across 18 LLMs, accuracy is 84.9% on single-step arithmetic but 31.7% on core items requiring one number after three to seven updates. From 50 updates on, no model exceeds 10% accuracy. Core accuracy reaches 88.0% under a larger budget and instructions to write steps and place the answer on the last line, mainly due to the instruction changes rather than the budget. Core accuracy also correlates positively with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard scores. These findings show that strong single-step arithmetic does not ensure reliable cumulative tracking and that output protocols substantially change measured accuracy. We release the generator, items, scoring code, and responses for reproducible comparisons across depths, query types, and protocols.
evidence_items.title: WMIP: A Working-Memory-Inspired Programmable Probe of Cumulative State Tracking in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Attention remains a substantial computational cost in Transformer training, particularly at long context lengths. NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs provide high-throughput low-precision matrix multiplication, but exploiting it in attention requires addressing quantization overhead, causal information leakage through shared scales, and numerical inconsistencies between the forward and backward passes. We present FLAMIA, a family of attention kernels for Blackwell with MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 training paths. Our design combines token-block scaling that reuses quantized operands across matrix orientations, targeted safeguards against scale-induced leakage, and consistent forward and backward computations. Fused quantization and architecture-specific kernel optimizations reduce overhead, while document-local scaling and workload-aware scheduling support variable-length documents directly in packed layouts without repacking. Across various causal packed-document workloads, the MXFP8 path accelerates the combined forward and backward attention call, including quantization, by factors of 1.10--1.40times on B200 and 1.06--1.42times on B300 relative to the fastest evaluated baseline for each workload. We validate training stability and quality preservation on pretraining Llama-style models. These results show how jointly designing quantization, training numerics, and document scheduling translates low-bit hardware throughput into practical attention acceleration.
evidence_items.title: FLAMIA: FLAsh MIcroscaling Attention for Fast and Causally Safe Training on Blackwell

evidence_items.summary: We introduce SIMIT, a test-time self-improvement framework in which a vision-language model creates its own query-specific training data before answering an unlabeled test query. Our goal is to improve performance on a given target test set without annotations or external models. To pursue this goal, some test-time methods improve answers through longer reasoning or repeated sampling but leave the model unchanged. Others update the model using rewards based on majority agreement among multiple candidate answers or the model's own judgments of correctness, but such rewards can reinforce existing mistakes. SIMIT instead imagines similar problems whose solutions it controls: a model need not correctly solve the target query to construct useful practice examples. It synthesizes diverse (question, answer, image) triplets by specifying each answer before realizing its image. To support diverse multimodal tasks, SIMIT combines native image generation with an extensible skill library for structured visuals, including documents, charts, and diagrams. Within this pipeline, multi-stage verification checks that images support their assigned answers, while difficulty filtering retains informative examples. Adaptive budgeting further targets this practice by allocating more samples to queries the model is less confident in answering. The resulting data can improve the model in-context (SIMIT-ICL) or in-weight (SIMIT-FT). Across 17 diverse benchmarks, SIMIT outperforms existing self-improvement methods. Its best configuration achieves a +7.20% mean relative gain over BAGEL-7B, while training-free SIMIT-ICL achieves +6.98%.
evidence_items.title: SIMIT: Self-Improving Vision-Language Models via Imagination at Test-Time

evidence_items.summary: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.
evidence_items.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly capable of writing and executing code, suggesting a natural paradigm for tool-augmented agents: expressing tool use as programs rather than isolated calls. Programmatic tool calling (PTC) captures this idea through loops, batching, abstraction, and structured computation, but existing PTC approaches are largely stateless, limiting their ability to reuse intermediate results and adapt over time. This is problematic for real-world tasks, where tool environments and problem-solving processes are inherently stateful. We therefore present I-PTC, an interactive framework that executes stateful PTC: models issue code snippets that call tools, maintain reusable state, and evolve the tool interface through API corrections. To evaluate the effectiveness of I-PTC and the general PTC setting, we introduce PTC-Bench, a benchmark of long-tail, production-style user requests whose difficulty comes from large initial environments, many dependent API interactions, extended planning, and recovery across follow-ups and transient failures. Experiments on PTC-Bench show that I-PTC improves performance on complex multi-step tasks with large tool sets while substantially reducing token consumption over conventional tool-calling baselines and the original PTC baseline, highlighting stateful programmatic tool calling as a promising direction for scalable tool-augmented agents.
evidence_items.title: I-PTC: Interactive Programmatic Tool Calling for Stateful Tool-Augmented Agents

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents solve repository issues through long sequences of exploration, editing, and validation. These trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so how they are collected shapes what the trained model learns. A common approach is to sample multiple trajectories independently for each issue and then select or curate them. However, as more trajectories are sampled independently, later trajectories become increasingly redundant, even though earlier trajectories could guide where subsequent collection effort should be spent. A natural way to use this history is to expose it to the coding agent as advice. But training on such trajectories can make the model rely on advice that is unavailable at test time, creating a train-test mismatch. Instead, we argue that history should guide where collection effort is spent, while the coding agent decides what to generate. We introduce SWE-Trail, a trajectory collector that uses earlier trajectories to guide subsequent collection while keeping that history outside the coding agent's context. During a new rollout, SWE-Trail uses history to identify a state where additional collection effort may be useful. There, the coding agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context, and SWE-Trail briefly executes them from the same checkpoint to decide which route continues. We evaluate collection approaches by training student models on the trajectories they produce. For a 124B student initialized from Ling-3.0-flash-base, SWE-Trail improves mean resolution over independent sampling by 2.33 and 1.60 percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-bench Pro, respectively. Without history, the same pipeline produces more resolved trajectories than independent sampling, but improves by only 0.11 points on Multilingual. These results show the value of using history to guide collection without exposing it to the coding agent.
evidence_items.title: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training

evidence_items.summary: Computer graphics is built on code. Large language model (LLM) agents can now generate graphics code and iteratively refine it through various feedback. This capability opens the door to a potentially new paradigm of computer graphics, with graphics algorithms increasingly built around agentic systems to automate progressively complex tasks. Over the past years, research on agentic graphics has expanded rapidly across a diverse range of tasks. This rapid growth makes it increasingly difficult for manual literature reviews to keep pace with new developments. At the same time, similar ideas are often described using different terminology across these tasks, further complicating efforts to develop a systematic understanding of the field. In this report, we address these challenges through two contributions. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy for characterizing agentic systems across diverse computer graphics tasks. Second, we develop an agentic literature system that can assist human researchers in analyzing existing and newly published papers at scale. Building on these contributions, we analyze emerging research trends and discuss open challenges in coordinating agents and tools across graphics tasks, designing interfaces and representations for human-agent collaboration, sustaining long-horizon planning and refinement, and reliably evaluating interactive graphics systems.
evidence_items.title: Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics

evidence_items.summary: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.
evidence_items.title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?

evidence_items.summary: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.
evidence_items.title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale

evidence_items.summary: Robot agents built on vision-language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher's harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher's trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining. On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors' harnesses. It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher's accelerator time.
evidence_items.title: TinyAstral: Transferring Self-Evolving Harnesses to Tiny Generalist Manipulation Agents

evidence_items.summary: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.
evidence_items.title: Self-Improvement with Auxiliary Rewards: Learning from Verified Traces and Evaluating Transfer

evidence_items.summary: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through the agent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First, agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third, recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.
evidence_items.title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement

evidence_items.summary: As publications and products on time series forecasting (TSF) proliferate, researchers face a growing burden of analyzing existing work. First, not all publications release code. For instance, only about 20% of arXiv TSF papers have a code link in the surveyed period. Second, released code also requires manual maintenance. Thus, TSF researchers must constantly adapt or implement existing works. However, independent implementations can differ in experimental settings and are difficult to maintain. We therefore propose to use AI agents for benchmarking TSF research and even supporting autoresearch, e.g., developing new TSF models. Yet directly applying existing coding agents, such as Claude Code and Codex, is suboptimal: prohibitive costs, limited scalability to large research projects (e.g., benchmarking), and lack of self-maintenance. To address these challenges, we propose TSFLab, a self-improving agent-agnostic "workbench" that equips compatible coding agents with shared resources and tools for low-cost TSF research and continuous maintenance of research resources. Our experiments cover reproduction, benchmarking, and new method development. In reproduction and benchmarking, TSFLab improves task completion by 20-163% and cuts fresh tokens per completed task by 11-66% across baselines. A pilot study of agent-driven method development also shows improved forecasting accuracy via TSFLab, with 32.8-73.6% fewer fresh tokens and 9.2-68.8% less development time than the other settings.
evidence_items.title: TSFLab: A Self-Improving Agent-Agnostic Workbench for Time Series Forecasting Research

evidence_items.summary: On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy. In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the training-inference mismatch between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs. Evaluating the trainer at the sampler's weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a numerical discrepancy of the engine and a policy lag of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer's own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the discrepancy-lag correction (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler's prefixes does not detect.
evidence_items.title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and τ-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.
evidence_items.title: GEPA-Curator: Curated Learning for Self Improving Agents

evidence_items.summary: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.
evidence_items.title: Think Twice: The Metis-1.6 Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.
evidence_items.title: Learning Quality-Controllable Robot Policies with Iterative Hindsight Relabeling

evidence_items.summary: In recent years, agentic orchestration has been widely applied to solve complex human tasks. However, existing orchestration learning still faces key challenges, including hand-designed curricula, advantage collapse when a task's rollouts all reach the same outcome, and unreliable evaluation signals that judge each skill by one noisy score. To address these challenges, we propose R^2Orch, a new paradigm of Recursive Self-Play Orchestration: an inner loop of self-play that improves the orchestrator on self-chosen tasks, and an outer loop that improves how the inner loop improves. To support this paradigm, we introduce Recursive Learnability, a training objective that rewards a Proposer for choosing tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn. Built on this objective, we further propose Skill Withdrawal, in which the outer loop withdraws each skill once a controlled evaluation within self-play shows that the orchestrator performs as well without it. Moreover, the two loops form one cycle: failures are distilled into skills, skills into parameters, and withdrawals lead the Proposer to new failures, so the orchestrator moves toward zero-skill deployment. Experimental results on twelve datasets show that R^2Orch consistently outperforms baselines across question answering, math, code, and interactive tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/R2Orch.
evidence_items.title: R^2Orch: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Orchestration via Self-Play within a Skill-Internalization Loop

evidence_items.summary: Face image quality assessment (FIQA) estimates the utility of a face image for automated face recognition and has been proposed as a morphing attack detection (MAD) signal that requires no morph-specific training. We evaluate 17 FIQA methods from all current FIQA categories on 20 morphing attack sets from two datasets, FRLL and FEI, including five diffusion-based attack sets. Each quality score is used directly as a MAD decision score. Unlike prior work, which inverted a quality measure when this lowered its error, we fix the score direction of each method in advance from its definition, so that cases in which morphs receive higher quality than bona fide samples remain visible. On FRLL, DifFIQA(R) achieves a mean D-EER of 11.42%, and together with CLIB-FIQA and eDifFIQA(L) clearly outperforms all other FIQA methods. A strong separation of bona fide and morph scores does not imply good detection performance: on the diffusion-based attacks, up to 11 of 17 methods assign higher quality to morphs than to bona fide samples, and the largest reversed separation in the study coincides with the worst detection result of the study. Performance also depends strongly on the attack: GraFIQs(L), the best detector of DCMorph and Arc2Morph on FRLL, performs poorly on the landmark-based and GAN-based attacks. On FEI, the lowest mean D-EER is 39.75%, and a threshold set on the bona fide data of one dataset does not transfer to the other.
evidence_items.title: When Morphs Look Better: Face Image Quality as a Training-Free Signal for Morphing Attack Detection

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This paper proposes a multiagent large language model (LLM)–based system for early-stage building layout planning, which enables flexible design requirement inputs and robust spatial reasoning. Existing generative methods often depend on structured inputs, and perform poorly when faced with incomplete requirements or regulatory constraints. Moreover, although LLMs excel at understanding language, they typically lack the spatial reasoning capabilities required for layout generation. To address these limitations, the proposed system includes five core modules: a requirement interpreter that standardizes design requirements and employs multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to fetch similar layouts; a planner module composed of specialized LLM agents such as an architect, accessibility expert, and user experience advocate; a layout executor that transforms planning strategies into bubble diagrams; and an evaluation module that combines rule-based checks and LLM-based feedback. All modules are coordinated by a director module using multichain-of-thought reasoning to iteratively refine the design process. The system supports natural language prompts, layout boundaries, and optional reference layouts, making it suitable for both incomplete and detailed design scenarios. After a bubble diagram is finalized, a diffusion-based generative model produces a complete architectural layout. Experimental results using the Tell2Design data set demonstrated significant improvements in both geometric quality and semantic alignment over a baseline LLM-only system. Case studies of office and multiapartment buildings further validated the system’s adaptability and effectiveness in complex design contexts.
evidence_items.title: A Multiagent Large Language Model–Based System for Early-Stage Building Layout Planning

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The paper investigates the turbulent flow generated by a wall jet. A numerical benchmark of six turbulence closures including two-equation and seven-equation models in their high- or low-Reynolds number formulations, is performed. The Standard k - ε , Realizable k - ε , k - ω SST, the linear and quadratic pressure-strain Reynolds Stress Models (RSM) and RSM based on ω available within Ansys Fluent 2023R2 and OpenFOAM v11 are systematically compared with reference experimental data available from the literature for the jet Reynolds number of R e j = 9,600 . Generally, the specific dissipation rate ω appears to be a better candidate than ε to determine the length scale of the turbulence for this particular configuration. Thus, the k - ω SST and RSM- ω models perform better than the others to predict the wall jet spreading rate, maximum Reynolds number or friction coefficient. The linear pressure-strain RSM fails to predict the mean streamwise velocity profile, exhibiting a large deficit in the log region. A budget analysis of the turbulence kinetic energy transport equation is also performed for the low-Reynolds number models. The intriguing behavior of the linear pressure-strain RSM is confirmed by the production term’s profile, which peaks earlier than the other models at about y + ≃ 5 . Overall, the k - ω SST model can be recommended because it offers a good trade-off between accuracy and computational efforts.
evidence_items.title: Turbulent Plane Wall Jet Flows: A Numerical Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Phishing detectors trained on public benchmarks score highly in-domain yet miss scams aimed at university users. We audit TF-IDF, MiniLM and RoBERTa detectors with 5146 scams published by five U.S. universities, 594 scams posted since 2023, 2684 legitimate university announcements and mailing-list messages, and 17,880 labelled job advertisements. In one benchmark, message year separates phishing from legitimate mail; in both, donor-identifying terms, 2% of the vocabulary, carry 14–16% of the legitimacy weight. Trained on that benchmark, TF-IDF and RoBERTa detect scams containing academic vocabulary about 15 percentage points less often. Thresholds set for a 5% false-positive rate on benchmark mail flag between 1.0% and 87.8% of legitimate job advertisements. Calibrated instead on job advertisements grouped by company, TF-IDF flags 2.1% of university announcements but 65.3% of short legitimate financial messages, and appended legitimate-looking words cut its recall from 0.828 to 0.123. Bounding legitimacy evidence yields closed-form certificates for whitespace-delimited appends, prepends and interior insertions. A budget-split ensemble certifies 0.259 recall against appends or prepends of any length at 0.706 clean recall, whereas adversarially trained TF-IDF falls to 0.078 under a 40-token white-box append. Monotone components, however, flag many long formal letters.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Shortcuts and Append Robustness in Phishing Detection: Evidence from University Scam Emails

evidence_items.summary: A GUI command can be correct at the interface level yet still produce an incorrect assembly. An agent must identify the relevant components, respect their structural relationships, and determine which parts should move during recovery. We introduce MAGAR-Bench, a benchmark of 4,000 multimodal samples from 26 assembly families that separates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action, and Minimal Rework. For rework, the objective counts distinct moved parts within the validated recovery candidate set for each state, rather than the number of actions. We also introduce MAGAR, a selective correction framework built on a frozen policy obtained by supervised fine-tuning. Its key design matches correction granularity to output dependencies. Structured candidates revise assembly fields and rework scope, while complete action candidates keep native GUI primitives coupled with their parameters. A learned selector retains the original prediction unless a candidate passes a task-specific intervention threshold. On recorded states from held-out assembly families, MAGAR improves Overall, the task-balanced aggregate, from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks. Across 209 interventions, 70 correct an error and 22 introduce one. These results support task-specific correction while highlighting the remaining tradeoff between fixing errors and preserving reliable predictions.
evidence_items.title: MAGAR: Multimodal Agents for GUI-Based 3D Mechanical Assembly and Minimal Rework

evidence_items.summary: AI-generated videos often depict people within detailed scenes while leaving their small facial regions poorly resolved. Visual super-resolution can sharpen these regions without resolving whether the recovered lips and teeth agree with the spoken audio. We present an audio-guided facial video restoration framework that addresses this ambiguity within a reference-guided video flow model. Source--noise mixing initializes reconstruction from a partially preserved observation, and structured reference injection separates appearance anchors from continuous motion context. Training combines restoration of degraded images and videos with correction of degraded dubbed sources under target audio. Appearance and synchronization supervision allow the model to recover facial detail and support visual dubbing when the audio is replaced. On talking-head restoration benchmarks, our method achieves the best paired perceptual similarity and synchronization scores among the compared restoration methods. Component comparisons examine audio conditioning, the reconstruction formulation, and reference injection. Native AIGC examples further illustrate the recovery of lip contours, dental structure, and surrounding facial texture in scene-level footage. injection. Native AIGC examples further illustrate the recovery of lip contours, dental structure, and surrounding facial texture in scene-level footage.

evidence_items.summary: Traditional image cropping assumes the photograph already contains the composition worth keeping, and asks only where to crop. A full 360^{circ} scene offers no such guarantee: the viewing direction in a scene has to be discovered before anything can be framed. We present PhotoGuider, a measure-then-frame method that answers both questions with compact learned scorers over one shared set of composition-aware features. The designed features are extracted using foundation and task-specific vision models and structured into four photographic tokens: Subject, Composition, Aesthetics, and Integrity. Our MLLM explainer is fine-tuned to generate composition-related explanations conditioned on images and measured token assessments. To our knowledge, PhotoGuider is the first method to combine explicit composition-based direction selection in 360^{circ} panoramas with refined framing, camera-parameter output for native re-rendering, and measurement-conditioned explanations. On two standard 2D cropping benchmarks, PhotoGuider achieves the highest average mIoU performance against ground-truth crops. In a blind ranking study, 120 participants ranked three cropping methods over 100 panoramic scenes from the public Poly Haven HDRI library, placing our framings first in 53.2% of cases, against 27.3% and 19.5% for two strong alternatives. Project page: https://ntuneillee.github.io/research/photoguider/
evidence_items.title: PhotoGuider: Composition-Aware Cropping and 360^{circ} View Framing with Explainable Photographic Assessments

evidence_items.summary: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.
evidence_items.title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
